docs.title: pyramids-mesh
docs.text: Reads and writes the file formats of hydrodynamic and hydraulic mesh models — 2DM, Selafin, DFSU, XMDF, PLY and more — as pyramids UGRID objects. pyramids-core already ships the mesh data model and every operation that follows from a topology in hand; what it cannot do is open other people's mesh files. That is this package's only job.

docs.title: The layer boundary
docs.text:
The split is the point of the package, so it is worth stating precisely. pyramids-core owns the mesh data model and everything that follows from a topology already in hand:

Concern Lives in Mesh2d, Mesh1d, MeshDataset, Connectivity pyramids.netcdf.ugrid UGRID-compliant NetCDF read / write pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.io Connectivity derivation, graph algorithms, boundary extraction pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.graph Sampling, rasterize_like, mesh-to-mesh regridding, time interpolation pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.regrid Construction from a raster grid or a polygon layer pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.construct Mesh ↔ vector, gap filling, xarray / zarr hand-off pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.{vector_ops,fill,interop_xarray} Mesh rendering pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.plot → cleopatra MeshGlyph

pyramids-mesh adds the one thing that is missing from that list — the ability to open other people's mesh files:

Concern Lives in Reading 2DM, Selafin, DFSU, XMDF, XDMF, DAT, FLO-2D, 3Di, PLY, TIN, … pyramids_mesh.drivers Writing 2DM, Selafin, DAT, PLY, Mike21 pyramids_mesh.drivers Driver discovery via the pyramids.mesh_drivers entry points pyramids-core reads, this package registers

A survey of the mesh-format landscape found pyramids-core reads exactly one of the eighteen driver families the established mesh I/O libraries cover (UGRID NetCDF). The other seventeen are what this package is for. In the other direction those libraries do no interpolation, regridding, reprojection or graph analysis, all of which pyramids-core already has.

Anything that belongs on the left-hand side of the first table is a change to pyramids-core, not a feature of this package. Report it upstream rather than duplicating it here.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
0.1.0 is the repository scaffold — packaging, CI, docs, and the import contract that pins import pyramids first so the vendored osgeo bindings are active before anything else loads. The public surface is empty; pyramids_mesh.__version__ is all it exports.

>>> import pyramids_mesh
>>> pyramids_mesh.__version__
'0.1.0'

docs.title: Where to next
docs.text:
• Installation — Pixi environments and what each one carries.
  • Reference — the API surface, as it lands.
  • Change log
  • Architecture Decision Records — including the scope boundary above, as ADR-0003.

Source: https://github.com/serapeum-org/pyramids-mesh

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
A primary goal of Hapi is to be inclusive to the largest number of contributors, with the most varied and diverse backgrounds possible. As such, we are committed to providing a friendly, safe and welcoming environment for all, regardless of gender, sexual orientation, ability, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and religion (or lack thereof).

This code of conduct outlines our expectations for all those who participate in our community, as well as the consequences for unacceptable behavior.

We invite all those who participate in Hapi to help us create safe and positive experiences for everyone.

docs.title: 2. Open [Source/Culture/Tech] Citizenship
docs.text:
A supplemental goal of this Code of Conduct is to increase open [source/culture/tech] citizenship by encouraging participants to recognize and strengthen the relationships between our actions and their effects on our community.

Communities mirror the societies in which they exist and positive action is essential to counteract the many forms of inequality and abuses of power that exist in society.

If you see someone who is making an extra effort to ensure our community is welcoming, friendly, and encourages all participants to contribute to the fullest extent, we want to know.

docs.title: 3. Expected Behavior
docs.text:
The following behaviors are expected and requested of all community members:

  • Participate in an authentic and active way. In doing so, you contribute to the health and longevity of this community.
  • Exercise consideration and respect in your speech and actions.
  • Attempt collaboration before conflict.
  • Refrain from demeaning, discriminatory, or harassing behavior and speech.
  • Be mindful of your surroundings and of your fellow participants. Alert community leaders if you notice a dangerous situation, someone in distress, or violations of this Code of Conduct, even if they seem inconsequential.
  • Remember that community event venues may be shared with members of the public; please be respectful to all patrons of these locations.

docs.title: 4. Unacceptable Behavior
docs.text:
The following behaviors are considered harassment and are unacceptable within our community:

  • Violence, threats of violence or violent language directed against another person.
  • Sexist, racist, homophobic, transphobic, ableist or otherwise discriminatory jokes and language.
  • Posting or displaying sexually explicit or violent material.
  • Posting or threatening to post other people's personally identifying information ("doxing").
  • Personal insults, particularly those related to gender, sexual orientation, race, religion, or disability.
  • Inappropriate photography or recording.
  • Inappropriate physical contact. You should have someone's consent before touching them.
  • Unwelcome sexual attention. This includes, sexualized comments or jokes; inappropriate touching, groping, and unwelcomed sexual advances.
  • Deliberate intimidation, stalking or following (online or in person).
  • Advocating for, or encouraging, any of the above behavior.
  • Sustained disruption of community events, including talks and presentations.

docs.title: 5. Weapons Policy
docs.text: No weapons will be allowed at Hapi events, community spaces, or in other spaces covered by the scope of this Code of Conduct. Weapons include but are not limited to guns, explosives (including fireworks), and large knives such as those used for hunting or display, as well as any other item used for the purpose of causing injury or harm to others. Anyone seen in possession of one of these items will be asked to leave immediately, and will only be allowed to return without the weapon. Community members are further expected to comply with all state and local laws on this matter.

docs.title: 6. Consequences of Unacceptable Behavior
docs.text:
Unacceptable behavior from any community member, including sponsors and those with decision-making authority, will not be tolerated.

Anyone asked to stop unacceptable behavior is expected to comply immediately.

If a community member engages in unacceptable behavior, the community organizers may take any action they deem appropriate, up to and including a temporary ban or permanent expulsion from the community without warning (and without refund in the case of a paid event).

docs.title: 7. Reporting Guidelines
docs.text:
If you are subject to or witness unacceptable behavior, or have any other concerns, please notify a community organizer as soon as possible. .

Additionally, community organizers are available to help community members engage with local law enforcement or to otherwise help those experiencing unacceptable behavior feel safe. In the context of in-person events, organizers will also provide escorts as desired by the person experiencing distress.

docs.title: 8. Addressing Grievances
docs.text: If you feel you have been falsely or unfairly accused of violating this Code of Conduct, you should notify with a concise description of your grievance. Your grievance will be handled in accordance with our existing governing policies.

docs.title: 9. Scope
docs.text:
We expect all community participants (contributors, paid or otherwise; sponsors; and other guests) to abide by this Code of Conduct in all community venues--online and in-person--as well as in all one-on-one communications pertaining to community business.

This code of conduct and its related procedures also applies to unacceptable behavior occurring outside the scope of community activities when such behavior has the potential to adversely affect the safety and well-being of community members.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
This page covers installation of pyramids-mesh and its native dependencies.

Item Value Distribution name pyramids-mesh Python import name pyramids_mesh Current version 0.1.0 Supported Python 3.11 – 3.14 License GPL v3

Not published yet. 0.1.0 exists only in this repository — there is no PyPI or conda-forge release to install from. Use the from-source route below.

docs.title: Runtime
docs.text:
• pyramids-core >= 0.70.0 (provides the pyramids import and the mesh-driver registry; pulled from PyPI)
  • numpy >= 2.0.0

GDAL is deliberately absent from that list. It is not a dependency of this package: the pyramids-core wheel vendors its own osgeo bindings, and import pyramids is what puts them on sys.path. Nothing here installs or pins a separate GDAL.

scipy, shapely and geopandas are not declared either. The UGRID subsystem requires all three, so they arrive with pyramids-core — but that is its requirement, not a promise to this package. Each gets declared here the moment a module under src/pyramids_mesh/ imports it directly.

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text: Extra Purpose Pulls viz mesh rendering / colour tables pyramids-core[viz], cleopatra[tiles]

docs.title: Development dependency groups
docs.text:
dev, docs and notebook are PEP 735 dependency groups, not extras — they are local tooling and are deliberately not published in the package metadata. Pixi resolves a group by name wherever an environment lists it, so an environment is a set of groups and extras rather than a single same-named group: dev is py314 + dev + viz, docs is py314 + docs. notebook is currently referenced by no environment.

pixi install -e dev      # tests, linting, build tooling
pixi install -e docs     # mkdocs toolchain

docs.title: Recommended: Pixi
docs.text:
This repository ships a Pixi configuration that resolves every dependency from PyPI, GDAL included — the pyramids-core wheel vendors its own, so no conda channel is involved and the usual GDAL-wheel headaches do not arise.

Prerequisites: install Pixi.

git clone https://github.com/serapeum-org/pyramids-mesh.git
cd pyramids-mesh

# Solve and install the dev environment
pixi install -e dev

# Drop into a shell with everything available
pixi shell -e dev

# Or run a task directly
pixi run main          # main test suite
pixi run plot          # plot/visualization tests
pixi run test-all      # everything, with a terminal coverage report
pixi run notebooks     # validate example notebooks

docs.title: Available Pixi environments
docs.text:
Environment Features Purpose default py314 minimal runtime dev py314, dev, viz tests, linting, build tooling docs py314, docs docs site (mkdocs serve) py311 py311, dev, viz pinned Python 3.11 py312 py312, dev, viz pinned Python 3.12 py313 py313, dev, viz pinned Python 3.13 py314 py314, dev, viz pinned Python 3.14

default, dev and docs are not unpinned — they reuse the py314 feature, so they resolve Python 3.14 like the matrix environment of that name. viz is a PEP 621 extra; dev, docs and notebook are PEP 735 dependency groups. The definitions live in pyproject.toml under [tool.pixi.environments].

The 3.13 and 3.14 pins carry a build glob (*_cp313 / *_cp314) that excludes the free-threaded interpreter: pyramids-core ships no cp313t / cp314t wheel, and with no conda GDAL underneath, resolving one of those would fail at import rather than at solve time.

docs.title: Where the environments live
docs.text: .pixi/config.toml sets detached-environments to C:/python-environments/pixi/envs, keeping the multi-GB solved environments off the Google-Drive-synced checkout. That file is local-only (pixi writes a .pixi/.gitignore holding *), so each machine chooses its own location; without it, pixi puts the environments in .pixi/envs/ inside the repository.

docs.title: Editable / development install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/serapeum-org/pyramids-mesh.git
cd pyramids-mesh
pixi install -e dev
pixi run -e dev pre-commit install

The package itself is registered as an editable pixi pypi-dependency, so pixi install -e dev already puts your checkout on the path — there is no separate editable-install step.

docs.title: Quick check
docs.text:
>>> import pyramids_mesh
>>> pyramids_mesh.__version__
'0.1.0'
>>> from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import Mesh2d, MeshDataset   # the tier this extends

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• pyramids (conda-forge name) and pyramids-core (PyPI name) are the same package. pyramids-mesh depends on the PyPI distribution name (pyramids-core) so it works regardless of how pyramids itself was installed.
  • Documentation: https://serapeum-org.github.io/pyramids-mesh/latest
  • Source repository: https://github.com/serapeum-org/pyramids-mesh

docs.title: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
docs.text:
This section collects significant architectural decisions for the pyramids-mesh project, using the MADR format.

  • ADR-0001: Documentation stack
  • ADR-0002: Type checking approach
  • ADR-0003: Scope boundary with pyramids-core — superseded by 0005
  • ADR-0004: Versioned documentation strategy
  • ADR-0005: pyramids-mesh is a file-format driver package

Each ADR includes context, decision, and consequences. New ADRs should follow the numbering convention and be immutable once accepted.

docs.title: ADR-0001: Documentation stack
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-13

docs.title: Context
docs.text: We need a robust, contributor-friendly documentation stack that supports API reference, diagrams, tutorials, and versioned publishing — and that matches the rest of the stack, so a contributor moving between repositories does not relearn it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Use MkDocs with the Material theme as the primary docs framework.
  • Use mkdocstrings[python] for auto-generating API reference from docstrings.
  • Prefer Mermaid fenced blocks for diagrams; allow PlantUML if complexity requires it.
  • Use mike to publish versioned documentation on GitHub Pages.
  • Execute example notebooks ahead of time and render their stored outputs (mkdocs-jupyter with execute: false); pixi run notebooks is what proves they still run.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Contributors document code with Google-style docstrings.
  • Diagrams render client-side in the site; heavy diagrams can be split or pre-rendered if needed.
  • CI builds the docs on pull requests, pushes to main, and releases, publishing with mike.

docs.title: ADR-0002: Type checking approach
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-13

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Static analysis improves reliability and developer experience, but the runtime stack underneath this package (GDAL via the vendored osgeo bindings, and the UGRID types it extends) is only partially typed, so full strictness is not reachable from day one.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Adopt gradual typing with standard Python type hints; annotate public APIs first.
  • mypy is installed in the dev group and may be run by contributors; it is not enforced in CI yet.
  • Prefer Google-style docstrings with type annotations to improve mkdocstrings output.
  • Mesh topology arrays are annotated with numpy.typing.NDArray, matching how pyramids annotates the same arrays, so signatures line up across the boundary.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Type hints are added progressively rather than in one sweep.
  • Strictness can be enabled per-module later, and a type-coverage report added to CI, without reworking existing annotations.

docs.title: ADR-0003: Scope boundary with pyramids-core
docs.text:
• Status: Superseded by ADR-0005
  • Date: 2026-10-13

Superseded 2026-10-13. The three-concerns decision below (generation, quality, refinement) was written during scaffolding and was not the intended scope. This package is a file-format driver package; see ADR-0005, which restates every boundary rule from this ADR unchanged. Kept for the record; do not act on its Decision section.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
pyramids-core already ships UGRID support in pyramids.netcdf.ugrid: the data model (Mesh2d, Mesh1d, MeshDataset, Connectivity), UGRID-compliant NetCDF I/O, connectivity derivation and graph algorithms, sampling and mesh-to-mesh regridding, construction by flattening a raster grid or a polygon layer, mesh-to-vector conversion, gap filling, spatial indexing, and rendering through cleopatra. This repository exists because three things are missing from that list, not because the mesh model needs a second implementation.

Without a stated boundary, the obvious failure mode is re-deriving connectivity or re-wrapping the NetCDF I/O here, which gives the stack two mesh types that drift apart.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• pyramids-core remains the single owner of the mesh data model, its persistence, and every operation that follows from a topology already in hand. This package imports those types; it never redefines them.
  • pyramids-mesh owns three concerns:
    • Generation — producing a topology where none exists yet (as opposed to flattening a grid or polygon layer that already carries one, which is ugrid.construct).
    • Quality — per-element metrics (aspect ratio, skewness, orthogonality) and quality-driven smoothing.
    • Refinement — local refinement and coarsening of an existing mesh.
  • Public functions take and return pyramids.netcdf.ugrid types, so a result can go straight back into a MeshDataset and be written as UGRID NetCDF without a conversion step.
  • A gap or bug on the pyramids side of the boundary is reported and fixed upstream. A local workaround, if one is unavoidable, carries a comment naming the upstream issue and is removed when that lands.
  • Plotting goes through cleopatra, reached via pyramids — this package declares no plotting code of its own beyond the viz extra.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The dependency floor (pyramids-core >= 0.66.0) is an API floor: raising it is the normal way to pick up an upstream mesh fix.
  • Some features will be rejected here and routed upstream instead; the table in the docs home page is the quick test for which side a concern falls on.
  • Interoperability is free — anything this package produces is already a UGRID mesh that the rest of the stack reads.

docs.title: ADR-0004: Versioned documentation strategy
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-13

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Readers need documentation matching the version they have installed, and contributors need to preview docs changes on a pull request before they merge.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Use mike to publish versioned docs to GitHub Pages.
  • Track main as the development version; publish releases under their tag and alias latest.
  • Publish pull-request previews through the shared mkdocs-deploy action's pull_request trigger.
  • The release tag comes from pyproject.toml's version, which commitizen bumps — one source of truth for the package version, the git tag, and the docs version selector.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Contributors update docs alongside code and see a preview on the pull request.
  • Users browse historical docs aligned with releases.
  • A release that skips cz bump publishes docs under the wrong version, so version bumps stay commitizen-driven.

docs.title: ADR-0005: pyramids-mesh is a file-format driver package
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-13
  • Supersedes: ADR-0003

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR-0003 scoped this package to mesh generation, quality and refinement. That scope was written during scaffolding, before the gap analysis it was meant to serve, and it does not match the work this repository exists to do.

The actual gap is format breadth. A survey of the mesh-format landscape — the eighteen driver families the established mesh I/O libraries cover — found that pyramids-core reads exactly one of them: UGRID NetCDF. The other seventeen are the native file formats of hydrodynamic and hydraulic solvers — SMS, TUFLOW, TELEMAC, DHI MIKE, FLO-2D, 3Di, ANUGA, HEC-RAS — and none of them can be opened today.

That survey also found the comparison runs the other way for everything else: those libraries do no interpolation, regridding, reprojection, contouring, gap filling, mesh-to-vector conversion or graph analysis. pyramids-core already has all of it. So the only substantial capability they have over this stack is the ability to open other people's mesh files.

Reading a format is never out of scope for the stack, but seventeen parsers do not belong in pyramids-core itself: they carry dependencies the core must not take (mikeio alone pulls pandas, matplotlib, scipy and tqdm), and their test fixtures are binary files measured in megabytes against a PyPI project that already refills its 10 GB limit roughly every twelve releases.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
pyramids-mesh reads and writes the file formats of hydrodynamic and hydraulic mesh models — 2DM, Selafin, DFSU, XMDF, PLY and the rest of the hydrodynamic formats — as pyramids.netcdf.ugrid objects. It owns file-format drivers; every mesh operation belongs upstream in pyramids-core.

  • Generation, quality and refinement are dropped, not deferred. They were not an intended scope. If mesh generation is wanted later it gets its own package and its own argument.
  • Drivers are discovered by pyramids-core through the pyramids.mesh_drivers entry-point group. This package depends on pyramids-core; pyramids-core never imports this package. That registry shipped in pyramids-core 0.68.0, which is this package's floor, so registered drivers are discovered and dispatched to.
  • Each driver is a class declaring name, long_name, suffixes, api_version and a capabilities set, implementing can_open and mesh_names — which pyramids calls on every driver whatever it declares — plus either read (a format carrying topology) or read_data (a results-only format such as DAT, XMDF or XDMF, which carries values but no mesh). Only read_mesh, needs_mesh, write_mesh and write_data gate behaviour upstream; read_data, lazy_data and multi_mesh are declarative and require no method of their own.
  • The one dependency-backed driver family lives behind an extra — [dhi] (mikeio) — and a driver whose extra is absent is skipped at discovery, so a bare install stays small and useful. Mesh reading itself is never delegated to a third-party mesh library: that is pyramids-core's, and a generic capability missing there is added there. The [interchange] extra (meshio) was dropped for this reason; PLY and the TIN formats are parsed here. [hdf] (h5py) went the same way: HDF5 is read through the GDAL multidimensional API over the GDAL vendored in the pyramids-core wheel, which supplies group traversal, attributes and typed reads. mikeio remains because DFSU and DFS2 are proprietary DHI containers with no portable alternative.
  • Test fixtures are hand-built minimal files, committed, and kept out of the built distribution. Nothing special is needed for that: setuptools' sdist does not collect tests/data/*, and the wheel is built from src/ only. Vendor sample files are fetched in CI behind a marker, never committed.

docs.title: The boundary (carried over from ADR-0003 unchanged)
docs.text:
Every rule below was correct in ADR-0003 and is restated here because that ADR is superseded in full. Only its three-concerns decision was wrong.

  • pyramids-core remains the single owner of the mesh data model, its persistence, and every operation that follows from a topology already in hand. This package imports those types; it never redefines them.
  • Public functions take and return pyramids.netcdf.ugrid types, so a result can go straight back into a MeshDataset and be written as UGRID NetCDF without a conversion step.
  • A gap or bug on the pyramids side of the boundary is reported and fixed upstream. A local workaround, if one is unavoidable, carries a comment naming the upstream issue and is removed when that lands.
  • Plotting goes through cleopatra, reached via pyramids. This package declares no plotting code — and, with the viz extra removed, no plotting dependency either: a driver returns data, and the caller plots it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The pyramids-core floor is an API floor on the registry, not on the mesh model. The registry shipped in pyramids-core 0.68.0, so the floor is now >= 0.68.0 and this package's entry points are live: a driver it registers is dispatched to. The earlier hold on publishing to PyPI — kept while the registry was unreleased and the entry points inert — is lifted.
  • Three concerns these source formats carry and pyramids-core does not — ragged vertical levels (DataOnVolumes), per-timestep active/dry flags, and a dataset reference time — are upstream work. A driver meeting them carries the value through without fabricating data: it raises on a genuinely ragged vertical profile rather than padding it, and attaches an active mask as a sibling variable rather than folding it into the values as NaN.
  • DFS2 is a structured grid rather than a mesh, so it is the one in-scope format whose natural target is a raster Dataset. Whether it belongs here at all is deliberately left open.
  • The viz extra is removed, and generation/quality/refinement leave the documentation.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• planning/design.md — the full architecture: driver protocol, registry and dispatch, the model contract, per-format specifications, and the task plan.
  • the format-comparison notes in planning/ — the driver table and the capability comparison this decision rests on.

docs.title: Getting started with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
pyramids-mesh is a thin file-format layer. Hydrodynamic and hydraulic solvers each save their mesh in their own format — Gmsh .msh, SMS/TUFLOW .2dm, Telemac Selafin, DHI .dfsu, XMDF, and dozens more. pyramids-mesh registers a driver for each of these formats whose only job is to parse the file and hand back a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid object (a MeshDataset wrapping a Mesh2d / Mesh1d).

Why does that matter? Because once the mesh is a pyramids object, the entire pyramids GIS toolbox applies — bounds, CRS handling, conversion to a GeoDataFrame, bounding polygons, circumcenters, plotting through cleopatra, and so on. pyramids-mesh adds readers, not geometry algorithms: every mesh operation lives upstream in pyramids-gis.

This notebook walks the whole path end to end:

  1. the driver registry — how formats are discovered,
  2. MeshDataset.read_file — how a file is dispatched to the right driver,
  3. a first read → explore → plot on one real Gmsh mesh, and
  4. a couple of GIS operations that come for free from pyramids.

docs.title: 1. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 2. Locate the example data¶
docs.text: This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so the repo-root examples/data/ folder is two levels up. Paths inside a notebook are always written relative to the notebook itself. We will read a small Gmsh mesh, gmsh/insulated-2.2.msh.

docs.title: 3. The driver registry¶
docs.text: Every supported format is a driver, discovered through Python entry points and collected by mesh_drivers(). It returns a plain dict mapping a short driver name to its driver class. The number of entries is simply how many formats this install can read or write.

docs.title: 4. What a driver advertises¶
docs.text:
Each driver class exposes four descriptive attributes:

  • .name — the short key used in the registry and for forcing a driver,
  • .long_name — a human-readable format name,
  • .suffixes — the file extensions it claims, and
  • .capabilities — a set of verbs describing what it can do with that format.

We inspect the Gmsh driver, since that is the format we are about to read.

docs.title: 5. The full format table¶
docs.text: Capabilities and suffixes for every registered driver make a natural DataFrame. Rendering it as a table is the clearest way to see the plugin's reach at a glance — which formats are read-only, which can round-trip data, which carry multiple meshes.

docs.title: 6. Reading a file: automatic dispatch¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path) is the one entry point you normally call. It inspects the file's suffix and content, finds the matching driver in the registry, and runs it — you do not name a driver yourself. The result is a MeshDataset.

docs.title: 7. Forcing a specific driver¶
docs.text: When a suffix is ambiguous (several formats share .inp or .nc, for instance) you can override auto-detection with the driver= argument, naming any key from the registry. Here we force gmsh explicitly and confirm we get the identical mesh.

docs.title: 8. Exploring the dataset's metadata¶
docs.text:
A MeshDataset exposes summary properties that describe the mesh as a whole. The most useful on a first look:

  • n_node / n_face — size of the mesh,
  • crs / epsg — the coordinate reference system, if the format recorded one,
  • bounds — the spatial extent (minx, miny, maxx, maxy), and
  • data_variable_names — names of any field variables attached to the mesh.

docs.title: 9. File-level attributes¶
docs.text: Formats can also carry free-form metadata, surfaced as a dict on .global_attributes.

docs.title: 10. A statistical summary of the fields¶
docs.text: .summary() returns a DataFrame of per-variable statistics (count, min, max, mean, std). Because this mesh has no data variables yet, the summary is empty — a useful confirmation, not an error. We will populate it shortly.

docs.title: 11. The underlying Mesh2d¶
docs.text:
ds.mesh is the Mesh2d object holding the raw topology. The arrays you reach for most often:

  • node_x / node_y — node coordinates,
  • face_node_connectivity.data — the (n_face, k) table of node indices per face, and
  • face_areas — area of each face.

docs.title: 12. First plot: the mesh outline¶
docs.text: The simplest visualization needs no data at all -- just draw the wireframe with plot_outline(), which renders the mesh edges through cleopatra and returns a MeshGlyph wrapping the figure. Reading the file above flipped matplotlib to a non-interactive backend, so we let cleopatra choose it with Config.set_matplotlib_backend() (which picks inline in a notebook); from now on every plot embeds on its own.

docs.title: 13. A data map: attach and plot a field¶
docs.text: To draw a filled map we need a value per cell. This mesh has none, so we compute one — each cell's area — and attach it with with_variable(..., location="face"), which returns a new dataset carrying that field. (The original ds is left untouched.)

docs.title: 14. The summary, now populated¶
docs.text: With a field attached, .summary() on d2 reports real statistics — the same call that was empty in section 11.

docs.title: 15. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text:
Because the mesh is a pyramids object, pyramids' GIS layer applies directly. A few teasers:

bounds is the extent, and bounding_polygon() returns the extent as a shapely Polygon you can intersect, buffer, or export.

docs.title: Faces as a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every face into a polygon row of a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the standard vector structure for export to shapefile/GeoPackage or for joining against other spatial layers.

docs.title: Circumcenters¶
docs.text: circumcenters() returns an (n_face, 2) array of per-cell circumcenter coordinates — the points a finite-volume scheme places unknowns at. It is a mesh-derived geometry pyramids computes on demand.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• pyramids-mesh is a format layer: drivers parse mesh files into pyramids.netcdf.ugrid objects, and that is all they do — no GIS, no interpolation, no analysis.
  • mesh_drivers() is the registry of every supported format, each driver advertising its suffixes and capabilities.
  • MeshDataset.read_file(path) auto-dispatches to the right driver by suffix/content, with driver= as an override.
  • Once read, the mesh is a first-class pyramids object: explore it (n_node, bounds, summary()), plot it (plot_outline, plot), and run GIS operations (to_geodataframe, bounding_polygon, circumcenters) — all from pyramids, not from this package.

Next: see the per-format and domain notebooks in docs/examples/ for reading specific solver outputs (2DM, Selafin, DFSU, …), attaching real result fields, and the deeper GIS workflows pyramids provides.

docs.title: Reading SMS/TUFLOW 2DM meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
The 2DM format is the plain-text mesh of the Aquaveo SMS (Surface-water Modeling System) and is consumed by solvers such as TUFLOW, SRH-2D and HEC-RAS 2D. A 2DM file lists nodes (ND records) and elements (E3T triangles, E4Q quads, …), optionally with a material id per element. pyramids-mesh registers a 2dm driver that parses those records into a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset.

This notebook reads the bundled minimal.2dm — a unit square split into two triangles — and then puts it through the GIS toolkit. A tiny mesh keeps every table and figure readable.

docs.title: 3. Locate the data¶
docs.text: This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so the repo-root examples/data/ folder is two levels up. Paths are written relative to the notebook itself, as a Path object.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 4. Read the file¶
docs.text: A driver's only job is to parse the file and hand back a MeshDataset. We pass a pathlib.Path (never a str) and name the driver explicitly:

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes the mesh size, its coordinate reference system, and the data variables carried alongside the topology. None for crs/epsg simply means the source file declared no projection — the geometry is still valid, it is just unlocated in world space.

docs.title: Per-variable summary¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a pandas DataFrame — one row per data variable with count, min, max, mean and standard deviation. A std of 0 means that variable is uniform across the mesh.

docs.title: Global attributes¶
docs.text: Each driver stamps provenance into global_attributes so you can trace a dataset back to the format it came from after it has been converted.

docs.title: 6. The Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: node coordinates plus the face-node connectivity table. face_node_connectivity.data has shape (n_face, k) — row i lists the node indices of face i (padded for mixed element types). We also derive per-face areas and centroids from that topology.

docs.title: 7. Wireframe — the mesh skeleton¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare mesh: every face edge, no data coloring. This is the fastest way to eyeball connectivity, element shapes and the overall extent.

docs.title: 8. A data map¶
docs.text: minimal.2dm carries a per-element material id. We map it with ds.plot(...). This sample has a single material zone, so the map is uniform — on a real model the same call paints the roughness/landuse zones that drive the solver.

docs.title: 9. GIS operations¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is a first-class pyramids object, the full geospatial toolkit works on it directly — no conversion step. Below are several operations, each visualised or interpreted. (Operations that need a source CRS, such as to_crs, are skipped here: this sample declares none.)

docs.title: 9a. Faces as polygons — to_geodataframe()¶
docs.text: Every face becomes a shapely polygon in a GeoPandas GeoDataFrame, ready for a spatial join, an overlay, or export to any OGR vector format.

docs.title: 9b. Outer boundary — bounding_polygon() and exterior_edges()¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the faces into a single shapely polygon tracing the mesh outline, and exterior_edges() returns the indices of the mesh edges that lie on that boundary — their count is the boundary's edge length.

docs.title: 9c. Connectivity — connected_components()¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by the connected sub-mesh it belongs to. One unique label means the mesh is a single watertight piece; more than one would reveal detached islands. We attach the labels as a face variable and map them.

docs.title: 9d. Face adjacency — sparse_adjacency()¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() returns the face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix (two faces are adjacent when they share an edge). Its sparsity pattern is the dual graph a solver walks; nnz counts the directed face-neighbour links.

docs.title: 9e. Triangle circumcenters — circumcenters()¶
docs.text: For a triangular mesh, circumcenters() returns the circumcircle centre of each face (shape (2, n_face)) — the sample points of the dual Voronoi mesh that finite-volume schemes use. We scatter them over the wireframe.

docs.title: 9f. Clip to a sub-region — crop()¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) keeps only the faces inside a bounding box. We clip to the lower-left quarter of the extent.

docs.title: 9g. Round-trip through UGRID NetCDF — to_file()¶
docs.text: to_file(..., driver='ugrid') writes the mesh to the CF/UGRID NetCDF convention — the lossless lingua franca every tool in the stack reads back. We write it, re-read it, and confirm the topology survived.

docs.title: 10. Takeaway¶
docs.text: The 2dm driver turns an SMS/TUFLOW mesh into a MeshDataset in one call. From there the mesh is a full pyramids citizen: vectorise it, clip it, inspect its connectivity, and round-trip it through UGRID NetCDF — all without the driver doing any GIS itself.

docs.title: 3Di results with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
3Di is a hydrodynamic flood model whose results NetCDF stores values on a staggered sub-grid rather than an explicit polygon mesh. The pyramids-mesh 3Di driver is a needs-mesh driver: it reconstructs the 2D cell grid itself from the file's geometry arrays, then presents it as a standard MeshDataset.

(3Di files can also carry a coupled 1D network; pyramids represents the 2D mesh and warns that the 1D part is dropped.)

docs.title: Quickstart read¶
docs.text: Pass driver="3di" explicitly. The driver rebuilds the 2D grid and loads the Mesh2D_* result variables. The UserWarning about a coupled 1D network is expected for this file.

docs.title: Explore the dataset¶
docs.text:
A MeshDataset wraps a UGRID-style unstructured mesh plus any data variables that ride on it. The scalar properties below describe the grid at a glance: how many nodes and faces it has, its coordinate reference system, and its spatial extent.

The reconstructed grid here is a compact 4x4 block of quad cells (25 nodes, 16 faces).

docs.title: Data variables¶
docs.text: data_variable_names lists every field attached to the mesh. These are the real model results - water levels, depths, velocities - that make a results file worth reading.

docs.title: The Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: the topology the data variables are defined on. Nodes carry the (x, y) coordinates; face_node_connectivity says which nodes form each face (a row per face, padded to the maximum vertex count).

docs.title: Wireframe - the bare mesh¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the mesh edges with no data colouring. It is the fastest way to see the grid's shape, resolution, and how faces are distributed before looking at any results.

docs.title: Mapping the real results¶
docs.text: The result variables carry a time axis (time_values shows the stored timesteps, in seconds). At t = 0 the model is still dry (Mesh2D_s1 is all fill value), so we select a later wet step with isel(time=...) before mapping.

docs.title: From mesh to GIS¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset is not a dead end - it converts into the vector and raster types the rest of a GIS workflow expects. Everything below is reached through pyramids; this package only supplies the file-format driver that built the mesh.

docs.title: Faces as vector polygons¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe(variable_name=...) turns every face into a polygon row carrying that variable's value - a standard GeoPandas GeoDataFrame you can join, filter, or export.

docs.title: Dissolving into zones¶
docs.text: polygonize(variable) merges neighbouring faces that share a value into larger polygons - handy for turning a noisy per-cell field into clean zones. It needs a single value per face, which is exactly what our working dataset holds.

docs.title: Sampling at points¶
docs.text: sample(variable, x, y) reads the value of the face that contains each query point. Here we probe the first few face centroids, so each query lands squarely inside a face.

docs.title: The mesh outline as one polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() returns a single shapely polygon tracing the mesh's outer boundary - the model's wetted footprint, useful as a clip mask or extent reference.

docs.title: Cropping to a sub-region¶
docs.text: subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) returns a new, smaller MeshDataset holding only the faces inside the box - the same object type, so every operation above still applies. We derive a box from the mesh envelope so it works on any extent.

docs.title: Connectivity as a sparse graph¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() exposes face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix, and connected_components() labels each face by which connected piece of the mesh it belongs to - the entry points for graph algorithms over the grid.

docs.title: Circumcenters - not applicable here¶
docs.text: circumcenters() is only defined for purely triangular meshes. This grid contains quad (or mixed-polygon) faces, so the call would raise ValueError. We note it and skip rather than force it.

docs.title: Self-contained rasterisation¶
docs.text: to_dataset(variable, cell_size=...) samples the mesh onto a regular raster grid and returns a pyramids Dataset. Unlike rasterize_like / regrid — which need an existing reference grid — this is self-contained: pick a cell size and pyramids builds the grid. We derive the cell size from the average face area so the raster has sub-face resolution regardless of the mesh density.

docs.title: Reprojection - skipped¶
docs.text: to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to project from. This 3Di result stores coordinates without a CRS, so ds.crs is None. With no source CRS, reprojection is undefined, so we skip it; assign a CRS first if your coordinates are georeferenced.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: The 3Di driver shows what a needs-mesh driver does: the file never stored an explicit polygon mesh, yet the driver reconstructs the 2D grid and serves it as an ordinary MeshDataset. Select a wet timestep with isel, then map water level and volume, convert faces to vectors, or crop - all through the shared pyramids API, with the 1D network reported-but-skipped rather than silently mangled.

docs.title: Reading Abaqus meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
Abaqus (Dassault Systèmes) input decks (.inp) drive one of the most widely used finite-element solvers. They are keyword ASCII files: a *NODE block lists coordinates, and *ELEMENT, TYPE=... blocks list connectivity.

Our sample uses TYPE=CPS3 — 3-node plane-stress triangles. Coordinates are in the model's engineering frame with no projection, so crs=None.

We use nle1xf3c.inp: a small all-triangle plane-stress patch.

Source: meshio test suite (tests/meshes/abaqus/), MIT.

docs.title: Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: Quickstart: read the Abaqus file¶
docs.text:
driver="abaqus" parses the keyword grammar (*NODE / *ELEMENT).

The one rule that matters: pass a pathlib.Path, never a str — read_file keys its driver dispatch off the Path type. MeshDataset.read_file(...) returns a MeshDataset, the in-memory UGRID container every pyramids-mesh driver produces.

docs.title: What did we get?¶
docs.text: A few scalar properties describe the dataset at a glance: node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, and the planar bounding box.

docs.title: Summary table¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a pandas DataFrame with per-variable statistics (count / min / max / mean / std). With no data variables the table is empty — confirming a geometry-only deck.

docs.title: The mesh geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: node coordinates plus the face-node connectivity, an (n_face, k) integer table where k is the largest number of nodes any face has. Triangles fill 3 columns; quadrilaterals fill 4 (a shorter face pads the spare slot). face_areas and face_centroids are derived on demand.

docs.title: Wireframe¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare mesh edges — the quickest way to eyeball the topology and the element shapes before colouring anything.

docs.title: A derived field: cell area¶
docs.text: These engineering files usually carry no cell data we can colour by — so we compute one ourselves. with_variable attaches face_areas as a face-located variable, giving a non-destructive copy of the dataset that plot can render as a filled colour map.

docs.title: Treating the mesh as GIS¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is just nodes and polygonal faces, pyramids exposes the usual vector-GIS toolbox on it. First, every face as a GeoPandas polygon:

docs.title: The outer boundary¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the triangles into the patch outline.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) returns a new MeshDataset with only the faces inside the box — handy for zooming into a region of a large mesh. We crop to the left half of the extent.

docs.title: The face-adjacency graph¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() gives the face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix, and connected_components() labels which faces are reachable from which. plt.spy shows the sparsity pattern — the fingerprint of how the faces are wired together.

docs.title: A triangle-only operation: circumcenters¶
docs.text: Every CPS3 element is a triangle, so circumcenters() is defined. We overlay the circumcenters (red) on the area-weighted centroids (blue) — note how they diverge for the more skewed triangles.

docs.title: Converting out: other drivers¶
docs.text: to_file(path, driver=...) re-serialises the mesh through any writer in the driver table — here a round-trip to the 2dm format in a temp file.

docs.title: What we cannot do here: reprojection & regridding¶
docs.text: to_crs(epsg) reprojects between coordinate systems — but this mesh has crs=None (model-local coordinates, no datum), so there is nothing to reproject from; we skip it. Likewise rasterize_like(...) and regrid(...) map a data field onto a raster or another mesh; with no meaningful field and no georeferencing on an engineering mesh they are out of scope. These belong on georeferenced hydrodynamic meshes, not FEM/CFD decks.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• driver="abaqus" reads a keyword .inp deck (*NODE + *ELEMENT TYPE=CPS3) into a MeshDataset.
  • An all-triangle plane-stress patch, geometry-only (crs=None, no data variables).
  • All GIS operations work, and because it is triangular, circumcenters does too.
  • No CRS → reprojection and regridding do not apply.

docs.title: Reading ADCIRC grids with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
ADCIRC is a coastal-ocean circulation and storm-surge model. Its mesh lives in a plain-text fort.14 grid file: a header, then one line per node (id lon lat depth), then one line per triangular element (id n a b c), then open- and land-boundary sections. Water-surface results (zeta) are written to a companion NetCDF fort.63.nc.

pyramids-mesh registers an adcirc driver whose only job is to parse those files and hand back a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset wrapping a Mesh2d. Once the grid is a pyramids object, the whole pyramids GIS toolbox applies — bounds, CRS handling, GeoDataFrame conversion, bounding polygons, plotting through cleopatra. This notebook reads the public-domain Shinnecock Inlet example and works through read → explore → plot → GIS.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the data¶
docs.text: This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so the repo-root examples/data/ folder is two levels up. Paths inside a notebook are always written relative to the notebook itself. The ADCIRC folder holds the fort.14 grid and the fort.63.nc result file. We pass a pathlib.Path to the reader — never a string.

docs.title: 4. Read the grid¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file dispatches on the driver we name. We pass driver="adcirc" explicitly; the returned object is a MeshDataset. (The reader may warn that it reversed some clockwise faces to counter-clockwise — that is the UGRID winding convention being enforced, not an error.)

docs.title: 5. Explore the mesh¶
docs.text: A handful of properties describe the grid: node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, the data variables the driver attached, and the bounding box. ADCIRC grids store longitude/latitude, but fort.14 declares no CRS, so crs / epsg come back None — we treat the coordinates as geographic degrees but pyramids will not assume so.

docs.title: 6. Mesh geometry¶
docs.text: The Mesh2d behind the dataset exposes the raw topology: node coordinates, the (n_face, 3) face-node connectivity table (each triangle's three node indices), per-face areas and centroids. These are plain numpy arrays.

docs.title: 7. Wireframe¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the mesh skeleton — every element edge, no data colouring. It is the quickest way to see the grid's shape and where it is refined. Shinnecock Inlet's mesh is far denser around the inlet channel than offshore.

docs.title: 8. Data map — surface elevation¶
docs.text: plot(variable) colours each element by a data variable. zeta is time-varying (57 steps, 3070 nodes); the mesh renderer draws the first time step. This is the modelled sea-surface elevation across the domain at the start of the run.

docs.title: 9. GIS operations for free¶
docs.text: Because the grid is a pyramids object, pyramids' vector/GIS layer applies unchanged. First, convert to a GeoDataFrame — one polygon per element, ready for geopandas, spatial joins or export. to_geodataframe() returns just the geometry column, so we attach each element's area and let geopandas colour by it — the small cells pick out the refined inlet.

docs.title: 10. What needs more than a grid¶
docs.text:
Two families of operation are deliberately skipped here:

  • to_crs(epsg) reprojects coordinates, but it needs a source CRS. fort.14 declares none, so ds.epsg is None and to_crs raises Cannot reproject: source CRS is unknown. The coordinates are lon/lat (EPSG:4326) by convention, but the file does not say so, so pyramids will not guess.
  • rasterize_like / regrid need a reference grid to sample onto; with only the mesh in hand there is nothing to target, so they are out of scope for this read-only tour.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver="adcirc") turns a fort.14 grid (plus its fort.63.nc results) into a first-class pyramids mesh. From there, exploration, plotting, GeoDataFrame conversion, bounding polygons, connectivity analysis, spatial subsetting and export are all inherited from pyramids — pyramids-mesh only added the reader.

docs.title: Reading AVS-UCD meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
AVS-UCD (Unstructured Cell Data) is the ASCII mesh format of the AVS visualization system, also emitted by mesh generators such as LaGriT. It lists nodes, then cells of mixed type, then optional node/cell data.

driver="avsucd" reads it. Coordinates are model-local — crs=None.

This sample, 02_tet_mesh.inp from LaGriT, is deliberately instructive: it is a tetrahedral (volumetric) mesh — 1122 nodes, 4800 tets. A MeshDataset models a 2D surface, so each tet face is flattened into the plane. That projection produces many overlapping and degenerate (zero-area) faces, and pyramids warns about it on read. This notebook shows both how to read such a file and why a volumetric mesh is the wrong shape for a surface container.

Source: LANL LaGriT tutorial data, BSD-3-Clause.

docs.title: Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: Quickstart: read the AVS-UCD file¶
docs.text:
driver="avsucd" parses the UCD grammar. Expect a burst of warnings about re-wound and degenerate faces — the direct consequence of flattening a 3D tet mesh into 2D. They are warnings, not errors.

The one rule that matters: pass a pathlib.Path, never a str — read_file keys its driver dispatch off the Path type. MeshDataset.read_file(...) returns a MeshDataset, the in-memory UGRID container every pyramids-mesh driver produces.

docs.title: What did we get?¶
docs.text: A few scalar properties describe the dataset at a glance: node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, and the planar bounding box.

docs.title: Summary table¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a pandas DataFrame with per-variable statistics (count / min / max / mean / std). It reports node_z, whose range hints at the original 3D extent.

docs.title: The mesh geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: node coordinates plus the face-node connectivity, an (n_face, k) integer table where k is the largest number of nodes any face has. Triangles fill 3 columns; quadrilaterals fill 4 (a shorter face pads the spare slot). face_areas and face_centroids are derived on demand.

docs.title: Wireframe¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare mesh edges — the quickest way to eyeball the topology and the element shapes before colouring anything.

docs.title: A derived field: cell area¶
docs.text: These engineering files usually carry no cell data we can colour by — so we compute one ourselves. with_variable attaches face_areas as a face-located variable, giving a non-destructive copy of the dataset that plot can render as a filled colour map.

docs.title: Treating the mesh as GIS¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is just nodes and polygonal faces, pyramids exposes the usual vector-GIS toolbox on it. First, every face as a GeoPandas polygon:

docs.title: The outer boundary — and why it fails here¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves all faces into one polygon. On this projected tet mesh the faces self-intersect, so the geometry union raises a topology error. We catch it and report it — another concrete sign that this volumetric mesh does not form a valid 2D surface.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) returns a new MeshDataset with only the faces inside the box — handy for zooming into a region of a large mesh. We crop to the left half of the extent.

docs.title: The face-adjacency graph¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() gives the face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix, and connected_components() labels which faces are reachable from which. plt.spy shows the sparsity pattern — the fingerprint of how the faces are wired together.

docs.title: Why circumcenters are skipped here¶
docs.text: The face table is 4-wide (not purely triangular), so circumcenters() raises ValueError. We catch it.

docs.title: Converting out: other drivers¶
docs.text: to_file(path, driver=...) re-serialises the mesh through any writer in the driver table — here a round-trip to the 2dm format in a temp file.

docs.title: What we cannot do here: reprojection & regridding¶
docs.text: to_crs(epsg) reprojects between coordinate systems — but this mesh has crs=None (model-local coordinates, no datum), so there is nothing to reproject from; we skip it. Likewise rasterize_like(...) and regrid(...) map a data field onto a raster or another mesh; with no meaningful field and no georeferencing on an engineering mesh they are out of scope. These belong on georeferenced hydrodynamic meshes, not FEM/CFD decks.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• driver="avsucd" reads an AVS-UCD ASCII mesh into a MeshDataset.
  • This sample is volumetric (tetrahedra). Reading it as a 2D surface works but produces degenerate faces, a self-intersecting boundary, and a mesh that fragments into hundreds of components — all signalled by read-time warnings.
  • The lesson: MeshDataset is a surface model. Feed it surface meshes (like the VTK, CGNS, MED, Nastran and Abaqus examples); a solid mesh is the wrong shape.
  • crs=None throughout → no reprojection or regridding.

docs.title: Reading CGNS (CFD) meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
CGNS — the CFD General Notation System — is the standard interchange format of computational fluid dynamics. Solvers and grid generators across the CFD world write it, storing the mesh (and flow solution) as a SIDS node tree inside an HDF5 container.

Passing driver="cgns" forces pyramids-mesh down the HDF5 path, reading the grid through the vendored GDAL HDF5 multidimensional driver. A CGNS grid is defined in the solver's own Cartesian coordinates with no map projection, so again crs=None.

We use cgnslib_vers-4400.cgns from the official CGNS repository: a structured block of quadrilateral cells.

Source: CGNS/CGNS src/tests/data/, zlib licence.

docs.title: Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: Quickstart: read the CGNS file¶
docs.text:
driver="cgns" forces the HDF5 reader. You may see a warning that some faces were re-wound to counter-clockwise — that is pyramids normalising the winding order, not an error.

The one rule that matters: pass a pathlib.Path, never a str — read_file keys its driver dispatch off the Path type. MeshDataset.read_file(...) returns a MeshDataset, the in-memory UGRID container every pyramids-mesh driver produces.

docs.title: What did we get?¶
docs.text: A few scalar properties describe the dataset at a glance: node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, and the planar bounding box.

docs.title: Summary table¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a pandas DataFrame with per-variable statistics (count / min / max / mean / std). Here it reports node_z, so you can see its range directly.

docs.title: The mesh geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: node coordinates plus the face-node connectivity, an (n_face, k) integer table where k is the largest number of nodes any face has. Triangles fill 3 columns; quadrilaterals fill 4 (a shorter face pads the spare slot). face_areas and face_centroids are derived on demand.

docs.title: Wireframe¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare mesh edges — the quickest way to eyeball the topology and the element shapes before colouring anything.

docs.title: A derived field: cell area¶
docs.text: These engineering files usually carry no cell data we can colour by — so we compute one ourselves. with_variable attaches face_areas as a face-located variable, giving a non-destructive copy of the dataset that plot can render as a filled colour map.

docs.title: Treating the mesh as GIS¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is just nodes and polygonal faces, pyramids exposes the usual vector-GIS toolbox on it. First, every face as a GeoPandas polygon:

docs.title: The outer boundary¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves all faces into the single enclosing polygon — the outline of the structured block.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) returns a new MeshDataset with only the faces inside the box — handy for zooming into a region of a large mesh. We crop to the left half of the extent.

docs.title: The face-adjacency graph¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() gives the face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix, and connected_components() labels which faces are reachable from which. plt.spy shows the sparsity pattern — the fingerprint of how the faces are wired together.

docs.title: Why circumcenters are skipped here¶
docs.text: circumcenters() is defined only for triangular meshes (a quad has no unique circumscribed circle). This grid is quadrilateral, so the call raises ValueError: circumcenters is only defined for triangular meshes. We demonstrate the guard rather than forcing it.

docs.title: Converting out: other drivers¶
docs.text: to_file(path, driver=...) re-serialises the mesh through any writer in the driver table — here a round-trip to the 2dm format in a temp file.

docs.title: What we cannot do here: reprojection & regridding¶
docs.text: to_crs(epsg) reprojects between coordinate systems — but this mesh has crs=None (model-local coordinates, no datum), so there is nothing to reproject from; we skip it. Likewise rasterize_like(...) and regrid(...) map a data field onto a raster or another mesh; with no meaningful field and no georeferencing on an engineering mesh they are out of scope. These belong on georeferenced hydrodynamic meshes, not FEM/CFD decks.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• driver="cgns" reads the CFD-standard HDF5 CGNS container into a MeshDataset.
  • The grid is quadrilateral and geometry-only (crs=None); its one variable node_z is the nodal elevation.
  • GIS operations — polygon export, bounding polygon, cropping, the adjacency graph — all work; triangle-only circumcenters is correctly refused.
  • Winding-normalisation warnings on read are informational, not failures.

docs.title: Attaching SMS .dat results to a mesh — the needs_mesh pattern¶
docs.text:
Some formats store only values, no topology. The SMS ASCII .dat dataset is one: it lists a scalar (or vector) per node or per cell, for one or more time steps, but says nothing about where the nodes are. A file like that is useless on its own — it needs a mesh to hang the numbers on.

pyramids-mesh models this with the needs_mesh capability. A needs_mesh driver does not implement read (it cannot build a mesh); it implements read_data, reached through MeshDataset.read_file(mesh).attach_data(results). You read the geometry from a mesh file first, then attach the results onto it. This notebook reads minimal.2dm for the topology and attaches the matching minimal.dat depth series.

docs.title: 3. Locate the data¶
docs.text: Two files, same folder: the mesh (minimal.2dm) and the results (minimal.dat). Both paths are relative to this notebook.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 4. Read the mesh, then attach the data¶
docs.text: Step one reads the topology from the 2DM file. Step two calls attach_data() with the .dat path: the needs_mesh driver reads the per-node values and binds them onto the mesh we already hold, returning a new MeshDataset. Note what happens to the variable list — the depth series from the .dat appears alongside the mesh's own material/node_z.

docs.title: 5. Explore the attached dataset¶
docs.text: The depth variable spans two time steps (its count is 2 x n_node). summary() shows its range; the mesh-side variables remain uniform on this minimal square.

docs.title: Provenance¶
docs.text: attach_data keeps the mesh's own global attributes and does not let the results file overwrite them, so the dataset still reads as an SMS 2DM mesh.

docs.title: 6. The Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: node coordinates plus the face-node connectivity table. face_node_connectivity.data has shape (n_face, k) — row i lists the node indices of face i (padded for mixed element types). We also derive per-face areas and centroids from that topology.

docs.title: 7. Wireframe — the mesh skeleton¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare mesh: every face edge, no data coloring. This is the fastest way to eyeball connectivity, element shapes and the overall extent.

docs.title: 8. A data map¶
docs.text: Now the payoff: we map the attached depth field. These are the numbers from the .dat file, drawn on the geometry from the .2dm file — the two halves joined by attach_data. plot shows the first time step by default.

docs.title: 9. GIS operations¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is a first-class pyramids object, the full geospatial toolkit works on it directly — no conversion step. Below are several operations, each visualised or interpreted. (Operations that need a source CRS, such as to_crs, are skipped here: this sample declares none.)

docs.title: 9a. Faces as polygons — to_geodataframe()¶
docs.text: Every face becomes a shapely polygon in a GeoPandas GeoDataFrame, ready for a spatial join, an overlay, or export to any OGR vector format.

docs.title: 9b. Outer boundary — bounding_polygon() and exterior_edges()¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the faces into a single shapely polygon tracing the mesh outline, and exterior_edges() returns the indices of the mesh edges that lie on that boundary — their count is the boundary's edge length.

docs.title: 9c. Connectivity — connected_components()¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by the connected sub-mesh it belongs to. One unique label means the mesh is a single watertight piece; more than one would reveal detached islands. We attach the labels as a face variable and map them.

docs.title: 9d. Face adjacency — sparse_adjacency()¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() returns the face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix (two faces are adjacent when they share an edge). Its sparsity pattern is the dual graph a solver walks; nnz counts the directed face-neighbour links.

docs.title: 9e. Triangle circumcenters — circumcenters()¶
docs.text: For a triangular mesh, circumcenters() returns the circumcircle centre of each face (shape (2, n_face)) — the sample points of the dual Voronoi mesh that finite-volume schemes use. We scatter them over the wireframe.

docs.title: 9f. Clip to a sub-region — crop()¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) keeps the faces inside a box; the attached depth values ride along with the clipped mesh.

docs.title: 9g. Round-trip through UGRID NetCDF — to_file()¶
docs.text: to_file(..., driver='ugrid') writes the mesh to the CF/UGRID NetCDF convention — the lossless lingua franca every tool in the stack reads back. We write it, re-read it, and confirm the topology survived.

docs.title: 10. Takeaway¶
docs.text: Results-only formats declare needs_mesh: you read a mesh, then attach_data() the values onto it. The same pattern powers the XMDF and other solver-output readers. Once attached, the field is an ordinary data variable — mappable, clippable and exportable like any other.

docs.title: Reading a 1D network (Deltares D-Flow FM) with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
Most mesh files describe a 2D surface — a sheet of triangles or quads. But hydraulic models of rivers and channels store a 1D network: nodes joined by edges, with no faces at all. This notebook reads a Deltares D-Flow FM UGRID *_net.nc file — the korte-woerden channel schematic — as a 1D network.

Why this case is special. pyramids' built-in UGRID reader always builds a 2D Mesh2d, whatever topology dimension a file declares — so MeshDataset.read_file on a pure-1D file fails (it looks for a face table that is not there). The network is read through the deltares1d driver instead: Mesh1d.read_file(path, driver="deltares1d") parses the UGRID mesh1d topology — the node coordinates and the edge-node table — straight into a Mesh1d, with no manual array handling.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: We import Mesh1d and MeshDataset. The split matters here: a 2D driver hands back a MeshDataset (which wraps a Mesh2d), but a 1D network is read with Mesh1d.read_file and comes back as a bare Mesh1d — which is exactly what this notebook does. Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook — just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the data¶
docs.text: The Deltares folder holds several UGRID samples. We use the pure-1D korte-woerden-1d_FlowFM_net.nc (network topology, no results).

docs.title: 4. Why MeshDataset.read_file refuses¶
docs.text: Pointing MeshDataset.read_file at a 1D file raises — the reader tries to build a 2D mesh and finds no face table. We catch it so the notebook keeps running.

docs.title: 5. Read the network¶
docs.text: Mesh1d.read_file with driver="deltares1d" reads the 1D discretisation directly — nodes, edge connectivity, CRS — all through the pyramids GDAL substrate, with no external libraries.

docs.title: 7. Draw the network by hand¶
docs.text: A Mesh1d has no plot() of its own, so we draw it as a graph: loop the edge table, draw each edge as a line segment between its two node coordinates, then scatter the nodes on top. Equal aspect keeps the geometry true (the CRS is in metres).

docs.title: 8. The network as vectors¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns the network into a geopandas GeoDataFrame — one LineString per edge (location="edge") or one Point per node (location="node"), CRS-stamped from the network. That is the bridge to the whole vector-GIS ecosystem: spatial joins, export to shapefile/GeoPackage, overlay with other layers.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: A 1D network is a graph, not a surface. pyramids keeps it in a dedicated Mesh1d class, and the deltares1d driver reads a D-Flow FM UGRID .nc straight into it — Mesh1d.read_file(path, driver="deltares1d") — with no manual array parsing. From there you get edge lengths, bounds, nearest-neighbour trees, a GeoDataFrame of lines or points, and — for a directed network — topological ordering. There are no faces, areas or centroids, and that is correct: a channel network has none.

docs.title: DHI MIKE DFSU results with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text: DFSU is DHI's flexible-mesh format for MIKE 21/3 hydrodynamic results. It stores an unstructured mesh (mixed triangles and quads) with time-varying variables such as surface elevation and depth-averaged velocity. pyramids-mesh reads it through mikeio under the hood and presents a standard MeshDataset.

docs.title: Quickstart read¶
docs.text: Pass driver="dfsu". This is the classic MIKE OdenseHD2D estuary example - 535 nodes, 724 faces.

docs.title: Explore the dataset¶
docs.text:
A MeshDataset wraps a UGRID-style unstructured mesh plus any data variables that ride on it. The scalar properties below describe the grid at a glance: how many nodes and faces it has, its coordinate reference system, and its spatial extent.

The coordinates are a projected UTM grid (metres), even though no CRS is embedded.

docs.title: Data variables¶
docs.text: data_variable_names lists every field attached to the mesh. These are the real model results - water levels, depths, velocities - that make a results file worth reading.

docs.title: The Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: the topology the data variables are defined on. Nodes carry the (x, y) coordinates; face_node_connectivity says which nodes form each face (a row per face, padded to the maximum vertex count).

docs.title: Wireframe - the bare mesh¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the mesh edges with no data colouring. It is the fastest way to see the grid's shape, resolution, and how faces are distributed before looking at any results.

docs.title: Mapping the real results¶
docs.text: Surface elevation and the velocity components are time-varying (time_values lists the stored times, in seconds since the start). We pick a mid-simulation step with isel and map the tide level and the U-velocity.

docs.title: From mesh to GIS¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset is not a dead end - it converts into the vector and raster types the rest of a GIS workflow expects. Everything below is reached through pyramids; this package only supplies the file-format driver that built the mesh.

docs.title: Faces as vector polygons¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe(variable_name=...) turns every face into a polygon row carrying that variable's value - a standard GeoPandas GeoDataFrame you can join, filter, or export.

docs.title: Dissolving into zones¶
docs.text: polygonize(variable) merges neighbouring faces that share a value into larger polygons - handy for turning a noisy per-cell field into clean zones. It needs a single value per face, which is exactly what our working dataset holds.

docs.title: Sampling at points¶
docs.text: sample(variable, x, y) reads the value of the face that contains each query point. Here we probe the first few face centroids, so each query lands squarely inside a face.

docs.title: The mesh outline as one polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() returns a single shapely polygon tracing the mesh's outer boundary - the model's wetted footprint, useful as a clip mask or extent reference.

docs.title: Cropping to a sub-region¶
docs.text: subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) returns a new, smaller MeshDataset holding only the faces inside the box - the same object type, so every operation above still applies. We derive a box from the mesh envelope so it works on any extent.

docs.title: Connectivity as a sparse graph¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() exposes face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix, and connected_components() labels each face by which connected piece of the mesh it belongs to - the entry points for graph algorithms over the grid.

docs.title: Circumcenters - not applicable here¶
docs.text: circumcenters() is only defined for purely triangular meshes. This grid contains quad (or mixed-polygon) faces, so the call would raise ValueError. We note it and skip rather than force it.

docs.title: Self-contained rasterisation¶
docs.text: to_dataset(variable, cell_size=...) samples the mesh onto a regular raster grid and returns a pyramids Dataset. Unlike rasterize_like / regrid - which need an existing reference grid and are therefore skipped here - this is self-contained: you only choose a cell size.

docs.title: Reprojection - skipped¶
docs.text: to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to project from. MIKE stores the projection in a side file, so ds.crs comes back None here even though the coordinates are UTM metres. With no source CRS, reprojection is undefined, so we skip it; assign a CRS first if your coordinates are georeferenced.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: DFSU brings DHI's flexible mesh into the same MeshDataset shape as every other driver. Its mixed triangle/quad topology rules out circumcenters(), but surface elevation and velocity map cleanly once a timestep is selected, and the vector/raster conversions behave identically. pyramids-mesh owns only the DFSU parsing; the analysis lives in pyramids.
