docs.title: Reading ESMF unstructured meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
ESMF (Earth System Modeling Framework) defines a NetCDF unstructured-mesh convention used to describe grids for regridding between Earth-system model components. The file lists node coordinates (nodeCoords) and an element–node connectivity table (elementConn with numElementConn nodes per element), tagged gridType = unstructured.

This notebook reads the canonical ESMF example grid — ne4np4-esmf.nc, 866 nodes / 936 elements — into a pyramids MeshDataset and tours the supported operations. Coordinates are in degrees of longitude/latitude.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the example file¶
docs.text:
This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so examples/data/ is two levels up. The ESMF sample is esmf/ne4np4-esmf.nc, the canonical ESMF example mesh (classic CDF-1 NetCDF, readable by the vendored GDAL).

Paths inside a notebook are always written relative to the notebook itself, and pyramids' read_file accepts a pathlib.Path directly — we pass the Path, never str(path).

docs.title: 4. Read the mesh¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver="esmf") dispatches the file to the esmf driver, which parses it and hands back a MeshDataset — the same pyramids type produced from a native UGRID NetCDF file. We name the driver explicitly here because several formats share the .nc suffix; read_file can auto-detect, but being explicit is unambiguous.

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes summary properties describing the whole mesh: n_node / n_face (size), crs / epsg (georeferencing, if the format recorded any), bounds (spatial extent), and data_variable_names (any attached fields).

docs.title: 6. Coordinates are in DEGREES¶
docs.text: ESMF node coordinates are in degrees of longitude/latitude (not radians like MPAS/ICON). The ranges confirm it: longitude up to ≈ 354, latitude the full −90 → 90.

docs.title: 7. The underlying Mesh2d topology¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d holding the raw topology. The arrays you reach for most often are node_x/node_y (node coordinates), face_node_connectivity.data — the (n_face, k) table listing the node indices of each face — and face_areas (one value per face).

docs.title: 8. The wireframe¶
docs.text: The simplest visualization needs no data — just draw the cell edges. plot_outline() renders the mesh skeleton through cleopatra; it is the fastest sanity check that a file read in correctly.

docs.title: 9. A data map: per-cell area¶
docs.text: An ESMF mesh file carries no field values, so we synthesise one. We compute each cell's area from the geometry and attach it as a face-located variable with with_variable(...), which returns a new dataset (the original ds is left untouched). Colouring by it produces the generic pyramids data-map that any per-cell field (depth, velocity, …) would use.

docs.title: 10. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because the mesh is a pyramids object, the pyramids GIS layer applies directly — none of these methods live in pyramids-mesh. We tour a few.

docs.title: Faces as a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every face into a polygon row of a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the standard vector structure for export to shapefile/GeoPackage or for spatial joins.

docs.title: Bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the elements into the mesh outline. For this global ne4np4 mesh it returns a shapely Polygon.

docs.title: Circumcenters — not applicable¶
docs.text: circumcenters() is defined only for triangular meshes. ESMF is a quadrilateral mesh, so calling it raises ValueError: circumcenters is only defined for triangular meshes. We show the guard rather than force it — a circumcenter has no unique definition for a polygon with more than three sides.

docs.title: Boundary edges and face adjacency¶
docs.text: exterior_edges() returns the indices of the edges that lie on the mesh boundary (each interior edge is shared by two faces; a boundary edge by one). sparse_adjacency() returns the face–face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix — the graph a flow solver walks.

docs.title: Connected components¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by which connected piece of the adjacency graph it belongs to. The number of distinct labels tells you whether the mesh is one contiguous surface or several disjoint pieces.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)) returns a new MeshDataset holding only the faces inside the box — the mesh equivalent of a spatial window. (subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) does the same with positional arguments.) We crop to one quadrant of the extent and plot the result.

docs.title: Writing the mesh back out¶
docs.text: to_file(path, driver=...) serialises the mesh through any write-capable driver. We round-trip to Stanford PLY (driver="ply"), which stores arbitrary polygon faces, into a temp file and read it back to confirm the topology survived.

docs.title: 11. What we cannot do here, and why¶
docs.text:
Two pyramids operations are unavailable on this mesh, and the reasons are instructive:

  • to_crs(epsg) — skipped. This grid carries no CRS (crs is None above), so pyramids refuses to reproject: to_crs raises "Cannot reproject: source CRS is unknown." You would first assign the known CRS (these global grids are geographic lon/lat on a sphere) and only then reproject.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) — out of scope here. Burning the mesh onto a raster grid or remapping between meshes is a genuine pyramids capability, but it needs a target raster/mesh and a resampling choice to be meaningful — a topic for a dedicated regridding tutorial, not this format tour.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• The esmf driver reads an ESMF unstructured-mesh NetCDF into a pyramids MeshDataset from its nodeCoords + elementConn tables.
  • ne4np4 elements are quadrilaterals (k = 4) with coordinates in degrees — so circumcenters is skipped (triangles only).
  • The mesh is grid-only (no CRS, no fields); we attached a geometric face_area for a data map.
  • The full pyramids GIS layer applies — to_geodataframe, bounding_polygon, adjacency, components, crop, PLY round-trip — while to_crs is skipped (no CRS recorded).

docs.title: Reading ESRI TIN datasets with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
An ESRI TIN (Triangulated Irregular Network) is not a single file but a directory of Arc/Info .adf binaries — tnod.adf, tnxy.adf, tedg.adf, tnz.adf and friends — that together store a triangulated surface: node coordinates, edges, and per-node elevation. It is ArcGIS's native vector-surface format.

pyramids-mesh registers an esri_tin driver. Because the dataset is a folder, we point the reader at the directory, not a file. This notebook reads a small dem TIN and walks read → explore → plot → GIS.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the data¶
docs.text: The notebook lives in docs/examples/, so examples/data/ is two levels up. We pass a pathlib.Path to the reader (never a string).

docs.title: 4. Read the mesh¶
docs.text: We name the driver explicitly: driver="esri_tin". read_file dispatches to it and returns a MeshDataset wrapping a Mesh2d.

docs.title: 5. Explore the mesh¶
docs.text: Node/face counts, CRS, the attached data variables and the bounding box. This TIN has 281 nodes and 528 triangles. The coordinates are small local planar values and the format declares no EPSG code here, so crs/epsg are None.

docs.title: 6. Mesh geometry¶
docs.text: The Mesh2d exposes node coordinates, the (n_face, k) face-node connectivity, per-face areas and centroids — all plain numpy arrays.

docs.title: 7. Wireframe¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare element skeleton — the fastest way to read the mesh's shape and where it is refined.

docs.title: 8. Data map¶
docs.text: node_z is the per-node surface elevation. Note in summary() the min is a huge negative number (-3.4e38): that is GDAL's nodata fill on nodes outside the valid hull, which we mask before plotting (next section).

docs.title: 9. GIS operations for free¶
docs.text: The mesh is a pyramids object, so the vector/GIS layer applies unchanged. Convert to a GeoDataFrame — one polygon per element. to_geodataframe() returns just the geometry column, so we attach each element's area and let geopandas colour by it; smaller cells reveal where the mesh is refined.

docs.title: 10. What needs more than a mesh¶
docs.text:
• to_crs(epsg) needs a source CRS. this TIN declares no EPSG code, so ds.epsg is None, so to_crs is skipped.
  • rasterize_like / regrid need a reference grid to sample onto; with only the mesh in hand there is no target, so they are out of scope for this read-only tour.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver="esri_tin") turns the native esri_tin grid into a first-class pyramids mesh. Exploration, plotting, GeoDataFrame conversion, bounding polygons, connectivity analysis, spatial subsetting and export are all inherited from pyramids — pyramids-mesh only added the reader.

docs.title: Reading an Exodus II finite-element mesh¶
docs.text:
Exodus II is the Sandia/Trilinos finite-element model and results format, stored as NetCDF (CDF-2) underneath. It is the interchange format for libMesh, MOOSE, Sierra and much of the Trilinos ecosystem. pyramids-mesh reads the mesh into a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset.

This sample is a libMesh test mesh, nontrivial_node_num_map.exo — a small, clean planar QUAD4 mesh (4 cells, 9 nodes) with a non-trivial node-numbering map, which the reader resolves transparently (LGPL-licensed data). The directory also holds geom_2.exo, a 3-D TETRA mesh.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the example data¶
docs.text: This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so the repo-root examples/data/ folder is two levels up. Paths inside a notebook are written relative to the notebook itself. The critical rule for read_file is to pass a pathlib.Path, never str(...). We read exodus/nontrivial_node_num_map.exo.

docs.title: 4. Quickstart: read the file¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver=...) parses the file and returns a MeshDataset — the same type pyramids produces from a NetCDF UGRID file. We name the "exodus" driver explicitly; passing the Path object (not a string) is the supported call.

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes summary properties: n_node / n_face (mesh size), crs / epsg (georeferencing if the format recorded any), bounds (the (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) extent), and data_variable_names (attached field variables).

docs.title: 6. Face-degree distribution¶
docs.text: ds.mesh.face_node_connectivity.data is the (n_face, k) table of node indices per face, where k is the widest polygon. Cells with fewer nodes than k are padded with -1 (fill). Counting the non-negative entries per row gives each face's number of nodes — its degree.

docs.title: 7. The underlying geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d holding the raw arrays: node_x / node_y (coordinates), the connectivity table, face_areas (one area per cell) and face_centroids (shape (2, n_face)). Everything geometric is derived from the connectivity plus the node coordinates.

docs.title: 8. Wireframe: plot_outline()¶
docs.text: The simplest view needs no data — just the mesh edges. plot_outline() draws the wireframe through cleopatra and embeds it inline. This is the fastest sanity check that a file read in correctly.

docs.title: 9. A data map: attach and colour a field¶
docs.text: To draw a filled map we need a value per cell. These mesh files carry geometry only, so we compute one — each cell's area — and attach it with with_variable(..., location="face"), which returns a new dataset (the original ds is untouched). Then plot colours the mesh by it.

docs.title: The statistical summary¶
docs.text: With a field attached, .summary() reports per-variable statistics (count, min, max, mean, std). On the bare ds it is an empty frame; on d2 it has a real row.

docs.title: 10. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because the mesh is now a first-class pyramids object, the pyramids GIS layer applies directly — pyramids-mesh itself adds none of this. The next cells each run one operation and interpret it.

docs.title: Faces as a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every face into a polygon row of a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the standard vector structure for export to shapefile/GeoPackage or spatial joins.

docs.title: Bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the cells into a single shapely polygon of the meshed footprint — the gateway to the shapely/geopandas ecosystem for clipping and spatial joins.

docs.title: Circumcenters — explain and skip¶
docs.text: circumcenters() is only defined for triangular meshes. This mesh is not all-triangle, so the call raises ValueError; we catch it rather than crash. (Use cell centroids instead for such grids.)

docs.title: Exterior edges¶
docs.text: exterior_edges() returns the node indices of the mesh boundary — the edges that belong to exactly one cell. Its length is a quick measure of how much perimeter the mesh has.

docs.title: Cell adjacency and connected components¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() is the cell-to-cell adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix (nnz = twice the number of shared internal edges). connected_components() labels which cells are mutually reachable through that adjacency.

docs.title: Subset by a bounding box¶
docs.text: subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) keeps only the cells inside a window (note the four positional coordinates, not a tuple). We take the centred 60% window and plot the result — a clean clip that returns a new MeshDataset. (crop(bbox=...) does the same thing with a tuple argument.)

docs.title: Export: NetCDF round-trip¶
docs.text: to_file(path) writes a NetCDF UGRID file — the canonical pyramids on-disk form that any UGRID reader can load back.

docs.title: 11. CRS-dependent operations — explain and skip¶
docs.text:
This format records no CRS (crs / epsg were None above), so coordinate-aware steps have nothing to work from:

  • to_crs(...) — a reprojection needs a source CRS; with None there is nothing to reproject from, so we skip it. In practice you would first assign the CRS you know the model used.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) — these burn the mesh onto, or resample it to, a target raster grid. That is the job of the pyramids-gis raster layer (you supply a target Dataset); it is out of scope for a format-reader tutorial, so we only name it here.

docs.title: 12. Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• Exodus II .exo = Trilinos/libMesh FE interchange format (NetCDF underneath), read into a MeshDataset.
  • This sample is a clean planar QUAD4 patch (degree 4, no -1 fill) with a non-trivial node map resolved on read; geom_2.exo in the same folder is the 3-D TETRA counterpart.
  • Quads, so circumcenters() is skipped; no CRS, so reprojection/rasterisation are skipped.
  • Explore, plot and the full GIS toolbox apply to the FE mesh as to any MeshDataset.

docs.title: Reading a FEFLOW finite-element groundwater mesh¶
docs.text:
FEFLOW (DHI) is a finite-element simulator for subsurface flow and transport. Its classic ASCII .fem file carries the finite-element mesh: a node list plus element connectivity (here 2-D triangular elements). pyramids-mesh reads that mesh into a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset, so a FEFLOW model domain becomes an ordinary pyramids object.

This sample is disv_nodes.fem from the MODFLOW 6 examples (the ATES heat-storage case) — a CLASS v7.501 mesh of 2496 nodes and 4842 triangles (public-domain data).

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the example data¶
docs.text: This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so the repo-root examples/data/ folder is two levels up. Paths inside a notebook are written relative to the notebook itself. The critical rule for read_file is to pass a pathlib.Path, never str(...). We read feflow/disv_nodes.fem.

docs.title: 4. Quickstart: read the file¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver=...) parses the file and returns a MeshDataset — the same type pyramids produces from a NetCDF UGRID file. We name the "feflow" driver explicitly; passing the Path object (not a string) is the supported call.

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes summary properties: n_node / n_face (mesh size), crs / epsg (georeferencing if the format recorded any), bounds (the (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) extent), and data_variable_names (attached field variables).

docs.title: 6. Face-degree distribution¶
docs.text: ds.mesh.face_node_connectivity.data is the (n_face, k) table of node indices per face, where k is the widest polygon. Cells with fewer nodes than k are padded with -1 (fill). Counting the non-negative entries per row gives each face's number of nodes — its degree.

docs.title: 7. The underlying geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d holding the raw arrays: node_x / node_y (coordinates), the connectivity table, face_areas (one area per cell) and face_centroids (shape (2, n_face)). Everything geometric is derived from the connectivity plus the node coordinates.

docs.title: 8. Wireframe: plot_outline()¶
docs.text: The simplest view needs no data — just the mesh edges. plot_outline() draws the wireframe through cleopatra and embeds it inline. This is the fastest sanity check that a file read in correctly.

docs.title: 9. A data map: attach and colour a field¶
docs.text: To draw a filled map we need a value per cell. These mesh files carry geometry only, so we compute one — each cell's area — and attach it with with_variable(..., location="face"), which returns a new dataset (the original ds is untouched). Then plot colours the mesh by it.

docs.title: The statistical summary¶
docs.text: With a field attached, .summary() reports per-variable statistics (count, min, max, mean, std). On the bare ds it is an empty frame; on d2 it has a real row.

docs.title: 10. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because the mesh is now a first-class pyramids object, the pyramids GIS layer applies directly — pyramids-mesh itself adds none of this. The next cells each run one operation and interpret it.

docs.title: Faces as a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every face into a polygon row of a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the standard vector structure for export to shapefile/GeoPackage or spatial joins.

docs.title: Bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the cells into a single shapely polygon of the meshed footprint — the gateway to the shapely/geopandas ecosystem for clipping and spatial joins.

docs.title: Circumcenters¶
docs.text: circumcenters() returns an (n_face, 2) array of per-cell circumcenters — the points a finite-volume scheme places unknowns at. Defined only for triangular meshes, which this is.

docs.title: Exterior edges¶
docs.text: exterior_edges() returns the node indices of the mesh boundary — the edges that belong to exactly one cell. Its length is a quick measure of how much perimeter the mesh has.

docs.title: Cell adjacency and connected components¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() is the cell-to-cell adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix (nnz = twice the number of shared internal edges). connected_components() labels which cells are mutually reachable through that adjacency.

docs.title: Subset by a bounding box¶
docs.text: subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) keeps only the cells inside a window (note the four positional coordinates, not a tuple). We take the centred 60% window and plot the result — a clean clip that returns a new MeshDataset. (crop(bbox=...) does the same thing with a tuple argument.)

docs.title: Export: NetCDF round-trip¶
docs.text: to_file(path) writes a NetCDF UGRID file — the canonical pyramids on-disk form that any UGRID reader can load back.

docs.title: 11. CRS-dependent operations — explain and skip¶
docs.text:
This format records no CRS (crs / epsg were None above), so coordinate-aware steps have nothing to work from:

  • to_crs(...) — a reprojection needs a source CRS; with None there is nothing to reproject from, so we skip it. In practice you would first assign the CRS you know the model used.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) — these burn the mesh onto, or resample it to, a target raster grid. That is the job of the pyramids-gis raster layer (you supply a target Dataset); it is out of scope for a format-reader tutorial, so we only name it here.

docs.title: 12. Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• FEFLOW .fem = finite-element groundwater mesh: node list + element connectivity, read into a MeshDataset.
  • This ATES sample is a dense all-triangular 2-D mesh (2496 nodes, 4842 faces; degree 3, no -1 fill).
  • Triangular, so circumcenters() works; no CRS, so reprojection/rasterisation are skipped.
  • The full explore / plot / GIS toolbox applies unchanged once the mesh is a pyramids object.

docs.title: Reading FLAC3D grids with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
FLAC3D (Itasca) is a geomechanics solver; its .f3grid ASCII format lists G gridpoints and Z zones (hexahedra, wedges, ...). pyramids-mesh provides a driver that parses the grid into a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset; the mesh analysis lives upstream in pyramids.

Our sample is flac3d/flac3d_mesh_ex.f3grid (meshio test data, MIT): 160 gridpoints and 108 zones, whose faces carry up to 8 nodes. It is geometry only, crs=None, and — unusually — it splits into several disconnected zone groups, which we highlight below.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the sample file¶
docs.text:
This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so the repo-root examples/data/ folder is two levels up. Paths are written relative to the notebook itself. We will read the FLAC3D grid flac3d/flac3d_mesh_ex.f3grid.

Pass a pathlib.Path, never a string. read_file keys its driver dispatch off Path objects; a bare str is not accepted.

docs.title: 4. Read it in one line¶
docs.text: Each Z line names a zone type and its gridpoint indices. We name the driver explicitly with driver="flac3d" and hand read_file the Path. What comes back is a MeshDataset — the same mesh container every other pyramids mesh uses.

docs.title: 5. Inspect the dataset¶
docs.text: A handful of attributes describe the mesh at a glance: the node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, the list of data variables, and the planar bounding box (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax). FLAC3D grids use engineering coordinates, so crs and epsg are None.

docs.title: A statistical summary of the data variables¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a small pandas table — one row per data variable with count, min, max, mean and std. The grid exposes a node_z variable (gridpoint elevation), summarised in one row.

docs.title: 6. The underlying geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d. Its node coordinates live in node_x / node_y, and its face-to-node table is face_node_connectivity.data — an (n_face, k) integer array where row i lists the node indices of face i. The connectivity is (n_face, 8) — these are 8-node hexahedral zones projected to the plane, so some rows pad or repeat indices. That non-planarity is why a few polygon-based operations below are skipped.

docs.title: 7. Draw the mesh outline (wireframe)¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the cell edges with no fill — the quickest way to see the topology we just read. The figure embeds in the notebook on its own.

docs.title: 8. A filled map: projected cell area¶
docs.text:
These are engineering meshes with no CRS and (usually) no field data, so there is nothing physical to colour by out of the box. A useful derived quantity is the projected 2-D area of each cell, available as mesh.face_areas. We attach it as a face variable with with_variable(...) and let plot(...) draw a filled colour map.

The 2-D projection of a 3-D hex grid gives a patchwork of overlapping cell footprints, so the area map reads as blocky rather than smooth — a faithful picture of a volume grid flattened onto a plane.

docs.title: 9. The pyramids GIS toolbox applies¶
docs.text: The payoff of turning a solver file into a pyramids object is that the whole GIS toolbox now works on it, even though this is a FEM/CFD mesh. Below we exercise several operations and interpret each result.

docs.title: Export to a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every cell into a shapely polygon inside a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the bridge to the entire vector-GIS ecosystem. Because the mesh has crs=None, the frame is unprojected (model units, not metres/degrees).

docs.title: Connected components (the headline for this mesh)¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by which face-adjacent group it belongs to. Most meshes are a single blob, but this one splits into several disjoint zone groups — exactly what the colour map below reveals.

docs.title: Boundary edges¶
docs.text: exterior_edges() returns the indices of edges that belong to exactly one cell — the mesh boundary. A closed surface (a watertight solid) has none; an open sheet exposes its rim. We report the count.

docs.title: Face-adjacency as a sparse matrix¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() returns the (n_face, n_face) SciPy CSR matrix of which cells share an edge — the connectivity graph solvers assemble their stencils from. We only report its shape and non-zero count.

docs.title: Crop to a sub-region¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)) keeps only the cells inside a window — the mesh equivalent of a spatial subset. Here we take the left half of the domain and re-draw it.

docs.title: What we skip, and why¶
docs.text:
Because this mesh carries crs=None, the reprojection and raster-bridge operations do not apply:

  • to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to reproject from — skipped (there is no datum to interpret the model's bare coordinates).
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) burn a mesh onto, or resample it against, a georeferenced raster grid — skipped here, as there is no spatial reference to align to.

These are first-class pyramids operations; they simply require a georeferenced mesh, which an engineering solver file is not.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
We read a FLAC3D .f3grid of 160 gridpoints / 108 zones, mapped projected cell area, and — the headline — found 6 disconnected zone groups via connected_components. We also ran vector export, boundary edges, the adjacency graph, and a crop. bounding_polygon and circumcenters are skipped: the projected 8-node faces are non-planar/self-overlapping (GEOS rejects their union) and circumcentres are triangle-only.

The pattern is always the same: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver=...) turns a solver file into a pyramids object, and from there the full GIS toolbox applies — even for a geometry-only, CRS-less engineering mesh. pyramids-mesh contributes only the driver; every mesh operation lives upstream in pyramids.

docs.title: FLO-2D results with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text: FLO-2D is a floodplain model on a square-cell grid. pyramids-mesh reads the pair TIMDEP.HDF5 (time series of FLOW DEPTH, velocity, water-surface elevation) together with DEPFP.OUT (per-element maximum floodplain depth), building one MeshDataset of square faces. This example is a 240-element flume (4 x 60 cells).

docs.title: What is on disk¶
docs.text: The driver uses both files together: the HDF5 time series and the OUT summary.

docs.title: Quickstart read¶
docs.text: Pass driver="flo2d" and point at the HDF5; the driver picks up the companion DEPFP.OUT from the same folder.

docs.title: Explore the dataset¶
docs.text:
A MeshDataset wraps a UGRID-style unstructured mesh plus any data variables that ride on it. The scalar properties below describe the grid at a glance: how many nodes and faces it has, its coordinate reference system, and its spatial extent.

The grid is a tall, narrow flume: 4 columns by 60 rows of 50-unit square cells.

docs.title: Data variables¶
docs.text: data_variable_names lists every field attached to the mesh. These are the real model results - water levels, depths, velocities - that make a results file worth reading.

docs.title: The Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: the topology the data variables are defined on. Nodes carry the (x, y) coordinates; face_node_connectivity says which nodes form each face (a row per face, padded to the maximum vertex count).

docs.title: Wireframe - the bare mesh¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the mesh edges with no data colouring. It is the fastest way to see the grid's shape, resolution, and how faces are distributed before looking at any results.

docs.title: Mapping the real results¶
docs.text: FLOW DEPTH carries a long time axis, so we select the final stored step (the fully developed flood) with isel. max_floodplain_depth is already a per-element peak and needs no timestep - it maps directly.

docs.title: From mesh to GIS¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset is not a dead end - it converts into the vector and raster types the rest of a GIS workflow expects. Everything below is reached through pyramids; this package only supplies the file-format driver that built the mesh.

docs.title: Faces as vector polygons¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe(variable_name=...) turns every face into a polygon row carrying that variable's value - a standard GeoPandas GeoDataFrame you can join, filter, or export.

docs.title: Dissolving into zones¶
docs.text: polygonize(variable) merges neighbouring faces that share a value into larger polygons - handy for turning a noisy per-cell field into clean zones. It needs a single value per face, which is exactly what our working dataset holds.

docs.title: Sampling at points¶
docs.text: sample(variable, x, y) reads the value of the face that contains each query point. Here we probe the first few face centroids, so each query lands squarely inside a face.

docs.title: The mesh outline as one polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() returns a single shapely polygon tracing the mesh's outer boundary - the model's wetted footprint, useful as a clip mask or extent reference.

docs.title: Cropping to a sub-region¶
docs.text: subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) returns a new, smaller MeshDataset holding only the faces inside the box - the same object type, so every operation above still applies. We derive a box from the mesh envelope so it works on any extent.

docs.title: Connectivity as a sparse graph¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() exposes face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix, and connected_components() labels each face by which connected piece of the mesh it belongs to - the entry points for graph algorithms over the grid.

docs.title: Circumcenters - not applicable here¶
docs.text: circumcenters() is only defined for purely triangular meshes. This grid contains quad (or mixed-polygon) faces, so the call would raise ValueError. We note it and skip rather than force it.

docs.title: Self-contained rasterisation¶
docs.text: to_dataset(variable, cell_size=...) samples the mesh onto a regular raster grid and returns a pyramids Dataset. Unlike rasterize_like / regrid — which need an existing reference grid — this is self-contained: pick a cell size and pyramids builds the grid. We derive the cell size from the average face area so the raster has sub-face resolution regardless of the mesh density.

docs.title: Reprojection - skipped¶
docs.text: to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to project from. FLO-2D stores grid coordinates without a CRS, so ds.crs is None. With no source CRS, reprojection is undefined, so we skip it; assign a CRS first if your coordinates are georeferenced.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: FLO-2D shows a driver stitching two files into one mesh: the HDF5 time series and the OUT summary land on the same square-cell grid. Select the last timestep for the evolving FLOW DEPTH, map the static max_floodplain_depth directly, then reuse the vector and raster conversions. File assembly is the driver's job; the mesh operations are pyramids'.

docs.title: Reading FVCOM native grids with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
FVCOM (Finite-Volume Community Ocean Model) stores its unstructured grid as a trio of ASCII files. The core one is *_grd.dat — a header with node and cell counts, then the triangle connectivity, then the node coordinates; *_dep.dat carries per-node bathymetry.

pyramids-mesh registers an fvcom driver that parses the grid into a MeshDataset/Mesh2d. This notebook reads the chn estuarine example and walks read → explore → plot → GIS.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the data¶
docs.text: The notebook lives in docs/examples/, so examples/data/ is two levels up. We pass a pathlib.Path to the reader (never a string).

docs.title: 4. Read the mesh¶
docs.text: We name the driver explicitly: driver="fvcom". read_file dispatches to it and returns a MeshDataset wrapping a Mesh2d.

docs.title: 5. Explore the mesh¶
docs.text: Node/face counts, CRS, the attached data variables and the bounding box. This grid has 871 nodes and 1620 triangles, in projected metres (bounds run 0–800000 m east, 0–400000 m north); the format declares no EPSG code, so crs/epsg are None.

docs.title: 6. Mesh geometry¶
docs.text: The Mesh2d exposes node coordinates, the (n_face, k) face-node connectivity, per-face areas and centroids — all plain numpy arrays.

docs.title: 7. Wireframe¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare element skeleton — the fastest way to read the mesh's shape and where it is refined.

docs.title: 8. Data map¶
docs.text: node_z is the per-node bathymetry read from the companion depth file. The summary() above shows it spanning 10–100 m.

docs.title: 9. GIS operations for free¶
docs.text: The mesh is a pyramids object, so the vector/GIS layer applies unchanged. Convert to a GeoDataFrame — one polygon per element. to_geodataframe() returns just the geometry column, so we attach each element's area and let geopandas colour by it; smaller cells reveal where the mesh is refined.

docs.title: 10. What needs more than a mesh¶
docs.text:
• to_crs(epsg) needs a source CRS. the FVCOM grid is in projected metres but declares no EPSG code, so ds.epsg is None, so to_crs is skipped.
  • rasterize_like / regrid need a reference grid to sample onto; with only the mesh in hand there is no target, so they are out of scope for this read-only tour.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver="fvcom") turns the native fvcom grid into a first-class pyramids mesh. Exploration, plotting, GeoDataFrame conversion, bounding polygons, connectivity analysis, spatial subsetting and export are all inherited from pyramids — pyramids-mesh only added the reader.

docs.title: Reading GEOS cubed-sphere grids with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
GEOS (the NASA Goddard Earth Observing System model) runs on a cubed-sphere grid: the sphere is tiled by six square panels, each a C x C array of cells. The native NetCDF-4 file stores the panel corners as corner_lons/corner_lats of shape (6, C+1, C+1); the driver reconstructs the quadrilateral connectivity by index arithmetic across the six panels.

This notebook reads the C12 test grid (6 × 12 × 12 = 864 cells) into a pyramids MeshDataset. A nice property falls out later: because the panels are stitched only within each face, connected_components recovers the six cube panels. Coordinates are in degrees.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the example file¶
docs.text:
This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so examples/data/ is two levels up. The GEOS sample is geos/test-c12.native.nc4, a C12 cubed-sphere grid (NetCDF-4) from the UXarray test suite.

Paths inside a notebook are always written relative to the notebook itself, and pyramids' read_file accepts a pathlib.Path directly — we pass the Path, never str(path).

docs.title: 4. Read the mesh¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver="geos") dispatches the file to the geos driver, which parses it and hands back a MeshDataset — the same pyramids type produced from a native UGRID NetCDF file. We name the driver explicitly here because several formats share the .nc4 suffix; read_file can auto-detect, but being explicit is unambiguous.

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes summary properties describing the whole mesh: n_node / n_face (size), crs / epsg (georeferencing, if the format recorded any), bounds (spatial extent), and data_variable_names (any attached fields).

docs.title: 6. Coordinates are in DEGREES¶
docs.text: GEOS corner coordinates are stored in degrees of longitude/latitude. The ranges confirm it: longitude roughly 0 → 358, latitude the full −90 → 90.

docs.title: 7. The underlying Mesh2d topology¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d holding the raw topology. The arrays you reach for most often are node_x/node_y (node coordinates), face_node_connectivity.data — the (n_face, k) table listing the node indices of each face — and face_areas (one value per face).

docs.title: 8. The wireframe¶
docs.text: The simplest visualization needs no data — just draw the cell edges. plot_outline() renders the mesh skeleton through cleopatra; it is the fastest sanity check that a file read in correctly.

docs.title: 9. A data map: per-cell area¶
docs.text: A native GEOS grid file carries no field values, so we synthesise one. We compute each cell's area from the geometry and attach it as a face-located variable with with_variable(...), which returns a new dataset (the original ds is left untouched). Colouring by it produces the generic pyramids data-map that any per-cell field (depth, velocity, …) would use.

docs.title: 10. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because the mesh is a pyramids object, the pyramids GIS layer applies directly — none of these methods live in pyramids-mesh. We tour a few.

docs.title: Faces as a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every face into a polygon row of a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the standard vector structure for export to shapefile/GeoPackage or for spatial joins.

docs.title: Bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the cells into the outer boundary. For the unrolled global C12 grid it returns a shapely Polygon.

docs.title: Circumcenters — not applicable¶
docs.text: circumcenters() is defined only for triangular meshes. GEOS is a quadrilateral mesh, so calling it raises ValueError: circumcenters is only defined for triangular meshes. We show the guard rather than force it — a circumcenter has no unique definition for a polygon with more than three sides.

docs.title: Boundary edges and face adjacency¶
docs.text: exterior_edges() returns the indices of the edges that lie on the mesh boundary (each interior edge is shared by two faces; a boundary edge by one). sparse_adjacency() returns the face–face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix — the graph a flow solver walks.

docs.title: Connected components¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by which connected piece of the adjacency graph it belongs to. The number of distinct labels tells you whether the mesh is one contiguous surface or several disjoint pieces.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)) returns a new MeshDataset holding only the faces inside the box — the mesh equivalent of a spatial window. (subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) does the same with positional arguments.) We crop to one quadrant of the extent and plot the result.

docs.title: Writing the mesh back out¶
docs.text: to_file(path, driver=...) serialises the mesh through any write-capable driver. We round-trip to Stanford PLY (driver="ply"), which stores arbitrary polygon faces, into a temp file and read it back to confirm the topology survived.

docs.title: 11. What we cannot do here, and why¶
docs.text:
Two pyramids operations are unavailable on this mesh, and the reasons are instructive:

  • to_crs(epsg) — skipped. This grid carries no CRS (crs is None above), so pyramids refuses to reproject: to_crs raises "Cannot reproject: source CRS is unknown." You would first assign the known CRS (these global grids are geographic lon/lat on a sphere) and only then reproject.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) — out of scope here. Burning the mesh onto a raster grid or remapping between meshes is a genuine pyramids capability, but it needs a target raster/mesh and a resampling choice to be meaningful — a topic for a dedicated regridding tutorial, not this format tour.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• The geos driver reconstructs a GEOS cubed-sphere grid from its (6, C+1, C+1) corner arrays into a pyramids MeshDataset.
  • C12 cells are quadrilaterals (k = 4, 864 = 6×12×12) with coordinates in degrees — so circumcenters is skipped (triangles only).
  • connected_components recovers the six cube panels (144 cells each) — a direct readout of the cubed-sphere topology.
  • The rest of the pyramids GIS layer applies — to_geodataframe, bounding_polygon, adjacency, crop, PLY round-trip — while to_crs is skipped (no CRS recorded).

docs.title: Reading the GiD / Iber mesh format with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text: The GiD ASCII mesh format (CIMNE's format, and the one the Iber 2D hydraulic model exports, since Iber is built on GiD) stores a mesh as MESH ... dimension D ElemType T Nnode N, then a Coordinates block of node_id x y [z] and an Elements block of el_id n1..nN [mat], all 1-based with # comments. It shares the .msh extension with Gmsh, so the driver must be given explicitly. The sample is a 2D triangular mesh of a tube cross-section. pyramids-mesh reads it into a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid object.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Read the file in one call¶
docs.text: Because .msh is shared with Gmsh, we must pass driver="gid" — suffix sniffing alone could not tell the two apart. The sample uses ElemType Triangle with Nnode 6 (quadratic triangles); the reader keeps the three corner nodes of each element, giving linear triangles.

docs.title: 4. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A handful of attributes describe what we loaded: node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, the names of any data variables, and the spatial extent.

docs.title: 5. A statistical summary of the fields¶
docs.text: summary() returns a pandas frame with one row per data variable (count, min, max, mean, std).

docs.title: 6. The underlying Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d object carrying the raw topology: node coordinates, the face-node connectivity table of shape (n_face, k) (row i lists the node indices of cell i), per-face areas, and cell centroids.

docs.title: 7. The mesh outline (wireframe)¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare cell edges, with no field attached — the quickest look at the raw geometry this driver produced.

docs.title: 8. A data map: attach and colour by cell area¶
docs.text: These surface formats carry no field data, so there is nothing to colour by yet. We attach a derived cell_area variable at the face location and plot it — turning the geometry into a proper choropleth.

docs.title: 9. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is a first-class pyramids object, a whole GIS toolkit comes along. First, every face as a row in a GeoDataFrame.

docs.title: Bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() returns a single shapely geometry: the dissolved outer footprint of the mesh.

docs.title: Derived topology and connectivity¶
docs.text: A few more derived quantities are a method call away. circumcenters() is defined only for triangular meshes; exterior_edges() indexes the boundary edges; connected_components() labels disjoint pieces; sparse_adjacency() is the face-to-face graph as a sparse matrix.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) keeps the faces that fall within (or touch) a rectangle, returning a new MeshDataset. Here we crop to the left portion of the extent and redraw it.

docs.title: Round-tripping through the driver table¶
docs.text: to_file(..., driver=...) writes the mesh back out in any writable driver (here the solver-neutral 2DM).

docs.title: 10. What we skip here, and why¶
docs.text:
• to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to reproject from, but GiD files carry no georeferencing (crs=None), so there is nothing to reproject. Attach a CRS first if the coordinates are known to be in a specific projection.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) require a reference grid (a raster or target mesh) to sample onto; with only this standalone mesh in hand there is no target, so they are out of scope for this tutorial.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: A GiD/Iber .msh reads into a MeshDataset only when the driver is named explicitly (the extension collides with Gmsh). Its quadratic triangles are reduced to their corner nodes, and because it is a bare 2D hydraulic mesh it carries no data variables at all — the clearest contrast with the elevation-bearing surface formats. Once read, it joins the same pyramids pipeline: derive a field, map it, export it, crop it.

docs.title: Reading Gmsh meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
Gmsh is the widely used open-source finite-element mesh generator; its .msh format is a common interchange for unstructured meshes feeding FE/FV solvers. Unlike the global climate grids in this series, a Gmsh mesh is a planar engineering mesh — raw (x, y) coordinates in model units, with no georeferencing. The gmsh driver supports both the legacy v2.2 ASCII and the v4.1 formats.

This notebook reads insulated-2.2.msh — a genuine Gmsh mesh of 111 triangles over 67 nodes — into a pyramids MeshDataset and tours the operations it supports. Being triangular, it supports circumcenters.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the example file¶
docs.text:
This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so examples/data/ is two levels up. The Gmsh sample is gmsh/insulated-2.2.msh, a 111-triangle mesh (Gmsh 2.2 ASCII) from the meshio test suite.

Paths inside a notebook are always written relative to the notebook itself, and pyramids' read_file accepts a pathlib.Path directly — we pass the Path, never str(path).

docs.title: 4. Read the mesh¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver="gmsh") dispatches the file to the gmsh driver, which parses it and hands back a MeshDataset — the same pyramids type produced from a native UGRID NetCDF file. We name the driver explicitly here because several formats share the .msh suffix; read_file can auto-detect, but being explicit is unambiguous.

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes summary properties describing the whole mesh: n_node / n_face (size), crs / epsg (georeferencing, if the format recorded any), bounds (spatial extent), and data_variable_names (any attached fields).

docs.title: 6. Coordinates are planar model units¶
docs.text: Gmsh coordinates are not geographic — they are raw (x, y) in whatever units the .geo model used (here roughly ±3). There is no radian-vs-degree question: the values are small planar numbers centred near the origin, and no CRS is attached.

docs.title: 7. The underlying Mesh2d topology¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d holding the raw topology. The arrays you reach for most often are node_x/node_y (node coordinates), face_node_connectivity.data — the (n_face, k) table listing the node indices of each face — and face_areas (one value per face).

docs.title: 8. The wireframe¶
docs.text: The simplest visualization needs no data — just draw the cell edges. plot_outline() renders the mesh skeleton through cleopatra; it is the fastest sanity check that a file read in correctly.

docs.title: 9. A data map: per-cell area¶
docs.text: This mesh carries no field values, so we synthesise one. We compute each cell's area from the geometry and attach it as a face-located variable with with_variable(...), which returns a new dataset (the original ds is left untouched). Colouring by it produces the generic pyramids data-map that any per-cell field (depth, velocity, …) would use.

docs.title: 10. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because the mesh is a pyramids object, the pyramids GIS layer applies directly — none of these methods live in pyramids-mesh. We tour a few.

docs.title: Faces as a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every face into a polygon row of a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the standard vector structure for export to shapefile/GeoPackage or for spatial joins.

docs.title: Bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the triangles into the mesh's outer boundary — a shapely Polygon. Because this is a small planar mesh with no periodic seam, it dissolves cleanly.

docs.title: Circumcenters¶
docs.text: circumcenters() returns an (n_face, 2) array of per-cell circumcenter coordinates — the points a finite-volume scheme places unknowns at. It is defined only for triangular meshes, and the Gmsh mesh is triangular, so it works here.

docs.title: Boundary edges and face adjacency¶
docs.text: exterior_edges() returns the indices of the edges that lie on the mesh boundary (each interior edge is shared by two faces; a boundary edge by one). sparse_adjacency() returns the face–face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix — the graph a flow solver walks.

docs.title: Connected components¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by which connected piece of the adjacency graph it belongs to. The number of distinct labels tells you whether the mesh is one contiguous surface or several disjoint pieces.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)) returns a new MeshDataset holding only the faces inside the box — the mesh equivalent of a spatial window. (subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) does the same with positional arguments.) We crop to one quadrant of the extent and plot the result.

docs.title: Writing the mesh back out¶
docs.text: to_file(path, driver=...) serialises the mesh through any write-capable driver. We round-trip to Stanford PLY (driver="ply"), which stores arbitrary polygon faces, into a temp file and read it back to confirm the topology survived.

docs.title: 11. What we cannot do here, and why¶
docs.text:
Two pyramids operations are unavailable on this mesh:

  • to_crs(epsg) — skipped. The Gmsh mesh has no CRS (crs is None), so pyramids refuses to reproject: to_crs raises "Cannot reproject: source CRS is unknown." Gmsh coordinates are planar model units; you would assign the real-world CRS (if the model's georeferencing is known) before reprojecting.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) — out of scope here. These are genuine pyramids capabilities but need a target raster/mesh and a resampling choice to be meaningful — a topic for a dedicated tutorial, not this format tour.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• The gmsh driver reads a .msh finite-element mesh (v2.2 or v4.1) into a pyramids MeshDataset.
  • Gmsh cells are triangles (k = 3) with planar, non-georeferenced coordinates (no CRS, no radian/degree question); being triangular, circumcenters() works.
  • The file is geometry-only; we attached a geometric face_area for a data map.
  • The pyramids GIS layer applies in full — to_geodataframe, bounding_polygon, circumcenters, adjacency, components, crop, PLY round-trip — while to_crs is skipped because no CRS is recorded.

docs.title: HEC-RAS 2D results with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
HEC-RAS (USACE) writes its 2D results into an HDF5 plan file (*.pNN.hdf). pyramids-mesh reads the 2D flow area's cell mesh and its summary results - Maximum Water Surface and Minimum Water Surface. This is the classic Bald Eagle Creek dam-break example.

The file holds two 2D flow areas; the driver reads the first (BaldEagleCr, 3,359 cells) and warns that selecting the other is not yet wired up.

docs.title: Quickstart read¶
docs.text: Pass driver="hecras". The UserWarning about the second flow area is expected - only BaldEagleCr is loaded.

docs.title: Explore the dataset¶
docs.text:
A MeshDataset wraps a UGRID-style unstructured mesh plus any data variables that ride on it. The scalar properties below describe the grid at a glance: how many nodes and faces it has, its coordinate reference system, and its spatial extent.

The cells are a mixed-polygon mesh (3 to 7 vertices per face) in projected feet.

docs.title: Data variables¶
docs.text: data_variable_names lists every field attached to the mesh. These are the real model results - water levels, depths, velocities - that make a results file worth reading.

docs.title: The Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: the topology the data variables are defined on. Nodes carry the (x, y) coordinates; face_node_connectivity says which nodes form each face (a row per face, padded to the maximum vertex count).

docs.title: Wireframe - the bare mesh¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the mesh edges with no data colouring. It is the fastest way to see the grid's shape, resolution, and how faces are distributed before looking at any results.

docs.title: Mapping the real results¶
docs.text: Both variables are per-cell summaries, so they map directly with no timestep to pick. The maximum water surface traces the dam-break flood extent; the minimum shows the lowest stage each cell saw.

docs.title: Mapping the real results¶
docs.text: These files carry genuine model output, so the point of the package is to see it. ds.plot(variable, cmap=..., colorbar=..., title=...) colours each face by its value and routes through cleopatra (reached via pyramids) for the actual rendering.

docs.title: From mesh to GIS¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset is not a dead end - it converts into the vector and raster types the rest of a GIS workflow expects. Everything below is reached through pyramids; this package only supplies the file-format driver that built the mesh.

docs.title: Faces as vector polygons¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe(variable_name=...) turns every face into a polygon row carrying that variable's value - a standard GeoPandas GeoDataFrame you can join, filter, or export.

docs.title: Dissolving into zones¶
docs.text: polygonize(variable) merges neighbouring faces that share a value into larger polygons - handy for turning a noisy per-cell field into clean zones. It needs a single value per face, which is exactly what our working dataset holds.

docs.title: Sampling at points¶
docs.text: sample(variable, x, y) reads the value of the face that contains each query point. Here we probe the first few face centroids, so each query lands squarely inside a face.

docs.title: The mesh outline as one polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() returns a single shapely polygon tracing the mesh's outer boundary - the model's wetted footprint, useful as a clip mask or extent reference.

docs.title: Cropping to a sub-region¶
docs.text: subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) returns a new, smaller MeshDataset holding only the faces inside the box - the same object type, so every operation above still applies. We derive a box from the mesh envelope so it works on any extent.

docs.title: Connectivity as a sparse graph¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() exposes face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix, and connected_components() labels each face by which connected piece of the mesh it belongs to - the entry points for graph algorithms over the grid.

docs.title: Circumcenters - not applicable here¶
docs.text: circumcenters() is only defined for purely triangular meshes. This grid contains quad (or mixed-polygon) faces, so the call would raise ValueError. We note it and skip rather than force it.

docs.title: Self-contained rasterisation¶
docs.text: to_dataset(variable, cell_size=...) samples the mesh onto a regular raster grid and returns a pyramids Dataset. Unlike rasterize_like / regrid - which need an existing reference grid and are therefore skipped here - this is self-contained: you only choose a cell size.

docs.title: Reprojection - skipped¶
docs.text: to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to project from. This HEC-RAS plan file reports no CRS to the driver, so ds.crs is None (the coordinates are projected feet). With no source CRS, reprojection is undefined, so we skip it; assign a CRS first if your coordinates are georeferenced.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: HEC-RAS stores a mixed-polygon 2D mesh with summary water-surface results in an HDF5 plan file. pyramids-mesh reads the first flow area (reporting the unread one), exposes Maximum/Minimum Water Surface as plain per-cell fields that map directly, and lets the whole pyramids GIS toolkit operate on the result. The driver parses the plan file; the mesh analysis belongs to pyramids.

docs.title: Reading ICON icosahedral grids with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
ICON (ICOsahedral Nonhydrostatic) is the joint DWD/MPI weather and climate model. Its horizontal grid is built by recursively bisecting the edges of an icosahedron and projecting onto the sphere, yielding a fully triangular global mesh. Cell and vertex positions (clon/clat, vlon/vlat) are stored in radians, and connectivity (vertex_of_cell) is 1-based.

This notebook reads a small subset of an R02B04 grid — the first 320 triangular cells and their 197 vertices, reindexed for the fixture — into a pyramids MeshDataset. Being triangular, ICON supports the full geometric toolbox including circumcenters.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the example file¶
docs.text:
This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so examples/data/ is two levels up. The ICON sample is icon/icon_grid_R02B04_subset.nc, a 320-cell triangular patch carved from the DWD/MPI R02B04 global grid.

Paths inside a notebook are always written relative to the notebook itself, and pyramids' read_file accepts a pathlib.Path directly — we pass the Path, never str(path).

docs.title: 4. Read the mesh¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver="icon") dispatches the file to the icon driver, which parses it and hands back a MeshDataset — the same pyramids type produced from a native UGRID NetCDF file. We name the driver explicitly here because several formats share the .nc suffix; read_file can auto-detect, but being explicit is unambiguous.

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes summary properties describing the whole mesh: n_node / n_face (size), crs / epsg (georeferencing, if the format recorded any), bounds (spatial extent), and data_variable_names (any attached fields).

docs.title: 6. Coordinates are in RADIANS¶
docs.text: ICON stores longitude/latitude in radians. Because this is a subset (a small patch, not the whole globe) the longitude span is narrow, but the latitude reaches right up to the north pole at π/2 ≈ 1.571 — the clinching evidence of radians rather than degrees.

docs.title: 7. The underlying Mesh2d topology¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d holding the raw topology. The arrays you reach for most often are node_x/node_y (node coordinates), face_node_connectivity.data — the (n_face, k) table listing the node indices of each face — and face_areas (one value per face).

docs.title: 8. The wireframe¶
docs.text: The simplest visualization needs no data — just draw the cell edges. plot_outline() renders the mesh skeleton through cleopatra; it is the fastest sanity check that a file read in correctly.

docs.title: 9. A data map: per-cell area¶
docs.text: This file already carries a native cell_area, but to keep the series uniform we also compute the geometric area from the triangle coordinates and attach it as face_area. We compute each cell's area from the geometry and attach it as a face-located variable with with_variable(...), which returns a new dataset (the original ds is left untouched). Colouring by it produces the generic pyramids data-map that any per-cell field (depth, velocity, …) would use.

docs.title: 10. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because the mesh is a pyramids object, the pyramids GIS layer applies directly — none of these methods live in pyramids-mesh. We tour a few.

docs.title: Faces as a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every face into a polygon row of a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the standard vector structure for export to shapefile/GeoPackage or for spatial joins.

docs.title: Bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the triangles into the outline of the patch. Because this ICON subset is a small, non-seam-crossing region it dissolves cleanly (returning a shapely MultiPolygon when the patch is in more than one piece).

docs.title: Circumcenters¶
docs.text: circumcenters() returns an (n_face, 2) array of per-cell circumcenter coordinates — the points a finite-volume scheme places unknowns at. It is defined only for triangular meshes, and ICON is triangular, so it works here.

docs.title: Boundary edges and face adjacency¶
docs.text: exterior_edges() returns the indices of the edges that lie on the mesh boundary (each interior edge is shared by two faces; a boundary edge by one). sparse_adjacency() returns the face–face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix — the graph a flow solver walks.

docs.title: Connected components¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by which connected piece of the adjacency graph it belongs to. The number of distinct labels tells you whether the mesh is one contiguous surface or several disjoint pieces.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)) returns a new MeshDataset holding only the faces inside the box — the mesh equivalent of a spatial window. (subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) does the same with positional arguments.) We crop to one quadrant of the extent and plot the result.

docs.title: Writing the mesh back out¶
docs.text: to_file(path, driver=...) serialises the mesh through any write-capable driver. We round-trip to Stanford PLY (driver="ply"), which stores arbitrary polygon faces, into a temp file and read it back to confirm the topology survived.

docs.title: 11. What we cannot do here, and why¶
docs.text:
Two pyramids operations are unavailable on this mesh, and the reasons are instructive:

  • to_crs(epsg) — skipped. This grid carries no CRS (crs is None above), so pyramids refuses to reproject: to_crs raises "Cannot reproject: source CRS is unknown." You would first assign the known CRS (these global grids are geographic lon/lat on a sphere) and only then reproject.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) — out of scope here. Burning the mesh onto a raster grid or remapping between meshes is a genuine pyramids capability, but it needs a target raster/mesh and a resampling choice to be meaningful — a topic for a dedicated regridding tutorial, not this format tour.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• The icon driver reads an ICON icosahedral grid into a pyramids MeshDataset, handling the 1-based vertex_of_cell connectivity.
  • ICON cells are triangles (k = 3) with coordinates in radians (latitude → π/2 at the pole); being triangular, circumcenters() works.
  • The file ships a native cell_area; we also attached a geometric one for a uniform data map.
  • connected_components found 2 disjoint patches in this subset — a real structural fact, not an artifact — while to_crs is skipped (no CRS) with an explained reason.

docs.title: Reading Kratos Multiphysics .mdpa meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
Kratos Multiphysics is an open-source multiphysics FEM framework; its .mdpa ASCII format declares Nodes and Elements blocks (Element3D4N, etc.). pyramids-mesh registers a driver that parses .mdpa into a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset.

Our sample is kratos/small_cube.mdpa (KratosMultiphysics/Kratos, BSD-3-Clause): 8 nodes and 6 faces — the six faces of a unit cube. It is geometry only, crs=None.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the sample file¶
docs.text:
This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so the repo-root examples/data/ folder is two levels up. Paths are written relative to the notebook itself. We will read the Kratos model-part file kratos/small_cube.mdpa.

Pass a pathlib.Path, never a string. read_file keys its driver dispatch off Path objects; a bare str is not accepted.

docs.title: 4. Read it in one line¶
docs.text: Begin Nodes / Begin Elements blocks delimit the coordinates and connectivity. We name the driver explicitly with driver="kratos" and hand read_file the Path. What comes back is a MeshDataset — the same mesh container every other pyramids mesh uses.

docs.title: 5. Inspect the dataset¶
docs.text: A handful of attributes describe the mesh at a glance: the node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, the list of data variables, and the planar bounding box (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax). Kratos model parts are defined in simulation units, so crs and epsg are None.

docs.title: A statistical summary of the data variables¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a small pandas table — one row per data variable with count, min, max, mean and std. The mesh carries a node_z variable (the nodes' third coordinate), so the table has one row.

docs.title: 6. The underlying geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d. Its node coordinates live in node_x / node_y, and its face-to-node table is face_node_connectivity.data — an (n_face, k) integer array where row i lists the node indices of face i. Four node indices per row: the six quadrilateral faces of the cube.

docs.title: 7. Draw the mesh outline (wireframe)¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the cell edges with no fill — the quickest way to see the topology we just read. The figure embeds in the notebook on its own.

docs.title: 8. A filled map: projected cell area¶
docs.text:
These are engineering meshes with no CRS and (usually) no field data, so there is nothing physical to colour by out of the box. A useful derived quantity is the projected 2-D area of each cell, available as mesh.face_areas. We attach it as a face variable with with_variable(...) and let plot(...) draw a filled colour map.

As with any closed box, projecting to X-Y collapses the side faces and keeps the top/bottom, so the area map shows a mix of zero and unit-area cells — expected for a flattened solid.

docs.title: 9. The pyramids GIS toolbox applies¶
docs.text: The payoff of turning a solver file into a pyramids object is that the whole GIS toolbox now works on it, even though this is a FEM/CFD mesh. Below we exercise several operations and interpret each result.

docs.title: Export to a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every cell into a shapely polygon inside a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the bridge to the entire vector-GIS ecosystem. Because the mesh has crs=None, the frame is unprojected (model units, not metres/degrees).

docs.title: Dissolve to a bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() unions all cells into the single outer footprint of the mesh — useful as a clip mask or domain outline. We overlay it (red) on the grey cell edges.

docs.title: Boundary edges¶
docs.text: exterior_edges() returns the indices of edges that belong to exactly one cell — the mesh boundary. A closed surface (a watertight solid) has none; an open sheet exposes its rim. We report the count.

docs.title: Connected components¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by its face-adjacent group. A single label across all faces means the mesh is one topologically connected piece.

docs.title: Crop to a sub-region¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)) keeps only the cells inside a window — the mesh equivalent of a spatial subset. Here we take the left half of the domain and re-draw it.

docs.title: Write it back out (round-trip)¶
docs.text: A driver reads and writes. to_file(..., driver="2dm") re-encodes the mesh in a different format — here SMS 2DM — proving the in-memory object is format-agnostic. We write to a temp file and report its size.

docs.title: What we skip, and why¶
docs.text:
Because this mesh carries crs=None, the reprojection and raster-bridge operations do not apply:

  • to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to reproject from — skipped (there is no datum to interpret the model's bare coordinates).
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) burn a mesh onto, or resample it against, a georeferenced raster grid — skipped here, as there is no spatial reference to align to.

These are first-class pyramids operations; they simply require a georeferenced mesh, which an engineering solver file is not.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
We read a Kratos .mdpa cube (8 nodes, 6 quad faces), mapped projected cell area, and ran GIS on it: vector export, outer footprint, boundary edges, connected components, a crop, and a 2DM round-trip. Circumcenters are skipped (quads, not triangles).

The pattern is always the same: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver=...) turns a solver file into a pyramids object, and from there the full GIS toolbox applies — even for a geometry-only, CRS-less engineering mesh. pyramids-mesh contributes only the driver; every mesh operation lives upstream in pyramids.

docs.title: Reading MED (Salome / code_aster) meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
The MED format is the native mesh-and-field container of the Salome platform and the code_aster finite-element solver. Like CGNS it is built on HDF5.

driver="med" forces the HDF5 reader. A MED mesh lives in the model's own coordinate frame — no projection — so pyramids-mesh reports crs=None.

We use cylinder.med, a small mixed triangle+quadrilateral surface written by Salome 9.2.2.

Source: meshio test suite (tests/meshes/med/), MIT.

docs.title: Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: Quickstart: read the MED file¶
docs.text:
driver="med" forces the HDF5 path, the same multidimensional driver used for CGNS.

The one rule that matters: pass a pathlib.Path, never a str — read_file keys its driver dispatch off the Path type. MeshDataset.read_file(...) returns a MeshDataset, the in-memory UGRID container every pyramids-mesh driver produces.

docs.title: What did we get?¶
docs.text: A few scalar properties describe the dataset at a glance: node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, and the planar bounding box.

docs.title: Summary table¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a pandas DataFrame with per-variable statistics (count / min / max / mean / std). It reports node_z here.

docs.title: The mesh geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: node coordinates plus the face-node connectivity, an (n_face, k) integer table where k is the largest number of nodes any face has. Triangles fill 3 columns; quadrilaterals fill 4 (a shorter face pads the spare slot). face_areas and face_centroids are derived on demand.

docs.title: Wireframe¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare mesh edges — the quickest way to eyeball the topology and the element shapes before colouring anything.

docs.title: A derived field: cell area¶
docs.text: These engineering files usually carry no cell data we can colour by — so we compute one ourselves. with_variable attaches face_areas as a face-located variable, giving a non-destructive copy of the dataset that plot can render as a filled colour map.

docs.title: Treating the mesh as GIS¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is just nodes and polygonal faces, pyramids exposes the usual vector-GIS toolbox on it. First, every face as a GeoPandas polygon:

docs.title: The outer boundary¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the faces into the outline of the cross-section.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) returns a new MeshDataset with only the faces inside the box — handy for zooming into a region of a large mesh. We crop to the left half of the extent.

docs.title: The face-adjacency graph¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() gives the face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix, and connected_components() labels which faces are reachable from which. plt.spy shows the sparsity pattern — the fingerprint of how the faces are wired together.

docs.title: Why circumcenters are skipped here¶
docs.text: This is a mixed tri/quad mesh. circumcenters() is defined only when every face is a triangle, so it raises ValueError — we catch it rather than forcing it.

docs.title: Converting out: other drivers¶
docs.text: to_file(path, driver=...) re-serialises the mesh through any writer in the driver table — here a round-trip to the 2dm format in a temp file.

docs.title: What we cannot do here: reprojection & regridding¶
docs.text: to_crs(epsg) reprojects between coordinate systems — but this mesh has crs=None (model-local coordinates, no datum), so there is nothing to reproject from; we skip it. Likewise rasterize_like(...) and regrid(...) map a data field onto a raster or another mesh; with no meaningful field and no georeferencing on an engineering mesh they are out of scope. These belong on georeferenced hydrodynamic meshes, not FEM/CFD decks.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• driver="med" reads the Salome/code_aster HDF5 MED container.
  • A mixed triangle+quad surface, geometry-only (crs=None), with a node_z variable.
  • Polygon export, bounding polygon, cropping and the adjacency graph all work; triangle-only circumcenters is refused on a mixed mesh.
  • No CRS → no reprojection or regridding.
