docs.title: Reading INRIA Medit meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
The Medit .mesh format is the ASCII mesh format of INRIA's Medit viewer and the Gmsh/FreeFem++ toolchain — a plain list of Vertices, Triangles, Tetrahedra and so on. pyramids-mesh registers a driver whose only job is to parse that file and hand back a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset; it does no GIS and no analysis of its own.

Our sample is medit/cube86.mesh (meshio test data, MIT): the triangulated surface of the unit cube — 39 vertices and 72 triangular faces. Like all FEM meshes it is geometry only, crs=None.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the sample file¶
docs.text:
This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so the repo-root examples/data/ folder is two levels up. Paths are written relative to the notebook itself. We will read the Medit surface mesh medit/cube86.mesh.

Pass a pathlib.Path, never a string. read_file keys its driver dispatch off Path objects; a bare str is not accepted.

docs.title: 4. Read it in one line¶
docs.text: Medit stores vertices and element blocks as whitespace-separated ASCII. We name the driver explicitly with driver="medit" and hand read_file the Path. What comes back is a MeshDataset — the same mesh container every other pyramids mesh uses.

docs.title: 5. Inspect the dataset¶
docs.text: A handful of attributes describe the mesh at a glance: the node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, the list of data variables, and the planar bounding box (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax). A Medit file carries no spatial reference, so crs and epsg are both None — the coordinates are raw model units.

docs.title: A statistical summary of the data variables¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a small pandas table — one row per data variable with count, min, max, mean and std. This mesh carries a node_z variable (the third coordinate of its 3-D vertices, kept as node data), so the table has one row.

docs.title: 6. The underlying geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d. Its node coordinates live in node_x / node_y, and its face-to-node table is face_node_connectivity.data — an (n_face, k) integer array where row i lists the node indices of face i. Each row holds 3 node indices — these are triangles. The reader may warn that it re-wound some clockwise faces to counter-clockwise; that is the normaliser making the winding consistent, not an error.

docs.title: 7. Draw the mesh outline (wireframe)¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the cell edges with no fill — the quickest way to see the topology we just read. The figure embeds in the notebook on its own.

docs.title: 8. A filled map: projected cell area¶
docs.text:
These are engineering meshes with no CRS and (usually) no field data, so there is nothing physical to colour by out of the box. A useful derived quantity is the projected 2-D area of each cell, available as mesh.face_areas. We attach it as a face variable with with_variable(...) and let plot(...) draw a filled colour map.

The cube's faces lie on its six sides, so projecting to the X-Y plane collapses four of the six sides to zero area and keeps two — expect a mix of zero and non-zero cells. That is a true consequence of flattening a 3-D surface, worth calling out rather than hiding.

docs.title: 9. The pyramids GIS toolbox applies¶
docs.text: The payoff of turning a solver file into a pyramids object is that the whole GIS toolbox now works on it, even though this is a FEM/CFD mesh. Below we exercise several operations and interpret each result.

docs.title: Export to a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every cell into a shapely polygon inside a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the bridge to the entire vector-GIS ecosystem. Because the mesh has crs=None, the frame is unprojected (model units, not metres/degrees).

docs.title: Dissolve to a bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() unions all cells into the single outer footprint of the mesh — useful as a clip mask or domain outline. We overlay it (red) on the grey cell edges.

docs.title: Triangle circumcenters¶
docs.text: circumcenters() returns the (n_face, 2) circumcentre of each triangular cell — the dual-mesh vertices that finite-volume schemes use. (It is defined only for triangle meshes; the quad/polyhedral notebooks skip it.)

docs.title: Connected components¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by its face-adjacent group. A single label across all faces means the mesh is one topologically connected piece.

docs.title: Crop to a sub-region¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)) keeps only the cells inside a window — the mesh equivalent of a spatial subset. Here we take the left half of the domain and re-draw it.

docs.title: Write it back out (round-trip)¶
docs.text: A driver reads and writes. to_file(..., driver="2dm") re-encodes the mesh in a different format — here SMS 2DM — proving the in-memory object is format-agnostic. We write to a temp file and report its size.

docs.title: What we skip, and why¶
docs.text:
Because this mesh carries crs=None, the reprojection and raster-bridge operations do not apply:

  • to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to reproject from — skipped (there is no datum to interpret the model's bare coordinates).
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) burn a mesh onto, or resample it against, a georeferenced raster grid — skipped here, as there is no spatial reference to align to.

These are first-class pyramids operations; they simply require a georeferenced mesh, which an engineering solver file is not.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
We read a .mesh surface, inspected its 39 nodes / 72 triangles, mapped projected cell area, and then treated it as GIS: vector export, outer footprint, triangle circumcenters, a crop, and a 2DM round-trip.

The pattern is always the same: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver=...) turns a solver file into a pyramids object, and from there the full GIS toolbox applies — even for a geometry-only, CRS-less engineering mesh. pyramids-mesh contributes only the driver; every mesh operation lives upstream in pyramids.

docs.title: Reading DHI MIKE 21 flexible meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
MIKE 21 FM (Flexible Mesh) is DHI's shallow-water modelling engine; its mesh generator writes a plain-text .mesh file. The header line records the number of nodes, a node-id base, and a projection string (here LONG/LAT); then come the node coordinates and the element table. pyramids-mesh registers a mike21 driver that parses it into a MeshDataset.

We read the bundled minimal.mesh (a unit square, two triangles) and exercise the toolkit.

docs.title: 3. Locate the data¶
docs.text: minimal.mesh sits in examples/data/, two levels up from this notebook; we address it with a Path.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 4. Read the file¶
docs.text: The LONG/LAT token in the header is MIKE's projection field; this minimal fixture leaves the CRS unset, which is why crs/epsg read None below. A driver's only job is to parse the file and hand back a MeshDataset. We pass a pathlib.Path (never a str) and name the driver explicitly:

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes the mesh size, its coordinate reference system, and the data variables carried alongside the topology. None for crs/epsg simply means the source file declared no projection — the geometry is still valid, it is just unlocated in world space.

docs.title: Per-variable summary¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a pandas DataFrame — one row per data variable with count, min, max, mean and standard deviation. A std of 0 means that variable is uniform across the mesh.

docs.title: Global attributes¶
docs.text: Each driver stamps provenance into global_attributes so you can trace a dataset back to the format it came from after it has been converted.

docs.title: 6. The Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: node coordinates plus the face-node connectivity table. face_node_connectivity.data has shape (n_face, k) — row i lists the node indices of face i (padded for mixed element types). We also derive per-face areas and centroids from that topology.

docs.title: 7. Wireframe — the mesh skeleton¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare mesh: every face edge, no data coloring. This is the fastest way to eyeball connectivity, element shapes and the overall extent.

docs.title: 8. A data map¶
docs.text: The .mesh format carries a node z value (bed level). On this flat fixture node_z is all zeros, so instead of a featureless map we derive a face variable — the cell area — with with_variable(...) and map that. This is the idiom for painting any computed quantity onto a mesh.

docs.title: 9. GIS operations¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is a first-class pyramids object, the full geospatial toolkit works on it directly — no conversion step. Below are several operations, each visualised or interpreted. (Operations that need a source CRS, such as to_crs, are skipped here: this sample declares none.)

docs.title: 9a. Faces as polygons — to_geodataframe()¶
docs.text: Every face becomes a shapely polygon in a GeoPandas GeoDataFrame, ready for a spatial join, an overlay, or export to any OGR vector format.

docs.title: 9b. Outer boundary — bounding_polygon() and exterior_edges()¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the faces into a single shapely polygon tracing the mesh outline, and exterior_edges() returns the indices of the mesh edges that lie on that boundary — their count is the boundary's edge length.

docs.title: 9c. Connectivity — connected_components()¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by the connected sub-mesh it belongs to. One unique label means the mesh is a single watertight piece; more than one would reveal detached islands. We attach the labels as a face variable and map them.

docs.title: 9d. Face adjacency — sparse_adjacency()¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() returns the face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix (two faces are adjacent when they share an edge). Its sparsity pattern is the dual graph a solver walks; nnz counts the directed face-neighbour links.

docs.title: 9e. Triangle circumcenters — circumcenters()¶
docs.text: For a triangular mesh, circumcenters() returns the circumcircle centre of each face (shape (2, n_face)) — the sample points of the dual Voronoi mesh that finite-volume schemes use. We scatter them over the wireframe.

docs.title: 9f. Clip to a sub-region — crop()¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) keeps the faces inside a bounding box; we clip to the lower-left quarter.

docs.title: 9g. Round-trip through UGRID NetCDF — to_file()¶
docs.text: to_file(..., driver='ugrid') writes the mesh to the CF/UGRID NetCDF convention — the lossless lingua franca every tool in the stack reads back. We write it, re-read it, and confirm the topology survived.

docs.title: 10. Takeaway¶
docs.text: The mike21 driver reads a DHI .mesh into a MeshDataset. Node bathymetry comes through as a variable, any computed field can be attached with with_variable, and the mesh then flows into the same vector/clip/round-trip toolkit as every other format.

docs.title: Reading a MODFLOW 6 DISU unstructured grid¶
docs.text:
MODFLOW 6 DISU (discretisation by unstructured cells) is the most general MODFLOW grid: cells are listed with an explicit connectivity table (the IA/JA adjacency) and need not tile the plane regularly at all. It is used for nested grids, cross-sections and vertically staggered columns where neither rows/columns nor a clean vertex tessellation fit.

pyramids-mesh parses the ASCII DISU file into a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset. This sample is the MODFLOW 6 test model test016_Keating_disu_250 — a vertical cross-section of 324 quadrilateral cells (public-domain USGS data).

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the example data¶
docs.text: This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so the repo-root examples/data/ folder is two levels up. Paths inside a notebook are written relative to the notebook itself. The critical rule for read_file is to pass a pathlib.Path, never str(...). We read modflow6_disu/keating.disu.

docs.title: 4. Quickstart: read the file¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver=...) parses the file and returns a MeshDataset — the same type pyramids produces from a NetCDF UGRID file. We name the "modflow6_disu" driver explicitly; passing the Path object (not a string) is the supported call.

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes summary properties: n_node / n_face (mesh size), crs / epsg (georeferencing if the format recorded any), bounds (the (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) extent), and data_variable_names (attached field variables).

docs.title: 6. Face-degree distribution¶
docs.text: ds.mesh.face_node_connectivity.data is the (n_face, k) table of node indices per face, where k is the widest polygon. Cells with fewer nodes than k are padded with -1 (fill). Counting the non-negative entries per row gives each face's number of nodes — its degree.

docs.title: 7. The underlying geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d holding the raw arrays: node_x / node_y (coordinates), the connectivity table, face_areas (one area per cell) and face_centroids (shape (2, n_face)). Everything geometric is derived from the connectivity plus the node coordinates.

docs.title: 8. Wireframe: plot_outline()¶
docs.text: The simplest view needs no data — just the mesh edges. plot_outline() draws the wireframe through cleopatra and embeds it inline. This is the fastest sanity check that a file read in correctly.

docs.title: 9. A data map: attach and colour a field¶
docs.text: To draw a filled map we need a value per cell. These mesh files carry geometry only, so we compute one — each cell's area — and attach it with with_variable(..., location="face"), which returns a new dataset (the original ds is untouched). Then plot colours the mesh by it.

docs.title: The statistical summary¶
docs.text: With a field attached, .summary() reports per-variable statistics (count, min, max, mean, std). On the bare ds it is an empty frame; on d2 it has a real row.

docs.title: 10. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because the mesh is now a first-class pyramids object, the pyramids GIS layer applies directly — pyramids-mesh itself adds none of this. The next cells each run one operation and interpret it.

docs.title: Faces as a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every face into a polygon row of a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the standard vector structure for export to shapefile/GeoPackage or spatial joins.

docs.title: Bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the cells into a single shapely polygon of the meshed footprint — the gateway to the shapely/geopandas ecosystem for clipping and spatial joins.

docs.title: Circumcenters — explain and skip¶
docs.text: circumcenters() is only defined for triangular meshes. This mesh is not all-triangle, so the call raises ValueError; we catch it rather than crash. (Use cell centroids instead for such grids.)

docs.title: Exterior edges¶
docs.text: exterior_edges() returns the node indices of the mesh boundary — the edges that belong to exactly one cell. Its length is a quick measure of how much perimeter the mesh has.

docs.title: Cell adjacency and connected components¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() is the cell-to-cell adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix (nnz = twice the number of shared internal edges). connected_components() labels which cells are mutually reachable through that adjacency.

docs.title: Subset by a bounding box¶
docs.text: subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) keeps only the cells inside a window (note the four positional coordinates, not a tuple). We take the centred 60% window and plot the result — a clean clip that returns a new MeshDataset. (crop(bbox=...) does the same thing with a tuple argument.)

docs.title: Export: NetCDF round-trip¶
docs.text: to_file(path) writes a NetCDF UGRID file — the canonical pyramids on-disk form that any UGRID reader can load back.

docs.title: 11. CRS-dependent operations — explain and skip¶
docs.text:
This format records no CRS (crs / epsg were None above), so coordinate-aware steps have nothing to work from:

  • to_crs(...) — a reprojection needs a source CRS; with None there is nothing to reproject from, so we skip it. In practice you would first assign the CRS you know the model used.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) — these burn the mesh onto, or resample it to, a target raster grid. That is the job of the pyramids-gis raster layer (you supply a target Dataset); it is out of scope for a format-reader tutorial, so we only name it here.

docs.title: 12. Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• DISU = fully unstructured: cells connected by an explicit table, read straight into a MeshDataset.
  • The Keating sample is a thin vertical cross-section of all-quad cells (degree 4, no -1 fill).
  • Quads, not triangles, so circumcenters() is skipped; the sparse edge topology yields empty exterior_edges() and many connected components — both genuine traits of unstructured grids.
  • Explore, plot and the box-subset still work exactly as for any MeshDataset.

docs.title: Reading MPAS meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
MPAS (Model for Prediction Across Scales) is the unstructured global modelling framework behind NCAR/DOE atmosphere and ocean models. Its horizontal grid is a Spherical Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation — a mostly-hexagonal mesh of cells on the sphere, with exactly twelve pentagons where the icosahedral seed points sit (the same reason a football has twelve pentagons). Coordinates are stored in radians of longitude/latitude, and the connectivity is 1-based with 0 as a fill value.

This notebook reads one real MPAS file — the quasi-uniform QU.1920km test mesh (162 cells) — into a pyramids MeshDataset, explores it, visualises it, and runs the pyramids GIS operations it supports. The mpas driver handles the 1-based/fill-value reindexing for you.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the example file¶
docs.text:
This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so the repo-root examples/data/ folder is two levels up. The MPAS sample is mpas/mesh.QU.1920km.151026.nc, a 162-cell quasi-uniform mesh from the UXarray test suite.

Paths inside a notebook are always written relative to the notebook itself, and pyramids' read_file accepts a pathlib.Path directly — we pass the Path, never str(path).

docs.title: 4. Read the mesh¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver="mpas") dispatches the file to the mpas driver, which parses it and hands back a MeshDataset — the same pyramids type produced from a native UGRID NetCDF file. We name the driver explicitly here because several formats share the .nc suffix; read_file can auto-detect, but being explicit is unambiguous.

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes summary properties describing the whole mesh: n_node / n_face (size), crs / epsg (georeferencing, if the format recorded any), bounds (spatial extent), and data_variable_names (any attached fields).

docs.title: 6. Coordinates are in RADIANS¶
docs.text: MPAS stores node longitude/latitude in radians, not degrees. The tell is the range: longitude runs 0 → 2π ≈ 6.283, latitude −π/2 → π/2 ≈ ±1.571. We print the extents against those constants to prove it.

docs.title: 7. The underlying Mesh2d topology¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d holding the raw topology. The arrays you reach for most often are node_x/node_y (node coordinates), face_node_connectivity.data — the (n_face, k) table listing the node indices of each face — and face_areas (one value per face).

docs.title: 8. The wireframe¶
docs.text: The simplest visualization needs no data — just draw the cell edges. plot_outline() renders the mesh skeleton through cleopatra; it is the fastest sanity check that a file read in correctly.

docs.title: 9. A data map: per-cell area¶
docs.text: This grid-only file carries no field values, so we synthesise one. We compute each cell's area from the geometry and attach it as a face-located variable with with_variable(...), which returns a new dataset (the original ds is left untouched). Colouring by it produces the generic pyramids data-map that any per-cell field (depth, velocity, …) would use.

docs.title: 10. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because the mesh is a pyramids object, the pyramids GIS layer applies directly — none of these methods live in pyramids-mesh. We tour a few.

docs.title: Faces as a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every face into a polygon row of a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the standard vector structure for export to shapefile/GeoPackage or for spatial joins.

docs.title: Bounding polygon — skipped on this mesh¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the faces into the mesh's outer boundary. On this MPAS grid it raises a GEOS TopologyException (side location conflict): the cells wrap across the longitude seam at 2π/0, and dissolving them in the flat radian plane produces a self-touching boundary GEOS cannot resolve. This is a real artifact of plotting a periodic global grid on a flat plane, so we skip it and use the rectangular bounds instead.

docs.title: Circumcenters — not applicable¶
docs.text: circumcenters() is defined only for triangular meshes. MPAS is a hexagon-dominant mesh, so calling it raises ValueError: circumcenters is only defined for triangular meshes. We show the guard rather than force it — a circumcenter has no unique definition for a polygon with more than three sides.

docs.title: Boundary edges and face adjacency¶
docs.text: exterior_edges() returns the indices of the edges that lie on the mesh boundary (each interior edge is shared by two faces; a boundary edge by one). sparse_adjacency() returns the face–face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix — the graph a flow solver walks.

docs.title: Connected components¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by which connected piece of the adjacency graph it belongs to. The number of distinct labels tells you whether the mesh is one contiguous surface or several disjoint pieces.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)) returns a new MeshDataset holding only the faces inside the box — the mesh equivalent of a spatial window. (subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) does the same with positional arguments.) We crop to one quadrant of the extent and plot the result.

docs.title: Writing the mesh back out¶
docs.text: to_file(path, driver=...) serialises the mesh through any write-capable driver. We round-trip to Stanford PLY (driver="ply"), which stores arbitrary polygon faces, into a temp file and read it back to confirm the topology survived.

docs.title: 11. What we cannot do here, and why¶
docs.text:
Two pyramids operations are unavailable on this mesh, and the reasons are instructive:

  • to_crs(epsg) — skipped. This grid carries no CRS (crs is None above), so pyramids refuses to reproject: to_crs raises "Cannot reproject: source CRS is unknown." You would first assign the known CRS (these global grids are geographic lon/lat on a sphere) and only then reproject.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) — out of scope here. Burning the mesh onto a raster grid or remapping between meshes is a genuine pyramids capability, but it needs a target raster/mesh and a resampling choice to be meaningful — a topic for a dedicated regridding tutorial, not this format tour.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• The mpas driver reads an MPAS SCVT grid into a pyramids MeshDataset, handling the 1-based connectivity and fill values.
  • MPAS cells are hexagons + 12 pentagons — visible as k = 6 connectivity and in the wireframe — with coordinates in radians (longitude → 2π, latitude → ±π/2).
  • The mesh is grid-only (no CRS, no fields); we attached a geometric face_area to get a data map.
  • GIS comes for free — to_geodataframe, adjacency, components, crop, PLY round-trip — while bounding_polygon fails at the periodic seam and to_crs/circumcenters are skipped with reasons.

docs.title: Reading Nastran meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
Nastran bulk-data decks are the classic input of structural finite-element analysis (MSC Nastran, NX Nastran, and compatible solvers). They are fixed-field ASCII text: GRID cards place nodes, CTRIA3/CQUAD4 cards define triangular and quadrilateral shell elements.

A deck is written in the model's engineering coordinate system — millimetres or inches, no map datum — so pyramids-mesh reports crs=None.

We use cylinder.fem: 33 GRID points, 4 CTRIA3 and 18 CQUAD4 elements.

Source: meshio test suite (tests/meshes/nastran/), MIT.

docs.title: Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: Quickstart: read the Nastran file¶
docs.text:
driver="nastran" parses the fixed-field bulk-data grammar (small-field GRID/CTRIA3/CQUAD4 cards).

The one rule that matters: pass a pathlib.Path, never a str — read_file keys its driver dispatch off the Path type. MeshDataset.read_file(...) returns a MeshDataset, the in-memory UGRID container every pyramids-mesh driver produces.

docs.title: What did we get?¶
docs.text: A few scalar properties describe the dataset at a glance: node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, and the planar bounding box.

docs.title: Summary table¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a pandas DataFrame with per-variable statistics (count / min / max / mean / std). It reports node_z here.

docs.title: The mesh geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: node coordinates plus the face-node connectivity, an (n_face, k) integer table where k is the largest number of nodes any face has. Triangles fill 3 columns; quadrilaterals fill 4 (a shorter face pads the spare slot). face_areas and face_centroids are derived on demand.

docs.title: Wireframe¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare mesh edges — the quickest way to eyeball the topology and the element shapes before colouring anything.

docs.title: A derived field: cell area¶
docs.text: These engineering files usually carry no cell data we can colour by — so we compute one ourselves. with_variable attaches face_areas as a face-located variable, giving a non-destructive copy of the dataset that plot can render as a filled colour map.

docs.title: Treating the mesh as GIS¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is just nodes and polygonal faces, pyramids exposes the usual vector-GIS toolbox on it. First, every face as a GeoPandas polygon:

docs.title: The outer boundary¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the shell elements into their single enclosing outline.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) returns a new MeshDataset with only the faces inside the box — handy for zooming into a region of a large mesh. We crop to the left half of the extent.

docs.title: The face-adjacency graph¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() gives the face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix, and connected_components() labels which faces are reachable from which. plt.spy shows the sparsity pattern — the fingerprint of how the faces are wired together.

docs.title: Why circumcenters are skipped here¶
docs.text: The deck mixes CTRIA3 and CQUAD4, so the mesh is not purely triangular and circumcenters() raises ValueError. We catch it.

docs.title: Converting out: other drivers¶
docs.text: to_file(path, driver=...) re-serialises the mesh through any writer in the driver table — here a round-trip to the 2dm format in a temp file.

docs.title: What we cannot do here: reprojection & regridding¶
docs.text: to_crs(epsg) reprojects between coordinate systems — but this mesh has crs=None (model-local coordinates, no datum), so there is nothing to reproject from; we skip it. Likewise rasterize_like(...) and regrid(...) map a data field onto a raster or another mesh; with no meaningful field and no georeferencing on an engineering mesh they are out of scope. These belong on georeferenced hydrodynamic meshes, not FEM/CFD decks.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• driver="nastran" reads a fixed-field bulk-data deck (GRID + CTRIA3/CQUAD4) into a MeshDataset.
  • A mixed tri/quad shell mesh, geometry-only (crs=None), with a node_z variable.
  • Polygon export, bounding polygon, cropping and adjacency all work; triangle-only circumcenters is refused.
  • Engineering units, no CRS → no reprojection or regridding.

docs.title: Reading Netgen volume meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
Netgen is the open-source mesh generator behind NGSolve; its .vol format records points, surface elements and volume elements for finite-element analysis. pyramids-mesh provides a driver that parses the .vol file into a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset and nothing more — the mesh operations all belong upstream in pyramids.

Our sample is netgen/periodic_3d.vol (meshio test data, MIT; NETGEN v6.2): a periodic 3-D test mesh — 65 points and 108 triangular surface elements. It is geometry only, crs=None.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the sample file¶
docs.text:
This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so the repo-root examples/data/ folder is two levels up. Paths are written relative to the notebook itself. We will read the Netgen mesh netgen/periodic_3d.vol.

Pass a pathlib.Path, never a string. read_file keys its driver dispatch off Path objects; a bare str is not accepted.

docs.title: 4. Read it in one line¶
docs.text: The .vol file is a keyword-blocked ASCII dump (surfaceelements, points, ...). We name the driver explicitly with driver="netgen" and hand read_file the Path. What comes back is a MeshDataset — the same mesh container every other pyramids mesh uses.

docs.title: 5. Inspect the dataset¶
docs.text: A handful of attributes describe the mesh at a glance: the node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, the list of data variables, and the planar bounding box (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax). Netgen meshes are defined in abstract geometry units, so crs and epsg are None.

docs.title: A statistical summary of the data variables¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a small pandas table — one row per data variable with count, min, max, mean and std. The mesh exposes a node_z variable (the vertices' third coordinate), so the summary has one row describing it.

docs.title: 6. The underlying geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d. Its node coordinates live in node_x / node_y, and its face-to-node table is face_node_connectivity.data — an (n_face, k) integer array where row i lists the node indices of face i. Three node indices per row confirms a triangular surface mesh. A winding-normalisation warning on read is expected and harmless.

docs.title: 7. Draw the mesh outline (wireframe)¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the cell edges with no fill — the quickest way to see the topology we just read. The figure embeds in the notebook on its own.

docs.title: 8. A filled map: projected cell area¶
docs.text:
These are engineering meshes with no CRS and (usually) no field data, so there is nothing physical to colour by out of the box. A useful derived quantity is the projected 2-D area of each cell, available as mesh.face_areas. We attach it as a face variable with with_variable(...) and let plot(...) draw a filled colour map.

This triangulation has genuinely non-zero projected areas across most cells, so the colour map varies smoothly — a good sanity check that the geometry parsed correctly.

docs.title: 9. The pyramids GIS toolbox applies¶
docs.text: The payoff of turning a solver file into a pyramids object is that the whole GIS toolbox now works on it, even though this is a FEM/CFD mesh. Below we exercise several operations and interpret each result.

docs.title: Export to a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every cell into a shapely polygon inside a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the bridge to the entire vector-GIS ecosystem. Because the mesh has crs=None, the frame is unprojected (model units, not metres/degrees).

docs.title: Dissolve to a bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() unions all cells into the single outer footprint of the mesh — useful as a clip mask or domain outline. We overlay it (red) on the grey cell edges.

docs.title: Triangle circumcenters¶
docs.text: circumcenters() returns the (n_face, 2) circumcentre of each triangular cell — the dual-mesh vertices that finite-volume schemes use. (It is defined only for triangle meshes; the quad/polyhedral notebooks skip it.)

docs.title: Face-adjacency as a sparse matrix¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() returns the (n_face, n_face) SciPy CSR matrix of which cells share an edge — the connectivity graph solvers assemble their stencils from. We only report its shape and non-zero count.

docs.title: Crop to a sub-region¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)) keeps only the cells inside a window — the mesh equivalent of a spatial subset. Here we take the left half of the domain and re-draw it.

docs.title: What we skip, and why¶
docs.text:
Because this mesh carries crs=None, the reprojection and raster-bridge operations do not apply:

  • to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to reproject from — skipped (there is no datum to interpret the model's bare coordinates).
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) burn a mesh onto, or resample it against, a georeferenced raster grid — skipped here, as there is no spatial reference to align to.

These are first-class pyramids operations; they simply require a georeferenced mesh, which an engineering solver file is not.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
We read a Netgen .vol, inspected its 65 nodes / 108 triangles, mapped projected cell area, then exercised GIS: vector export, outer footprint, circumcenters, the sparse adjacency graph, a crop.

The pattern is always the same: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver=...) turns a solver file into a pyramids object, and from there the full GIS toolbox applies — even for a geometry-only, CRS-less engineering mesh. pyramids-mesh contributes only the driver; every mesh operation lives upstream in pyramids.

docs.title: Reading the Wavefront OBJ format with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text: The Wavefront OBJ format is a long-lived text format for 3D geometry: v x y z vertex lines and f i j k ... face lines referencing them (1-based). It is everywhere in 3D graphics and asset pipelines. The sample is a real model — an elephant surface of 623 vertices and 1148 triangles — large enough that the plots and GIS operations actually have something to show. pyramids-mesh reads it into a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid object.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Read the file in one call¶
docs.text: This real model is not consistently wound, so the reader reports how many clockwise faces it reversed and how many degenerate faces it found — ordinary housekeeping for hand-built 3D assets. The 1-based f indices are converted to 0-based connectivity.

docs.title: 4. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A handful of attributes describe what we loaded: node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, the names of any data variables, and the spatial extent.

docs.title: 5. A statistical summary of the fields¶
docs.text: summary() returns a pandas frame with one row per data variable (count, min, max, mean, std).

docs.title: 6. The underlying Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d object carrying the raw topology: node coordinates, the face-node connectivity table of shape (n_face, k) (row i lists the node indices of cell i), per-face areas, and cell centroids.

docs.title: 7. The mesh outline (wireframe)¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare cell edges, with no field attached — the quickest look at the raw geometry this driver produced.

docs.title: 8. A data map: attach and colour by cell area¶
docs.text: These surface formats carry no field data, so there is nothing to colour by yet. We attach a derived cell_area variable at the face location and plot it — turning the geometry into a proper choropleth.

docs.title: 9. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is a first-class pyramids object, a whole GIS toolkit comes along. First, every face as a row in a GeoDataFrame.

docs.title: Bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() returns a single shapely geometry: the dissolved outer footprint of the mesh.

docs.title: Derived topology and connectivity¶
docs.text: A few more derived quantities are a method call away. circumcenters() is defined only for triangular meshes; exterior_edges() indexes the boundary edges; connected_components() labels disjoint pieces; sparse_adjacency() is the face-to-face graph as a sparse matrix.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) keeps the faces that fall within (or touch) a rectangle, returning a new MeshDataset. Here we crop to the left portion of the extent and redraw it.

docs.title: Round-tripping through the driver table¶
docs.text: to_file(..., driver=...) writes the mesh back out in any writable driver (here the solver-neutral 2DM).

docs.title: 10. What we skip here, and why¶
docs.text:
• to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to reproject from, but OBJ files carry no georeferencing (crs=None), so there is nothing to reproject. Attach a CRS first if the coordinates are known to be in a specific projection.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) require a reference grid (a raster or target mesh) to sample onto; with only this standalone mesh in hand there is no target, so they are out of scope for this tutorial.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: A substantial Wavefront OBJ model reads into a MeshDataset like any other mesh, its 1-based faces renumbered and its winding normalised. Because it is a real surface with over a thousand cells, it shows what the shared pyramids toolkit is actually for: meaningful area maps, a real vector layer, multiple connected components, and genuine spatial cropping — all from a format whose reader only ever parsed v and f lines.

docs.title: Reading the OFF (Object File Format) with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text: The OFF (Object File Format) is a minimal polygon-mesh format: a line OFF, then an nvert nface nedge count, the vertex coordinates, and one line per face giving its vertex count and indices (optionally trailed by an RGBA colour). The sample here is a cube — eight vertices, six quadrilateral faces — complete with inline # comments and per-face colours, both of which the reader tolerates. This notebook reads it into a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid object and explores the quirks that come with a 3D surface flattened into a 2D mesh model.

docs.title: 3. Read the file in one call¶
docs.text: Reading emits two warnings worth understanding: the reader reverses clockwise faces to counter-clockwise (a consistent winding a writer can round-trip) and flags degenerate faces that have no planar winding. Both are expected when a 3D cube's faces are projected onto the 2D plane — vertical faces collapse.

docs.text:
• to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to reproject from, but OFF files carry no georeferencing (crs=None), so there is nothing to reproject. Attach a CRS first if the coordinates are known to be in a specific projection.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) require a reference grid (a raster or target mesh) to sample onto; with only this standalone mesh in hand there is no target, so they are out of scope for this tutorial.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: OFF exercises two things the triangular surface formats do not: non-triangular (quad) faces and the winding/degeneracy normalisation a 3D-surface-in-2D triggers. The reader parses, normalises winding, and warns about degenerate faces, then hands back an ordinary MeshDataset. Triangle-only operations like circumcenters bow out cleanly on a quad mesh, while the rest of the pyramids toolkit works unchanged.

docs.title: Reading OpenFOAM polyMesh directories with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
OpenFOAM — the open-source CFD toolbox — does not store its mesh in one file but in a polyMesh/ directory of ASCII files (points, faces, owner, neighbour, boundary). pyramids-mesh registers a driver that reads the whole directory into a single pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset.

Our sample is openfoam/polyMesh (fluiddyn/fluidfoam, GPL-3.0; OpenFOAM 5.0 output): 260 points and 258 faces over a tiny domain (roughly 0.6 mm x 60 mm). It is geometry only, crs=None. Note the key difference from every other notebook: we pass the driver the directory path, not a file.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the sample file¶
docs.text:
This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so the repo-root examples/data/ folder is two levels up. Paths are written relative to the notebook itself. OpenFOAM's mesh is a directory, so mesh_file points at the polyMesh folder itself.

Pass a pathlib.Path, never a string. read_file keys its driver dispatch off Path objects; a bare str is not accepted.

docs.title: 4. Read it in one line¶
docs.text: We hand read_file the polyMesh directory Path; the driver stitches its five ASCII files into one mesh. We name the driver explicitly with driver="openfoam" and hand read_file the Path. What comes back is a MeshDataset — the same mesh container every other pyramids mesh uses.

docs.title: 5. Inspect the dataset¶
docs.text: A handful of attributes describe the mesh at a glance: the node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, the list of data variables, and the planar bounding box (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax). A CFD mesh has no geographic datum, so crs and epsg are None; the bounds are in model units (here millimetres).

docs.title: A statistical summary of the data variables¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a small pandas table — one row per data variable with count, min, max, mean and std. The reconstructed mesh exposes a node_z variable (point depth), so the table has one row.

docs.title: 6. The underlying geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d. Its node coordinates live in node_x / node_y, and its face-to-node table is face_node_connectivity.data — an (n_face, k) integer array where row i lists the node indices of face i. Four node indices per row: the faces file describes mostly quadrilateral mesh faces. A winding-normalisation warning on read is expected.

docs.title: 7. Draw the mesh outline (wireframe)¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the cell edges with no fill — the quickest way to see the topology we just read. The figure embeds in the notebook on its own.

docs.title: 8. A filled map: projected cell area¶
docs.text:
These are engineering meshes with no CRS and (usually) no field data, so there is nothing physical to colour by out of the box. A useful derived quantity is the projected 2-D area of each cell, available as mesh.face_areas. We attach it as a face variable with with_variable(...) and let plot(...) draw a filled colour map.

The domain is sub-millimetre in X, so absolute areas are tiny (order 1e-5) — the colour map still resolves the relative variation. The very small magnitudes are a unit artefact, not an error.

docs.title: 9. The pyramids GIS toolbox applies¶
docs.text: The payoff of turning a solver file into a pyramids object is that the whole GIS toolbox now works on it, even though this is a FEM/CFD mesh. Below we exercise several operations and interpret each result.

docs.title: Export to a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every cell into a shapely polygon inside a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the bridge to the entire vector-GIS ecosystem. Because the mesh has crs=None, the frame is unprojected (model units, not metres/degrees).

docs.title: Dissolve to a bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() unions all cells into the single outer footprint of the mesh — useful as a clip mask or domain outline. We overlay it (red) on the grey cell edges.

docs.title: Connected components¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by its face-adjacent group. A single label across all faces means the mesh is one topologically connected piece.

docs.title: Face-adjacency as a sparse matrix¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() returns the (n_face, n_face) SciPy CSR matrix of which cells share an edge — the connectivity graph solvers assemble their stencils from. We only report its shape and non-zero count.

docs.title: Crop to a sub-region¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)) keeps only the cells inside a window — the mesh equivalent of a spatial subset. Here we take the left half of the domain and re-draw it.

docs.title: What we skip, and why¶
docs.text:
Because this mesh carries crs=None, the reprojection and raster-bridge operations do not apply:

  • to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to reproject from — skipped (there is no datum to interpret the model's bare coordinates).
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) burn a mesh onto, or resample it against, a georeferenced raster grid — skipped here, as there is no spatial reference to align to.

These are first-class pyramids operations; they simply require a georeferenced mesh, which an engineering solver file is not.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
We read an OpenFOAM polyMesh directory (260 points, 258 faces) by passing the folder path, mapped projected cell area over its sub-millimetre domain, and ran GIS: vector export, footprint, connected components, the adjacency graph, a crop. Circumcenters are skipped (non-triangular faces).

The pattern is always the same: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver=...) turns a solver file into a pyramids object, and from there the full GIS toolbox applies — even for a geometry-only, CRS-less engineering mesh. pyramids-mesh contributes only the driver; every mesh operation lives upstream in pyramids.

docs.title: Reading the PLY (Stanford Polygon) format with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text: The PLY (Polygon File Format, a.k.a. Stanford Triangle Format) is a simple surface format born from 3D scanning: an ASCII or binary header declaring element vertex/element face blocks, followed by the coordinates and the polygon vertex lists. pyramids-mesh reads it straight into a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid object, so a scan mesh lands in the same data model as every other driver. This notebook reads a tiny two-triangle PLY, explores its geometry, and shows the GIS tools that then come for free.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Read the file in one call¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file takes the Path and an explicit driver="ply". Passing the driver skips suffix sniffing and guarantees the PLY reader is used.

docs.title: 4. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A handful of attributes describe what we loaded: node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, the names of any data variables, and the spatial extent.

docs.title: 5. A statistical summary of the fields¶
docs.text: summary() returns a pandas frame with one row per data variable (count, min, max, mean, std).

docs.title: 6. The underlying Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d object carrying the raw topology: node coordinates, the face-node connectivity table of shape (n_face, k) (row i lists the node indices of cell i), per-face areas, and cell centroids.

docs.title: 7. The mesh outline (wireframe)¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare cell edges, with no field attached — the quickest look at the raw geometry this driver produced.

docs.title: 8. A data map: attach and colour by cell area¶
docs.text: These surface formats carry no field data, so there is nothing to colour by yet. We attach a derived cell_area variable at the face location and plot it — turning the geometry into a proper choropleth.

docs.title: 9. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is a first-class pyramids object, a whole GIS toolkit comes along. First, every face as a row in a GeoDataFrame.

docs.title: Bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() returns a single shapely geometry: the dissolved outer footprint of the mesh.

docs.title: Derived topology and connectivity¶
docs.text: A few more derived quantities are a method call away. circumcenters() is defined only for triangular meshes; exterior_edges() indexes the boundary edges; connected_components() labels disjoint pieces; sparse_adjacency() is the face-to-face graph as a sparse matrix.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) keeps the faces that fall within (or touch) a rectangle, returning a new MeshDataset. Here we crop to the left portion of the extent and redraw it.

docs.title: Round-tripping through the driver table¶
docs.text: to_file(..., driver=...) writes the mesh back out in any writable driver (here the solver-neutral 2DM).

docs.title: 10. What we skip here, and why¶
docs.text:
• to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to reproject from, but PLY files carry no georeferencing (crs=None), so there is nothing to reproject. Attach a CRS first if the coordinates are known to be in a specific projection.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) require a reference grid (a raster or target mesh) to sample onto; with only this standalone mesh in hand there is no target, so they are out of scope for this tutorial.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: A PLY surface mesh reads in one line into the same MeshDataset as every other format. PLY itself contributes only the file parsing — node coordinates, face lists and the node_z elevation — and the moment it is a MeshDataset, the full pyramids mesh and GIS toolkit (plotting, GeoDataFrame export, bounding polygon, cropping, cross-format write-out) applies unchanged.

docs.title: Reading SCHISM hgrid.gr3 grids with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
SCHISM is a cross-scale hydrodynamic model. Its horizontal grid is the ASCII hgrid.gr3 file — the same node/element layout as ADCIRC's fort.14, plus open- and land-boundary sections. The per-node value column holds the bathymetric depth.

pyramids-mesh registers a schism driver that parses hgrid.gr3 into a MeshDataset/Mesh2d. This notebook reads the California DWR teaching grid and walks read → explore → plot → GIS.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the data¶
docs.text: The notebook lives in docs/examples/, so examples/data/ is two levels up. We pass a pathlib.Path to the reader (never a string).

docs.title: 4. Read the mesh¶
docs.text: We name the driver explicitly: driver="schism". read_file dispatches to it and returns a MeshDataset wrapping a Mesh2d.

docs.title: 5. Explore the mesh¶
docs.text: Node/face counts, CRS, the attached data variables and the bounding box. This grid has 2639 nodes and 4636 triangles, with coordinates in projected metres (bounds run 0–56000 m east, −10400–10400 m north) — though the file declares no EPSG code, so crs/epsg are None.

docs.title: 6. Mesh geometry¶
docs.text: The Mesh2d exposes node coordinates, the (n_face, k) face-node connectivity, per-face areas and centroids — all plain numpy arrays.

docs.title: 7. Wireframe¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare element skeleton — the fastest way to read the mesh's shape and where it is refined.

docs.title: 8. Data map¶
docs.text: node_z is the per-node bathymetric depth the driver read from hgrid.gr3's value column. The summary() above shows it spanning 0.5–10.0 in model units.

docs.title: 9. GIS operations for free¶
docs.text: The mesh is a pyramids object, so the vector/GIS layer applies unchanged. Convert to a GeoDataFrame — one polygon per element. to_geodataframe() returns just the geometry column, so we attach each element's area and let geopandas colour by it; smaller cells reveal where the mesh is refined.

docs.title: 10. What needs more than a mesh¶
docs.text:
• to_crs(epsg) needs a source CRS. hgrid.gr3 carries projected metres but declares no EPSG code, so ds.epsg is None, so to_crs is skipped.
  • rasterize_like / regrid need a reference grid to sample onto; with only the mesh in hand there is no target, so they are out of scope for this read-only tour.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver="schism") turns the native schism grid into a first-class pyramids mesh. Exploration, plotting, GeoDataFrame conversion, bounding polygons, connectivity analysis, spatial subsetting and export are all inherited from pyramids — pyramids-mesh only added the reader.

pd.Series({
    "n_node": ds.n_node,
    "n_face": ds.n_face,
    "crs": ds.crs,
    "epsg": ds.epsg,

n_node                                       407
n_face                                       384
crs                                         None
epsg                                        None
bounds                 (0.0, -90.0, 360.0, 90.0)

384 quadrilateral faces assembled from 407 unique nodes (shared corners are de-duplicated on read). crs/epsg are None — SCRIP records lon/lat with no CRS object — and data_variable_names is empty: a SCRIP grid is a geometry description, not a field dataset. The bounds of (0, -90, 360, 90) already hint these coordinates are in degrees.

In [6]: Copied!

pd.Series({
    "node_x min/max": (float(nx.min()), float(nx.max())),
    "node_y min/max": (float(ny.min()), float(ny.max())),
    "two_pi": float(2*np.pi), "half_pi": float(np.pi/2),
})
nx, ny = ds.mesh.node_x, ds.mesh.node_y pd.Series({ "node_x min/max": (float(nx.min()), float(nx.max())), "node_y min/max": (float(ny.min()), float(ny.max())), "two_pi": float(2*np.pi), "half_pi": float(np.pi/2), }) Out[6]:

node_y min/max    (-90.0, 90.0)

node_x spans the full 0 → 360 and node_y the full −90 → 90 — these are degrees, so (once a geographic CRS is assigned) they are already in the units most GIS tools expect, no radian conversion needed.

cx, cy = mesh.face_centroids

{

The connectivity shape is (384, 4): four nodes per face — SCRIP cubed-sphere cells are quadrilaterals. That k = 4 (versus 3 for a triangular grid) is why circumcenters will not apply.

if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)
_g = ds.plot_outline() if ds.epsg: add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)

The wireframe shows the cubed-sphere layout unrolled onto the lon/lat plane: six square panels whose quadrilateral cells distort toward the poles, where constant-degree spacing stretches them.

In [9]: Copied!

_g = d2.plot("face_area", cmap="viridis", colorbar=True, title="Per-cell area")

Each quad is shaded by area (in degree-squared units). The map brightens toward the equator and dims toward the poles — the familiar lon/lat distortion where equal angular steps enclose less area at high latitude.

Expected: the operation is simply undefined for this cell shape. A triangular dual mesh would be the prerequisite for finite-volume circumcenter schemes on this grid.

The adjacency matrix is (384, 384) with two non-zeros per shared edge; the boundary-edge count reflects the rim of the unrolled cubed sphere (cells that would meet across a cube edge are not stitched in the flat lon/lat layout).

One component: every cell connects to its neighbours, so the SCRIP grid reads back as a single contiguous surface.

docs.title: Reading SCRIP remapping grids with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
SCRIP (Spherical Coordinate Remapping and Interpolation Package) defines the NetCDF grid-description convention used across climate modelling to specify how to remap fields between grids. A SCRIP file does not store a solver mesh so much as a list of cells by their corners: grid_corner_lat/grid_corner_lon give each cell's vertices (here (384, 4) — 384 quadrilateral cells, 4 corners each), grid_center_lat/lon the centres, and grid_imask an active-cell mask.

This notebook reads the outCSne8 cubed-sphere SCRIP grid (an ne8 cube, 384 cells) into a pyramids MeshDataset and tours the operations it supports. Unlike MPAS/ICON, SCRIP corner coordinates are in degrees.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the example file¶
docs.text:
This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so examples/data/ is two levels up. The SCRIP sample is scrip/outCSne8.nc, a cubed-sphere ne8 remapping grid from the UXarray test suite.

Paths inside a notebook are always written relative to the notebook itself, and pyramids' read_file accepts a pathlib.Path directly — we pass the Path, never str(path).

docs.title: 4. Read the mesh¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver="scrip") dispatches the file to the scrip driver, which parses it and hands back a MeshDataset — the same pyramids type produced from a native UGRID NetCDF file. We name the driver explicitly here because several formats share the .nc suffix; read_file can auto-detect, but being explicit is unambiguous.

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes summary properties describing the whole mesh: n_node / n_face (size), crs / epsg (georeferencing, if the format recorded any), bounds (spatial extent), and data_variable_names (any attached fields).

docs.title: 6. Coordinates are in DEGREES¶
docs.text: SCRIP corner/centre coordinates are stored in degrees of longitude/latitude — unlike the radian MPAS and ICON grids. The range makes it obvious: longitude 0 → 360, latitude −90 → 90.

docs.title: 7. The underlying Mesh2d topology¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d holding the raw topology. The arrays you reach for most often are node_x/node_y (node coordinates), face_node_connectivity.data — the (n_face, k) table listing the node indices of each face — and face_areas (one value per face).

docs.title: 8. The wireframe¶
docs.text: The simplest visualization needs no data — just draw the cell edges. plot_outline() renders the mesh skeleton through cleopatra; it is the fastest sanity check that a file read in correctly.

docs.title: 9. A data map: per-cell area¶
docs.text: A SCRIP grid carries no field values, so we synthesise one. We compute each cell's area from the geometry and attach it as a face-located variable with with_variable(...), which returns a new dataset (the original ds is left untouched). Colouring by it produces the generic pyramids data-map that any per-cell field (depth, velocity, …) would use.

docs.title: 10. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because the mesh is a pyramids object, the pyramids GIS layer applies directly — none of these methods live in pyramids-mesh. We tour a few.

docs.title: Faces as a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every face into a polygon row of a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the standard vector structure for export to shapefile/GeoPackage or for spatial joins.

docs.title: Bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the cells into the grid's outer boundary. For this cubed-sphere grid, unrolled across the full 0–360 longitude range, it returns a shapely Polygon.

docs.title: Circumcenters — not applicable¶
docs.text: circumcenters() is defined only for triangular meshes. SCRIP is a quadrilateral mesh, so calling it raises ValueError: circumcenters is only defined for triangular meshes. We show the guard rather than force it — a circumcenter has no unique definition for a polygon with more than three sides.

docs.title: Boundary edges and face adjacency¶
docs.text: exterior_edges() returns the indices of the edges that lie on the mesh boundary (each interior edge is shared by two faces; a boundary edge by one). sparse_adjacency() returns the face–face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix — the graph a flow solver walks.

docs.title: Connected components¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by which connected piece of the adjacency graph it belongs to. The number of distinct labels tells you whether the mesh is one contiguous surface or several disjoint pieces.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)) returns a new MeshDataset holding only the faces inside the box — the mesh equivalent of a spatial window. (subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) does the same with positional arguments.) We crop to one quadrant of the extent and plot the result.

docs.title: Writing the mesh back out¶
docs.text: to_file(path, driver=...) serialises the mesh through any write-capable driver. We round-trip to Stanford PLY (driver="ply"), which stores arbitrary polygon faces, into a temp file and read it back to confirm the topology survived.

docs.title: 11. What we cannot do here, and why¶
docs.text:
Two pyramids operations are unavailable on this mesh, and the reasons are instructive:

  • to_crs(epsg) — skipped. This grid carries no CRS (crs is None above), so pyramids refuses to reproject: to_crs raises "Cannot reproject: source CRS is unknown." You would first assign the known CRS (these global grids are geographic lon/lat on a sphere) and only then reproject.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) — out of scope here. Burning the mesh onto a raster grid or remapping between meshes is a genuine pyramids capability, but it needs a target raster/mesh and a resampling choice to be meaningful — a topic for a dedicated regridding tutorial, not this format tour.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• The scrip driver reads a SCRIP remapping grid (corner-list convention) into a pyramids MeshDataset, de-duplicating shared corners into n_node nodes.
  • SCRIP cubed-sphere cells are quadrilaterals (k = 4) with coordinates in degrees (0–360 / −90–90), so circumcenters is skipped (triangles only).
  • The grid is geometry-only (no CRS, no fields); we attached a geometric face_area to map it.
  • GIS operations — to_geodataframe, bounding_polygon, adjacency/components, crop, PLY round-trip — all apply, while to_crs is skipped because no CRS is recorded.

docs.title: Reading TELEMAC Selafin (.slf) results with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
Selafin (a.k.a. SERAFIN) is the binary mesh-and-results format of the TELEMAC-MASCARET hydrodynamic suite. Unlike a pure geometry format, a Selafin file bundles the triangular mesh and one or more time-varying variables (water depth, velocity, …). pyramids-mesh registers a selafin driver that parses both the topology and the variables into a MeshDataset.

The bundled minimal.slf carries a WATER DEPTH variable over two time steps on a two-triangle mesh. We read it and map the depth field.

docs.title: 3. Locate the data¶
docs.text: minimal.slf lives in examples/data/, two levels up; addressed as a Path.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 4. Read the file¶
docs.text: A Selafin file is self-contained — mesh plus results — so a single read_file yields a dataset that already has a data variable. A driver's only job is to parse the file and hand back a MeshDataset. We pass a pathlib.Path (never a str) and name the driver explicitly:

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes the mesh size, its coordinate reference system, and the data variables carried alongside the topology. None for crs/epsg simply means the source file declared no projection — the geometry is still valid, it is just unlocated in world space.

docs.title: Per-variable summary¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a pandas DataFrame — one row per data variable with count, min, max, mean and standard deviation. A std of 0 means that variable is uniform across the mesh.

docs.title: Global attributes¶
docs.text: Each driver stamps provenance into global_attributes so you can trace a dataset back to the format it came from after it has been converted.

docs.title: 6. The Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: node coordinates plus the face-node connectivity table. face_node_connectivity.data has shape (n_face, k) — row i lists the node indices of face i (padded for mixed element types). We also derive per-face areas and centroids from that topology.

docs.title: 7. Wireframe — the mesh skeleton¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare mesh: every face edge, no data coloring. This is the fastest way to eyeball connectivity, element shapes and the overall extent.

docs.title: 8. A data map¶
docs.text: Selafin's headline variable is WATER DEPTH. We map it directly — these are real TELEMAC output values, varying across the mesh. plot renders the first time step by default; the summary() table above reported the full range across both steps.

docs.title: 9. GIS operations¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is a first-class pyramids object, the full geospatial toolkit works on it directly — no conversion step. Below are several operations, each visualised or interpreted. (Operations that need a source CRS, such as to_crs, are skipped here: this sample declares none.)

docs.title: 9a. Faces as polygons — to_geodataframe()¶
docs.text: Every face becomes a shapely polygon in a GeoPandas GeoDataFrame, ready for a spatial join, an overlay, or export to any OGR vector format.

docs.title: 9b. Outer boundary — bounding_polygon() and exterior_edges()¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the faces into a single shapely polygon tracing the mesh outline, and exterior_edges() returns the indices of the mesh edges that lie on that boundary — their count is the boundary's edge length.

docs.title: 9c. Connectivity — connected_components()¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by the connected sub-mesh it belongs to. One unique label means the mesh is a single watertight piece; more than one would reveal detached islands. We attach the labels as a face variable and map them.

docs.title: 9d. Face adjacency — sparse_adjacency()¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() returns the face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix (two faces are adjacent when they share an edge). Its sparsity pattern is the dual graph a solver walks; nnz counts the directed face-neighbour links.

docs.title: 9e. Triangle circumcenters — circumcenters()¶
docs.text: For a triangular mesh, circumcenters() returns the circumcircle centre of each face (shape (2, n_face)) — the sample points of the dual Voronoi mesh that finite-volume schemes use. We scatter them over the wireframe.

docs.title: 9f. Clip to a sub-region — crop()¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) clips the mesh — and the depth field with it — to a bounding box. We keep the lower-left quarter.

docs.title: 9g. Round-trip through UGRID NetCDF — to_file()¶
docs.text: to_file(..., driver='ugrid') writes the mesh to the CF/UGRID NetCDF convention — the lossless lingua franca every tool in the stack reads back. We write it, re-read it, and confirm the topology survived.

docs.title: 10. Takeaway¶
docs.text: The selafin driver reads a TELEMAC mesh-and-results file in one call: topology becomes a Mesh2d, each stored field becomes a mappable data variable, and the dataset then supports the full GIS toolkit — vectorise, clip, inspect connectivity, round-trip to UGRID NetCDF.

docs.title: Reading SRH-2D meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
SRH-2D (Sedimentation and River Hydraulics – 2D) is the USBR / Aquaveo finite-volume river model. A case is described by three companion files sharing a base name:

  • .srhgeom — the mesh (nodes + mixed triangular/quadrilateral/polygonal elements),
  • .srhhydro — the control deck (boundary conditions, run settings),
  • .srhmat — the material / roughness zones.

pyramids-mesh registers an srh2d driver keyed on the .srhgeom file; it reads the geometry and pulls the roughness from the sibling .srhmat automatically, returning one MeshDataset.

The bundled case is the public-domain USACE HEC-RAS "Muncie" example (via psu-efd/pyHMT2D): ~19,400 mixed elements over ~21,500 nodes, in feet. A real mesh — so the maps and the clip actually show something.

docs.title: 3. Locate the data¶
docs.text: The SRH-2D files live in their own examples/data/srh2d/ subfolder. We point the driver at Muncie.srhgeom; it finds the .srhmat sibling itself. (See the folder's SOURCE.txt for provenance.)

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 4. Read the file¶
docs.text: We pass the .srhgeom path; the driver reads the geometry and merges the manning_n field from the companion .srhmat. A driver's only job is to parse the file and hand back a MeshDataset. We pass a pathlib.Path (never a str) and name the driver explicitly:

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes the mesh size, its coordinate reference system, and the data variables carried alongside the topology. None for crs/epsg simply means the source file declared no projection — the geometry is still valid, it is just unlocated in world space.

docs.title: Per-variable summary¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a pandas DataFrame — one row per data variable with count, min, max, mean and standard deviation. A std of 0 means that variable is uniform across the mesh.

docs.title: Global attributes¶
docs.text: Each driver stamps provenance into global_attributes so you can trace a dataset back to the format it came from after it has been converted.

docs.title: 6. The Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: node coordinates plus the face-node connectivity table. face_node_connectivity.data has shape (n_face, k) — row i lists the node indices of face i (padded for mixed element types). We also derive per-face areas and centroids from that topology.

docs.title: 7. Wireframe — the mesh skeleton¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare mesh: every face edge, no data coloring. This is the fastest way to eyeball connectivity, element shapes and the overall extent.

docs.title: 8. A data map¶
docs.text: The headline field for a river model is Manning's n — the bed roughness, per element, read from the .srhmat. We map it. Distinct bands appear: the channel, banks and floodplain each carry a different roughness, exactly the zoning SRH-2D solves against.

docs.title: A second map — bed elevation (node_z)¶
docs.text: node_z is the terrain the flow runs over. Mapping it shows the valley form — the low channel threading through higher ground.

docs.title: 9. GIS operations¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is a first-class pyramids object, the full geospatial toolkit works on it directly — no conversion step. Below are several operations, each visualised or interpreted. (Operations that need a source CRS, such as to_crs, are skipped here: this sample declares none.)

docs.title: 9a. Faces as polygons — to_geodataframe()¶
docs.text: Every face becomes a shapely polygon in a GeoPandas GeoDataFrame, ready for a spatial join, an overlay, or export to any OGR vector format.

docs.title: 9b. Outer boundary — bounding_polygon() and exterior_edges()¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the faces into a single shapely polygon tracing the mesh outline, and exterior_edges() returns the indices of the mesh edges that lie on that boundary — their count is the boundary's edge length.

docs.title: 9c. Connectivity — connected_components()¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by the connected sub-mesh it belongs to. One unique label means the mesh is a single watertight piece; more than one would reveal detached islands. We attach the labels as a face variable and map them.

docs.title: 9d. Face adjacency — sparse_adjacency()¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() returns the face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix (two faces share an edge). For a mesh this large we report its size and non-zero count rather than plotting the pattern — nnz is the number of face-neighbour links in the dual graph.

docs.title: 9e. Triangle circumcenters — not applicable¶
docs.text: circumcenters() is defined only for purely triangular meshes. This mesh contains quads and higher-order polygons, so circumcenters() raises ValueError: circumcenters is only defined for triangular meshes. — we skip it rather than force a triangulation.

docs.title: 9f. Clip to a sub-region — crop()¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) extracts a sub-mesh inside a bounding box — essential on a mesh this size. We clip to the lower-left quadrant of the extent and plot just that piece.

docs.title: 9g. Round-trip through UGRID NetCDF — to_file()¶
docs.text: to_file(..., driver='ugrid') writes the mesh to the CF/UGRID NetCDF convention — the lossless lingua franca every tool in the stack reads back. We write it, re-read it, and confirm the topology survived.

docs.title: A note on writing back¶
docs.text: to_file(..., driver='ugrid') above succeeds because UGRID NetCDF stores arbitrary polygons. Writing this mesh to 2dm instead would raise FileFormatNotSupportedError — 2DM only defines element keywords for 3-, 4- and 6-node faces, and this mesh has 5-node polygons. The driver refuses rather than silently dropping them; pick a format whose element table can hold your topology.

docs.title: 10. Takeaway¶
docs.text: The srh2d driver reads a three-file SRH-2D case from its .srhgeom, merging the roughness from the .srhmat, into a single real-world MeshDataset. Its mixed element types gate a few triangle-only operations (circumcenters) but everything topology-general — vectorise, boundary, components, adjacency, clip, UGRID round-trip — works at full scale.
