docs.title: Reading the STL (stereolithography) format with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text: The STL (stereolithography) format is the lingua franca of 3D printing and CAD exchange: a bare triangle soup, each facet stored as a normal plus three vertices, in either ASCII or (as here) a compact binary layout. The sample is a binary STL of a cube — 12 triangles (two per cube face). pyramids-mesh reads it into a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid object, deduplicating the repeated vertices into a shared node table. This notebook reads it and explores what a closed 3D surface looks like inside a 2D mesh model.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Read the file in one call¶
docs.text: Like OFF, reading warns that some clockwise faces were reversed (winding normalisation) and some are degenerate — the cube's faces that stand perpendicular to the XY plane collapse to zero planar area when projected. The binary facets are parsed and their duplicated corner vertices merged into unique nodes.

docs.title: 4. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A handful of attributes describe what we loaded: node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, the names of any data variables, and the spatial extent.

docs.title: 5. A statistical summary of the fields¶
docs.text: summary() returns a pandas frame with one row per data variable (count, min, max, mean, std).

docs.title: 6. The underlying Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d object carrying the raw topology: node coordinates, the face-node connectivity table of shape (n_face, k) (row i lists the node indices of cell i), per-face areas, and cell centroids.

docs.title: 7. The mesh outline (wireframe)¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare cell edges, with no field attached — the quickest look at the raw geometry this driver produced.

docs.title: 8. A data map: attach and colour by cell area¶
docs.text: These surface formats carry no field data, so there is nothing to colour by yet. We attach a derived cell_area variable at the face location and plot it — turning the geometry into a proper choropleth.

docs.title: 9. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is a first-class pyramids object, a whole GIS toolkit comes along. First, every face as a row in a GeoDataFrame.

docs.title: Bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() returns a single shapely geometry: the dissolved outer footprint of the mesh.

docs.title: Derived topology and connectivity¶
docs.text: A few more derived quantities are a method call away. circumcenters() is defined only for triangular meshes; exterior_edges() indexes the boundary edges; connected_components() labels disjoint pieces; sparse_adjacency() is the face-to-face graph as a sparse matrix.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) keeps the faces that fall within (or touch) a rectangle, returning a new MeshDataset. Here we crop to the left portion of the extent and redraw it.

docs.title: Round-tripping through the driver table¶
docs.text: to_file(..., driver=...) writes the mesh back out in any writable driver (here the solver-neutral 2DM).

docs.title: 10. What we skip here, and why¶
docs.text:
• to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to reproject from, but STL files carry no georeferencing (crs=None), so there is nothing to reproject. Attach a CRS first if the coordinates are known to be in a specific projection.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) require a reference grid (a raster or target mesh) to sample onto; with only this standalone mesh in hand there is no target, so they are out of scope for this tutorial.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: A binary STL triangle soup reads into a MeshDataset with its duplicate vertices merged into a shared node table. STL's job ends at parsing facets and normals; the resulting mesh behaves like any other — but because it is a genuine 3D surface, projecting it to the 2D plane produces zero-area vertical facets, a feature the geometry and area map make plain.

docs.title: Reading an SU2 CFD mesh¶
docs.text:
SU2 is an open-source suite for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and PDE-constrained optimisation. Its native .su2 mesh format lists points and elements by VTK cell code (triangles = 5, quads = 9) and is 0-based. pyramids-mesh reads it into a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset, turning a CFD grid into an ordinary pyramids object.

This sample is 5x5Mesh.su2 from the SU2 test cases — a clean 5x5 grid of 25 quadrilateral cells on the unit square (LGPL data).

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the example data¶
docs.text: This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so the repo-root examples/data/ folder is two levels up. Paths inside a notebook are written relative to the notebook itself. The critical rule for read_file is to pass a pathlib.Path, never str(...). We read su2/5x5Mesh.su2.

docs.title: 4. Quickstart: read the file¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver=...) parses the file and returns a MeshDataset — the same type pyramids produces from a NetCDF UGRID file. We name the "su2" driver explicitly; passing the Path object (not a string) is the supported call.

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes summary properties: n_node / n_face (mesh size), crs / epsg (georeferencing if the format recorded any), bounds (the (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) extent), and data_variable_names (attached field variables).

docs.title: 6. Face-degree distribution¶
docs.text: ds.mesh.face_node_connectivity.data is the (n_face, k) table of node indices per face, where k is the widest polygon. Cells with fewer nodes than k are padded with -1 (fill). Counting the non-negative entries per row gives each face's number of nodes — its degree.

docs.title: 7. The underlying geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d holding the raw arrays: node_x / node_y (coordinates), the connectivity table, face_areas (one area per cell) and face_centroids (shape (2, n_face)). Everything geometric is derived from the connectivity plus the node coordinates.

docs.title: 8. Wireframe: plot_outline()¶
docs.text: The simplest view needs no data — just the mesh edges. plot_outline() draws the wireframe through cleopatra and embeds it inline. This is the fastest sanity check that a file read in correctly.

docs.title: 9. A data map: attach and colour a field¶
docs.text: To draw a filled map we need a value per cell. These mesh files carry geometry only, so we compute one — each cell's area — and attach it with with_variable(..., location="face"), which returns a new dataset (the original ds is untouched). Then plot colours the mesh by it.

docs.title: The statistical summary¶
docs.text: With a field attached, .summary() reports per-variable statistics (count, min, max, mean, std). On the bare ds it is an empty frame; on d2 it has a real row.

docs.title: 10. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because the mesh is now a first-class pyramids object, the pyramids GIS layer applies directly — pyramids-mesh itself adds none of this. The next cells each run one operation and interpret it.

docs.title: Faces as a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every face into a polygon row of a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the standard vector structure for export to shapefile/GeoPackage or spatial joins.

docs.title: Bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the cells into a single shapely polygon of the meshed footprint — the gateway to the shapely/geopandas ecosystem for clipping and spatial joins.

docs.title: Circumcenters — explain and skip¶
docs.text: circumcenters() is only defined for triangular meshes. This mesh is not all-triangle, so the call raises ValueError; we catch it rather than crash. (Use cell centroids instead for such grids.)

docs.title: Exterior edges¶
docs.text: exterior_edges() returns the node indices of the mesh boundary — the edges that belong to exactly one cell. Its length is a quick measure of how much perimeter the mesh has.

docs.title: Cell adjacency and connected components¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() is the cell-to-cell adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix (nnz = twice the number of shared internal edges). connected_components() labels which cells are mutually reachable through that adjacency.

docs.title: Subset by a bounding box¶
docs.text: subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) keeps only the cells inside a window (note the four positional coordinates, not a tuple). We take the centred 60% window and plot the result — a clean clip that returns a new MeshDataset. (crop(bbox=...) does the same thing with a tuple argument.)

docs.title: Export: NetCDF round-trip¶
docs.text: to_file(path) writes a NetCDF UGRID file — the canonical pyramids on-disk form that any UGRID reader can load back.

docs.title: 11. CRS-dependent operations — explain and skip¶
docs.text:
This format records no CRS (crs / epsg were None above), so coordinate-aware steps have nothing to work from:

  • to_crs(...) — a reprojection needs a source CRS; with None there is nothing to reproject from, so we skip it. In practice you would first assign the CRS you know the model used.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) — these burn the mesh onto, or resample it to, a target raster grid. That is the job of the pyramids-gis raster layer (you supply a target Dataset); it is out of scope for a format-reader tutorial, so we only name it here.

docs.title: 12. Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• SU2 .su2 = native CFD mesh: VTK-coded, 0-based points and elements, read into a MeshDataset.
  • This sample is a structured 5x5 block of quads (degree 4, no -1 fill); triangular SU2 meshes also exist.
  • Quads, so circumcenters() is skipped; no CRS, so reprojection/rasterisation are skipped.
  • Explore, plot and GIS (footprint, bounding polygon, box-subset) all work on the CFD grid as on any mesh.

docs.title: Reading ANUGA .sww results with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
ANUGA is a free shallow-water hydrodynamic model (Geoscience Australia / ANU) used for flood and tsunami inundation. It writes a .sww file — a NetCDF container holding the triangular mesh plus time-varying quantities, chiefly stage (water-surface elevation) and the bed elevation. pyramids-mesh registers an sww driver that reads both into a MeshDataset.

The bundled minimal.sww carries node_z (elevation) and a stage series on a two-triangle mesh. We read it and map the stage.

docs.title: 3. Locate the data¶
docs.text: minimal.sww is in examples/data/, two levels up from the notebook; addressed as a Path.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 4. Read the file¶
docs.text: Like Selafin, an .sww is self-describing — the mesh and the results arrive together from one read_file. A driver's only job is to parse the file and hand back a MeshDataset. We pass a pathlib.Path (never a str) and name the driver explicitly:

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes the mesh size, its coordinate reference system, and the data variables carried alongside the topology. None for crs/epsg simply means the source file declared no projection — the geometry is still valid, it is just unlocated in world space.

docs.title: Per-variable summary¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a pandas DataFrame — one row per data variable with count, min, max, mean and standard deviation. A std of 0 means that variable is uniform across the mesh.

docs.title: Global attributes¶
docs.text: Each driver stamps provenance into global_attributes so you can trace a dataset back to the format it came from after it has been converted.

docs.title: 6. The Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: node coordinates plus the face-node connectivity table. face_node_connectivity.data has shape (n_face, k) — row i lists the node indices of face i (padded for mixed element types). We also derive per-face areas and centroids from that topology.

docs.title: 7. Wireframe — the mesh skeleton¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare mesh: every face edge, no data coloring. This is the fastest way to eyeball connectivity, element shapes and the overall extent.

docs.title: 8. A data map¶
docs.text: ANUGA's primary output is stage — the water-surface elevation. We map it directly. These are real ANUGA values spanning the mesh; plot shows the first time step. (Water depth would be stage - node_z, computable with with_variable from the two arrays.)

docs.title: 9. GIS operations¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is a first-class pyramids object, the full geospatial toolkit works on it directly — no conversion step. Below are several operations, each visualised or interpreted. (Operations that need a source CRS, such as to_crs, are skipped here: this sample declares none.)

docs.title: 9a. Faces as polygons — to_geodataframe()¶
docs.text: Every face becomes a shapely polygon in a GeoPandas GeoDataFrame, ready for a spatial join, an overlay, or export to any OGR vector format.

docs.title: 9b. Outer boundary — bounding_polygon() and exterior_edges()¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the faces into a single shapely polygon tracing the mesh outline, and exterior_edges() returns the indices of the mesh edges that lie on that boundary — their count is the boundary's edge length.

docs.title: 9c. Connectivity — connected_components()¶
docs.text: connected_components() labels each face by the connected sub-mesh it belongs to. One unique label means the mesh is a single watertight piece; more than one would reveal detached islands. We attach the labels as a face variable and map them.

docs.title: 9d. Face adjacency — sparse_adjacency()¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() returns the face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix (two faces are adjacent when they share an edge). Its sparsity pattern is the dual graph a solver walks; nnz counts the directed face-neighbour links.

docs.title: 9e. Triangle circumcenters — circumcenters()¶
docs.text: For a triangular mesh, circumcenters() returns the circumcircle centre of each face (shape (2, n_face)) — the sample points of the dual Voronoi mesh that finite-volume schemes use. We scatter them over the wireframe.

docs.title: 9f. Clip to a sub-region — crop()¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) clips the mesh and the stage/node_z fields to a bounding box; we keep the lower-left quarter.

docs.title: 9g. Round-trip through UGRID NetCDF — to_file()¶
docs.text: to_file(..., driver='ugrid') writes the mesh to the CF/UGRID NetCDF convention — the lossless lingua franca every tool in the stack reads back. We write it, re-read it, and confirm the topology survived.

docs.title: 10. Takeaway¶
docs.text: The sww driver reads an ANUGA results file into a MeshDataset: the triangular mesh plus stage and node_z as data variables. From there it is an ordinary pyramids mesh — mappable, vectorisable, clippable, and exportable to UGRID NetCDF.

docs.title: Reading Tecplot FE meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
Tecplot's ASCII .tec/.dat format is a staple CFD post-processing format: a ZONE block listing nodal coordinates (here in FEBLOCK layout) followed by an element connectivity table. pyramids-mesh registers a driver that reads the finite-element zone into a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset.

Our sample is tecplot/quad_zone_space.tec (meshio test data, MIT): a deliberately tiny ET=QUADRILATERAL zone — 4 nodes and a single quad face. It is geometry only, crs=None, and carries no field variables, which makes it a clean minimal example of the driver contract.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the sample file¶
docs.text:
This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so the repo-root examples/data/ folder is two levels up. Paths are written relative to the notebook itself. We will read the Tecplot zone tecplot/quad_zone_space.tec.

Pass a pathlib.Path, never a string. read_file keys its driver dispatch off Path objects; a bare str is not accepted.

docs.title: 4. Read it in one line¶
docs.text: The FEBLOCK layout stores each coordinate column contiguously, then the element table. We name the driver explicitly with driver="tecplot" and hand read_file the Path. What comes back is a MeshDataset — the same mesh container every other pyramids mesh uses.

docs.title: 5. Inspect the dataset¶
docs.text: A handful of attributes describe the mesh at a glance: the node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, the list of data variables, and the planar bounding box (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax). A Tecplot zone has no geographic reference, so crs and epsg are None.

docs.title: A statistical summary of the data variables¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a small pandas table — one row per data variable with count, min, max, mean and std. This zone defines no data variables, so summary() returns an empty table — a correct, expected result, not a failure.

docs.title: 6. The underlying geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d. Its node coordinates live in node_x / node_y, and its face-to-node table is face_node_connectivity.data — an (n_face, k) integer array where row i lists the node indices of face i. The single connectivity row has 4 node indices: one quadrilateral cell.

docs.title: 7. Draw the mesh outline (wireframe)¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the cell edges with no fill — the quickest way to see the topology we just read. The figure embeds in the notebook on its own.

docs.title: 8. A filled map: projected cell area¶
docs.text:
These are engineering meshes with no CRS and (usually) no field data, so there is nothing physical to colour by out of the box. A useful derived quantity is the projected 2-D area of each cell, available as mesh.face_areas. We attach it as a face variable with with_variable(...) and let plot(...) draw a filled colour map.

With one unit quad lying in the plane, the map is a single cell of area 1.0 — trivial, but it confirms the area derivation and the colour pipeline work.

docs.title: 9. The pyramids GIS toolbox applies¶
docs.text: The payoff of turning a solver file into a pyramids object is that the whole GIS toolbox now works on it, even though this is a FEM/CFD mesh. Below we exercise several operations and interpret each result.

docs.title: Export to a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every cell into a shapely polygon inside a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the bridge to the entire vector-GIS ecosystem. Because the mesh has crs=None, the frame is unprojected (model units, not metres/degrees).

docs.title: Dissolve to a bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() unions all cells into the single outer footprint of the mesh — useful as a clip mask or domain outline. We overlay it (red) on the grey cell edges.

docs.title: Boundary edges¶
docs.text: exterior_edges() returns the indices of edges that belong to exactly one cell — the mesh boundary. A closed surface (a watertight solid) has none; an open sheet exposes its rim. We report the count.

docs.title: Face-adjacency as a sparse matrix¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() returns the (n_face, n_face) SciPy CSR matrix of which cells share an edge — the connectivity graph solvers assemble their stencils from. We only report its shape and non-zero count.

docs.title: Crop to a sub-region¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)) keeps only the cells inside a window — the mesh equivalent of a spatial subset. Here we take the left half of the domain and re-draw it.

docs.title: What we skip, and why¶
docs.text:
Because this mesh carries crs=None, the reprojection and raster-bridge operations do not apply:

  • to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to reproject from — skipped (there is no datum to interpret the model's bare coordinates).
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) burn a mesh onto, or resample it against, a georeferenced raster grid — skipped here, as there is no spatial reference to align to.

These are first-class pyramids operations; they simply require a georeferenced mesh, which an engineering solver file is not.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
We read a minimal Tecplot FE zone (4 nodes, 1 quad), saw that an empty summary() is the right answer for a field-less mesh, and still ran GIS on it: vector export, footprint, its 4 boundary edges, the adjacency matrix, a crop. Circumcenters are skipped — they are defined for triangles only.

The pattern is always the same: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver=...) turns a solver file into a pyramids object, and from there the full GIS toolbox applies — even for a geometry-only, CRS-less engineering mesh. pyramids-mesh contributes only the driver; every mesh operation lives upstream in pyramids.

docs.title: Reading a Triangle / TetGen mesh¶
docs.text:
Triangle (Shewchuk) is the classic 2-D quality mesh generator; TetGen is its 3-D tetrahedral counterpart, and both use the same .node (points) + .ele (elements) file pair. You point read_file at the .node file and the driver pulls in the matching .ele. pyramids-mesh returns a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset.

This sample is meshio's TetGen test mesh — a 3-D tetrahedral mesh (89 nodes, 304 tetrahedra), which makes it a good illustration of what happens when a genuinely 3-D volume mesh meets 2-D planar GIS operations (MIT-licensed data).

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the example data¶
docs.text: This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so the repo-root examples/data/ folder is two levels up. Paths inside a notebook are written relative to the notebook itself. The critical rule for read_file is to pass a pathlib.Path, never str(...). We read triangle/mesh.node.

docs.title: 4. Quickstart: read the file¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver=...) parses the file and returns a MeshDataset — the same type pyramids produces from a NetCDF UGRID file. We name the "triangle" driver explicitly; passing the Path object (not a string) is the supported call.

docs.title: 5. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset exposes summary properties: n_node / n_face (mesh size), crs / epsg (georeferencing if the format recorded any), bounds (the (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) extent), and data_variable_names (attached field variables).

docs.title: 6. Face-degree distribution¶
docs.text: ds.mesh.face_node_connectivity.data is the (n_face, k) table of node indices per face, where k is the widest polygon. Cells with fewer nodes than k are padded with -1 (fill). Counting the non-negative entries per row gives each face's number of nodes — its degree.

docs.title: 7. The underlying geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d holding the raw arrays: node_x / node_y (coordinates), the connectivity table, face_areas (one area per cell) and face_centroids (shape (2, n_face)). Everything geometric is derived from the connectivity plus the node coordinates.

docs.title: 8. Wireframe: plot_outline()¶
docs.text: The simplest view needs no data — just the mesh edges. plot_outline() draws the wireframe through cleopatra and embeds it inline. This is the fastest sanity check that a file read in correctly.

docs.title: 9. A data map: attach and colour a field¶
docs.text: To draw a filled map we need a value per cell. These mesh files carry geometry only, so we compute one — each cell's area — and attach it with with_variable(..., location="face"), which returns a new dataset (the original ds is untouched). Then plot colours the mesh by it.

docs.title: The statistical summary¶
docs.text: With a field attached, .summary() reports per-variable statistics (count, min, max, mean, std). On the bare ds it is an empty frame; on d2 it has a real row.

docs.title: 10. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because the mesh is now a first-class pyramids object, the pyramids GIS layer applies directly — pyramids-mesh itself adds none of this. The next cells each run one operation and interpret it.

docs.title: Faces as a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe() turns every face into a polygon row of a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the standard vector structure for export to shapefile/GeoPackage or spatial joins.

docs.title: Bounding polygon — explain and skip¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the cells into one shapely polygon. On this mesh it raises a GEOS TopologyException — the projected tetrahedra overlap, so dissolving them produces a self-intersecting (invalid) geometry. We therefore skip it and fall back to the numeric bounds extent.

docs.title: Circumcenters — explain and skip¶
docs.text: circumcenters() is only defined for triangular meshes. This mesh is not all-triangle, so the call raises ValueError; we catch it rather than crash. (Use cell centroids instead for such grids.)

docs.title: Exterior edges¶
docs.text: exterior_edges() returns the node indices of the mesh boundary — the edges that belong to exactly one cell. Its length is a quick measure of how much perimeter the mesh has.

docs.title: Cell adjacency and connected components¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() is the cell-to-cell adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix (nnz = twice the number of shared internal edges). connected_components() labels which cells are mutually reachable through that adjacency.

docs.title: Subset by a bounding box¶
docs.text: subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) keeps only the cells inside a window (note the four positional coordinates, not a tuple). We take the centred 60% window and plot the result — a clean clip that returns a new MeshDataset. (crop(bbox=...) does the same thing with a tuple argument.)

docs.title: Export: NetCDF round-trip¶
docs.text: to_file(path) writes a NetCDF UGRID file — the canonical pyramids on-disk form that any UGRID reader can load back.

docs.title: 11. CRS-dependent operations — explain and skip¶
docs.text:
This format records no CRS (crs / epsg were None above), so coordinate-aware steps have nothing to work from:

  • to_crs(...) — a reprojection needs a source CRS; with None there is nothing to reproject from, so we skip it. In practice you would first assign the CRS you know the model used.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) — these burn the mesh onto, or resample it to, a target raster grid. That is the job of the pyramids-gis raster layer (you supply a target Dataset); it is out of scope for a format-reader tutorial, so we only name it here.

docs.title: 12. Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• Triangle/TetGen = the .node + .ele pair from a 2-D/3-D mesh generator; point read_file at the .node file.
  • This sample is a 3-D tetrahedral mesh (degree-4 cells, a node_z field), not a flat triangulation.
  • 2-D planar ops degrade gracefully on a projected volume: circumcenters() (non-triangular) and bounding_polygon() (self-intersecting projection) are skipped, and the adjacency fragments into many components — all expected, all caught rather than crashing.
  • The read, explore, wireframe, cell-area map and box-subset still work on the projected mesh.

docs.title: TUFLOW FV results with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text: TUFLOW FV is a finite-volume flexible-mesh hydraulic model. Its results NetCDF stores a genuine unstructured triangular mesh together with a rich set of variables: both time-varying fields (D, H, V_x, V_y) and peak/summary fields (max_H, max_D, ZB, ...). Because the mesh is purely triangular, triangle-only operations such as circumcenters() are available.

docs.title: Quickstart read¶
docs.text: Pass driver="tuflowfv". The result is a MeshDataset over a triangular mesh of ~2,866 faces.

docs.title: Explore the dataset¶
docs.text:
A MeshDataset wraps a UGRID-style unstructured mesh plus any data variables that ride on it. The scalar properties below describe the grid at a glance: how many nodes and faces it has, its coordinate reference system, and its spatial extent.

This is a radial dam-break 'cone' test case on a fine triangular grid.

docs.title: Data variables¶
docs.text: data_variable_names lists every field attached to the mesh. These are the real model results - water levels, depths, velocities - that make a results file worth reading.

docs.title: The Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: the topology the data variables are defined on. Nodes carry the (x, y) coordinates; face_node_connectivity says which nodes form each face (a row per face, padded to the maximum vertex count).

docs.title: Wireframe - the bare mesh¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the mesh edges with no data colouring. It is the fastest way to see the grid's shape, resolution, and how faces are distributed before looking at any results.

docs.title: Mapping the real results¶
docs.text: We map two summary fields that need no time selection: max_H, the peak water level reached anywhere during the run, and ZB, the underlying bed elevation. Together they tell the flood story - where water went and the terrain beneath it.

docs.title: Mapping the real results¶
docs.text: These files carry genuine model output, so the point of the package is to see it. ds.plot(variable, cmap=..., colorbar=..., title=...) colours each face by its value and routes through cleopatra (reached via pyramids) for the actual rendering.

docs.title: From mesh to GIS¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset is not a dead end - it converts into the vector and raster types the rest of a GIS workflow expects. Everything below is reached through pyramids; this package only supplies the file-format driver that built the mesh.

docs.title: Faces as vector polygons¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe(variable_name=...) turns every face into a polygon row carrying that variable's value - a standard GeoPandas GeoDataFrame you can join, filter, or export.

docs.title: Dissolving into zones¶
docs.text: polygonize(variable) merges neighbouring faces that share a value into larger polygons - handy for turning a noisy per-cell field into clean zones. It needs a single value per face, which is exactly what our working dataset holds.

docs.title: Sampling at points¶
docs.text: sample(variable, x, y) reads the value of the face that contains each query point. Here we probe the first few face centroids, so each query lands squarely inside a face.

docs.title: The mesh outline as one polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() returns a single shapely polygon tracing the mesh's outer boundary - the model's wetted footprint, useful as a clip mask or extent reference.

docs.title: Cropping to a sub-region¶
docs.text: subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) returns a new, smaller MeshDataset holding only the faces inside the box - the same object type, so every operation above still applies. We derive a box from the mesh envelope so it works on any extent.

docs.title: Connectivity as a sparse graph¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() exposes face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix, and connected_components() labels each face by which connected piece of the mesh it belongs to - the entry points for graph algorithms over the grid.

docs.title: Circumcenters (triangular meshes)¶
docs.text: This mesh is triangular, so circumcenters() is defined: it returns the circumcentre of every triangle - the natural dual-grid points used by finite-volume schemes.

docs.title: Self-contained rasterisation¶
docs.text: to_dataset(variable, cell_size=...) samples the mesh onto a regular raster grid and returns a pyramids Dataset. Unlike rasterize_like / regrid - which need an existing reference grid and are therefore skipped here - this is self-contained: you only choose a cell size.

docs.title: Reprojection - skipped¶
docs.text: to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to project from. This TUFLOW FV file stores no CRS, so ds.crs is None. With no source CRS, reprojection is undefined, so we skip it; assign a CRS first if your coordinates are georeferenced.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: TUFLOW FV gives pyramids-mesh a true triangular finite-volume mesh with a full variable set. Summary fields like max_H map directly (no timestep to choose), the triangular topology unlocks circumcenters(), and the same GeoDataFrame / polygonize / crop / rasterise operations apply unchanged. The driver parses TUFLOW's NetCDF layout; the mesh science stays in pyramids.

docs.title: Reading VTK meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
The VTK legacy format is the lingua franca of scientific visualization — written by ParaView, the VTK library itself, and conversion tools such as meshio. It stores an unstructured grid of points and cells in a plain ASCII (or binary) container.

A VTK file describes geometry and topology only — points live in a model-local Cartesian frame with no datum or projection. pyramids-mesh therefore reports crs=None: there is no georeferencing to speak of.

This tutorial uses gh-935.vtk, a tiny classic-v3.0 file: a unit square split into two triangles. We deliberately pick a 2D-surface sample. The reader rejects a purely volumetric (tetrahedra) or line-only file with “no 2D surface cell”, because a MeshDataset models a 2D surface mesh, not a solid.

Source: meshio test suite (tests/meshes/vtk/), MIT.

docs.title: Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: Quickstart: read the VTK file¶
docs.text:
driver="vtk" selects the VTK reader, which recognises both the legacy ASCII grammar and the newer VTK 5.1 OFFSETS/CONNECTIVITY layout.

The one rule that matters: pass a pathlib.Path, never a str — read_file keys its driver dispatch off the Path type. MeshDataset.read_file(...) returns a MeshDataset, the in-memory UGRID container every pyramids-mesh driver produces.

docs.title: What did we get?¶
docs.text: A few scalar properties describe the dataset at a glance: node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, and the planar bounding box.

docs.title: Summary table¶
docs.text: ds.summary() returns a pandas DataFrame with per-variable statistics (count / min / max / mean / std). With no data variables, the table here is empty — which is itself the finding: this is a pure-geometry file.

docs.title: The mesh geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: node coordinates plus the face-node connectivity, an (n_face, k) integer table where k is the largest number of nodes any face has. Triangles fill 3 columns; quadrilaterals fill 4 (a shorter face pads the spare slot). face_areas and face_centroids are derived on demand.

docs.title: Wireframe¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare mesh edges — the quickest way to eyeball the topology and the element shapes before colouring anything.

docs.title: A derived field: cell area¶
docs.text: These engineering files usually carry no cell data we can colour by — so we compute one ourselves. with_variable attaches face_areas as a face-located variable, giving a non-destructive copy of the dataset that plot can render as a filled colour map.

docs.title: Treating the mesh as GIS¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is just nodes and polygonal faces, pyramids exposes the usual vector-GIS toolbox on it. First, every face as a GeoPandas polygon:

docs.title: The outer boundary¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() dissolves the faces into the single polygon that bounds the mesh — for this square, the unit square itself.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) returns a new MeshDataset with only the faces inside the box — handy for zooming into a region of a large mesh. We crop to the left half of the extent.

docs.title: The face-adjacency graph¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() gives the face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix, and connected_components() labels which faces are reachable from which. plt.spy shows the sparsity pattern — the fingerprint of how the faces are wired together.

docs.title: A triangle-only operation: circumcenters¶
docs.text: Because every face here is a triangle, circumcenters() is defined — it returns the centre of each triangle's circumscribed circle (the basis of a Voronoi dual). We overlay circumcenters (red) on area-weighted centroids (blue).

docs.title: Converting out: other drivers¶
docs.text: to_file(path, driver=...) re-serialises the mesh through any writer in the driver table — here a round-trip to the 2dm format in a temp file.

docs.title: What we cannot do here: reprojection & regridding¶
docs.text: to_crs(epsg) reprojects between coordinate systems — but this mesh has crs=None (model-local coordinates, no datum), so there is nothing to reproject from; we skip it. Likewise rasterize_like(...) and regrid(...) map a data field onto a raster or another mesh; with no meaningful field and no georeferencing on an engineering mesh they are out of scope. These belong on georeferenced hydrodynamic meshes, not FEM/CFD decks.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text:
• A VTK file is read with MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver="vtk") — pass a Path and point it at a 2D-surface sample.
  • It is geometry-only: crs=None, no data variables. We synthesised cell_area to get something to colour.
  • Once loaded it behaves like any other mesh: wireframe, polygon export, cropping, the adjacency graph, and (because it is triangular) circumcenters.
  • Reprojection/regridding do not apply — there is no CRS and no physical field.

docs.title: Reading XDMF time-series meshes with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
XDMF (eXtensible Data Model and Format) pairs a small XML file describing the mesh and its variables with a bulky .h5 HDF5 companion holding the actual arrays. It is the interchange format written by meshio and read by ParaView/VTK. A temporal collection stores the same mesh across several time steps with per-step node and cell variables.

pyramids-mesh registers an xdmf driver that parses out.xdmf (plus its out.h5) into a MeshDataset/Mesh2d. This notebook reads a genuine meshio fixture and walks read → explore → plot → GIS.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Locate the data¶
docs.text: The notebook lives in docs/examples/, so examples/data/ is two levels up. We pass a pathlib.Path to the reader (never a string).

docs.title: 4. Read the mesh¶
docs.text: We name the driver explicitly: driver="xdmf". read_file dispatches to it and returns a MeshDataset wrapping a Mesh2d.

docs.title: 5. Explore the mesh¶
docs.text: Node/face counts, CRS, the attached data variables and the bounding box. This fixture is deliberately tiny — 4 nodes, 2 triangles on the unit square — which makes it perfect for seeing the full connectivity table. It carries a node variable phi (time-varying, 5 steps) and a cell variable a; it declares no CRS, so crs/epsg are None.

docs.title: 6. Mesh geometry¶
docs.text: The Mesh2d exposes node coordinates, the (n_face, k) face-node connectivity, per-face areas and centroids — all plain numpy arrays.

docs.title: 7. Wireframe¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare element skeleton — the fastest way to read the mesh's shape and where it is refined.

docs.title: 8. Data map¶
docs.text: phi is a time-varying node field (5 steps × 4 nodes); a is a per-cell value. The summary() above shows both.

docs.title: 9. GIS operations for free¶
docs.text: The mesh is a pyramids object, so the vector/GIS layer applies unchanged. Convert to a GeoDataFrame — one polygon per element. to_geodataframe() returns just the geometry column, so we attach each element's area and let geopandas colour by it; smaller cells reveal where the mesh is refined.

docs.title: 10. What needs more than a mesh¶
docs.text:
• to_crs(epsg) needs a source CRS. the XDMF fixture declares no CRS, so ds.epsg is None, so to_crs is skipped.
  • rasterize_like / regrid need a reference grid to sample onto; with only the mesh in hand there is no target, so they are out of scope for this read-only tour.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver="xdmf") turns the native xdmf grid into a first-class pyramids mesh. Exploration, plotting, GeoDataFrame conversion, bounding polygons, connectivity analysis, spatial subsetting and export are all inherited from pyramids — pyramids-mesh only added the reader.

docs.title: XMDF mesh results with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text:
XMDF (eXtensible Model Data Format) is an HDF5 results container used by SMS/SRH-2D and other hydraulic tools. Crucially, an XMDF file stores values only - it has no mesh geometry of its own. pyramids-mesh therefore reads it in two steps: open the companion mesh (here a .2dm file), then attach the XMDF results to it.

This notebook reads minimal.xmdf together with its minimal.2dm mesh and showcases the pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset API end to end.

docs.title: What is on disk¶
docs.text: Two files: the mesh (minimal.2dm) and the results (minimal.xmdf).

docs.title: Quickstart: read the mesh, then attach the results¶
docs.text: Reading the .2dm gives a MeshDataset carrying the mesh plus its static fields (material, node_z). attach_data(<xmdf>) returns a new dataset with the XMDF result variables added on top of that same geometry.

docs.title: Explore the dataset¶
docs.text:
A MeshDataset wraps a UGRID-style unstructured mesh plus any data variables that ride on it. The scalar properties below describe the grid at a glance: how many nodes and faces it has, its coordinate reference system, and its spatial extent.

Note the small size (25 nodes, 16 quad faces): this is a deliberately minimal test mesh.

docs.title: Data variables¶
docs.text: data_variable_names lists every field attached to the mesh. These are the real model results - water levels, depths, velocities - that make a results file worth reading.

docs.title: The Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: the topology the data variables are defined on. Nodes carry the (x, y) coordinates; face_node_connectivity says which nodes form each face (a row per face, padded to the maximum vertex count).

docs.title: Wireframe - the bare mesh¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the mesh edges with no data colouring. It is the fastest way to see the grid's shape, resolution, and how faces are distributed before looking at any results.

docs.title: Mapping the real results¶
docs.text: node_z is the bed elevation defined on the mesh, and Minimum dt is a solver diagnostic attached from the XMDF file (it carries a time axis, so we select the first step with isel). Both are genuine per-cell fields.

docs.title: From mesh to GIS¶
docs.text: A MeshDataset is not a dead end - it converts into the vector and raster types the rest of a GIS workflow expects. Everything below is reached through pyramids; this package only supplies the file-format driver that built the mesh.

docs.title: Faces as vector polygons¶
docs.text: to_geodataframe(variable_name=...) turns every face into a polygon row carrying that variable's value - a standard GeoPandas GeoDataFrame you can join, filter, or export.

docs.title: Dissolving into zones¶
docs.text: polygonize(variable) merges neighbouring faces that share a value into larger polygons - handy for turning a noisy per-cell field into clean zones. It needs a single value per face, which is exactly what our working dataset holds.

docs.title: Sampling at points¶
docs.text: sample(variable, x, y) reads the value of the face that contains each query point. Here we probe the first few face centroids, so each query lands squarely inside a face.

docs.title: The mesh outline as one polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() returns a single shapely polygon tracing the mesh's outer boundary - the model's wetted footprint, useful as a clip mask or extent reference.

docs.title: Cropping to a sub-region¶
docs.text: subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) returns a new, smaller MeshDataset holding only the faces inside the box - the same object type, so every operation above still applies. We derive a box from the mesh envelope so it works on any extent.

docs.title: Connectivity as a sparse graph¶
docs.text: sparse_adjacency() exposes face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix, and connected_components() labels each face by which connected piece of the mesh it belongs to - the entry points for graph algorithms over the grid.

docs.title: Circumcenters - not applicable here¶
docs.text: circumcenters() is only defined for purely triangular meshes. This grid contains quad (or mixed-polygon) faces, so the call would raise ValueError. We note it and skip rather than force it.

docs.title: Self-contained rasterisation¶
docs.text: to_dataset(variable, cell_size=...) samples the mesh onto a regular raster grid and returns a pyramids Dataset. Unlike rasterize_like / regrid - which need an existing reference grid and are therefore skipped here - this is self-contained: you only choose a cell size.

docs.title: Reprojection - skipped¶
docs.text: to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to project from. This XMDF/2DM pair stores no CRS, so ds.crs is None. With no source CRS, reprojection is undefined, so we skip it; assign a CRS first if your coordinates are georeferenced.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: XMDF is a results-only format: pyramids-mesh reads the mesh first (the .2dm), then attach_data layers the XMDF values onto it, producing one MeshDataset. From there the mesh behaves like any other pyramids object - plot its fields, convert faces to a GeoDataFrame, dissolve zones, crop, or rasterise. The driver's only job is parsing the file; every mesh and GIS operation lives upstream in pyramids.

docs.title: Reading the XMS TIN format with pyramids-mesh¶
docs.text: The XMS TIN format is the triangulated-irregular-network format of Aquaveo's SMS/GMS modelling systems: a text file with a TIN/BEGT header, a VERT block of x y z vertices, and a TRI block of 1-based triangle vertex triples. It is the classic way to carry a terrain or bathymetric surface into a hydrodynamic study. pyramids-mesh parses it into a pyramids.netcdf.ugrid object. This notebook reads a minimal four-vertex TIN and walks through geometry, plotting and the GIS operations that follow.

docs.title: 2. Imports¶
docs.text: The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

docs.title: 3. Read the file in one call¶
docs.text: We pass driver="xmstin" explicitly. The TIN reader consumes the VERT/TRI blocks and converts the 1-based triangle indices to the 0-based connectivity pyramids uses.

docs.title: 4. Explore the dataset¶
docs.text: A handful of attributes describe what we loaded: node and face counts, the coordinate reference system, the names of any data variables, and the spatial extent.

docs.title: 5. A statistical summary of the fields¶
docs.text: summary() returns a pandas frame with one row per data variable (count, min, max, mean, std).

docs.title: 6. The underlying Mesh2d geometry¶
docs.text: ds.mesh is the Mesh2d object carrying the raw topology: node coordinates, the face-node connectivity table of shape (n_face, k) (row i lists the node indices of cell i), per-face areas, and cell centroids.

docs.title: 7. The mesh outline (wireframe)¶
docs.text: plot_outline() draws the bare cell edges, with no field attached — the quickest look at the raw geometry this driver produced.

docs.title: 8. A data map: attach and colour by cell area¶
docs.text: These surface formats carry no field data, so there is nothing to colour by yet. We attach a derived cell_area variable at the face location and plot it — turning the geometry into a proper choropleth.

docs.title: 9. GIS operations, for free¶
docs.text: Because a MeshDataset is a first-class pyramids object, a whole GIS toolkit comes along. First, every face as a row in a GeoDataFrame.

docs.title: Bounding polygon¶
docs.text: bounding_polygon() returns a single shapely geometry: the dissolved outer footprint of the mesh.

docs.title: Derived topology and connectivity¶
docs.text: A few more derived quantities are a method call away. circumcenters() is defined only for triangular meshes; exterior_edges() indexes the boundary edges; connected_components() labels disjoint pieces; sparse_adjacency() is the face-to-face graph as a sparse matrix.

docs.title: Cropping to a bounding box¶
docs.text: crop(bbox=...) keeps the faces that fall within (or touch) a rectangle, returning a new MeshDataset. Here we crop to the left portion of the extent and redraw it.

docs.title: Round-tripping through the driver table¶
docs.text: to_file(..., driver=...) writes the mesh back out in any writable driver (here the solver-neutral 2DM).

docs.title: 10. What we skip here, and why¶
docs.text:
• to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to reproject from, but XMS TIN files carry no georeferencing (crs=None), so there is nothing to reproject. Attach a CRS first if the coordinates are known to be in a specific projection.
  • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) require a reference grid (a raster or target mesh) to sample onto; with only this standalone mesh in hand there is no target, so they are out of scope for this tutorial.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: An Aquaveo XMS TIN reads straight into a MeshDataset, elevations and all. The driver's only job is to parse the VERT/TRI blocks and renumber to 0-based indices; everything downstream — plotting, the node_z terrain field, GeoDataFrame export, cropping, cross-format write-out — is the shared pyramids machinery, identical to every other mesh format.

docs.title: Reference

What this package publishes is drivers, not an API you call directly. A driver is registered with pyramids-core through the pyramids.mesh_drivers entry-point group, so installing this package is the whole integration: pyramids then dispatches a read of a format it does not handle itself to the driver that claims it.

from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import MeshDataset

mesh = MeshDataset.read_file("domain.2dm")   # resolved to this package's 2dm driver

docs.title: pyramids_mesh
docs.text:
Mesh file-format drivers for the pyramids stack.

pyramids-mesh reads and writes the file formats of hydrodynamic and hydraulic mesh models — 2DM, Selafin, DFSU, XMDF, PLY and the rest of the hydrodynamic formats — as pyramids.netcdf.ugrid objects. pyramids.netcdf.ugrid owns the UGRID data model (Mesh2d, Mesh1d, MeshDataset), its NetCDF I/O, and every operation that follows from a topology already in hand — connectivity and graph algorithms, regridding and sampling, gap filling, mesh-to-vector conversion, and construction from a raster or a polygon layer. What it cannot do is open other people's mesh files; that is this package's job, and its only job.

Drivers are discovered by pyramids-core through the pyramids.mesh_drivers entry-point group, so MeshDataset.read_file("model.slf") resolves to a driver here once this package is installed. Dependency-backed drivers sit behind extras ([dhi]) and are skipped at discovery when their extra is absent. See ADR-0005 for the scope decision.

The package root deliberately re-exports nothing: it carries __version__ and the import contract that activates the vendored osgeo bindings, and that is all. Installing the package is the whole integration, so nothing here needs importing. A driver class is still reachable by its module path (pyramids_mesh.drivers.sms.TwoDmDriver, which is how its entry point names it) for the rare case of wanting one directly.

Examples:

  • The root carries the installed version and nothing else. __all__ is empty because there is deliberately nothing to re-export:

    import pyramids_mesh pyramids_mesh.version.split(".")[0].isdigit() True pyramids_mesh.all []

  • A driver is reached by its module path, not from the root, and reports the suffixes it claims:

    from pyramids_mesh.drivers.sms import TwoDmDriver TwoDmDriver.name '2dm' TwoDmDriver.suffixes ('.2dm',)

docs.title: 2DM — SMS / TUFLOW mesh frame
docs.text:
The 2DM reader. Plain text, one record per line, and the reference implementation every other driver in this package follows.

Driver name 2dm Suffixes .2dm Capabilities read_mesh, read_data, multi_mesh, write_mesh, write_data read_data and multi_mesh are declarative — they describe the driver in info(drivers=True) and require no method. There is no read_data() to call: read_data here means the file carries values (material, elevation) that read returns alongside the topology. A results-only format declares needs_mesh instead and does implement the method. Extra required none Returns MeshDataset for the surface mesh, Mesh1d for the E2L network 
from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import MeshDataset

mesh = MeshDataset.read_file("domain.2dm")

docs.title: Files holding both a surface and a network
docs.text:
A 2DM may carry a surface mesh (E3T/E4Q/E6T), a 1D network (E2L), or both. The two are named separately, so mesh_names tells you what a file holds and mesh_name= picks one:

from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import Mesh1d, MeshDataset

MeshDataset.mesh_names("domain.2dm")            # ['mesh2d', 'network1d']
mesh = MeshDataset.read_file("domain.2dm")      # the surface mesh
channels = Mesh1d.read_file("domain.2dm", mesh_name="network1d")   # the 1D network

Reading the surface of a file that also holds E2L elements warns that the network is not in that result and names this route. The E2L elements are a separate 1D topology, not the surface mesh's edges, so they are never folded into edge_node_connectivity.

docs.title: What it reads
docs.text:
Record Meaning MESH2D the header; the file's first significant line must be this ND <id> <x> <y> <z> a node. z becomes a node_z variable, not a coordinate E3T <id> <n1..n3> <mat> a triangular face E4Q <id> <n1..n4> <mat> a quadrilateral face E6T <id> <n1..n6> <mat> a six-node face, read as such E2L <id> <n1> <n2> <mat> a 1D line element NUM_MATERIALS_PER_ELEM <k> switches the parser to k material columns

Node and element ids are resolved through an id map rather than by assuming id == index + 1: 2DM ids may have gaps and may be out of file order, and a tool that renumbers a mesh produces exactly that. The node count is the number of ND records, never the highest id.

The material id becomes a face-located material variable. With NUM_MATERIALS_PER_ELEM k the extra columns become material_2 … material_k, for k from 1 to 16 — each column costs an array and a variable, and the count comes from an untrusted file, so a larger one is refused rather than allocated.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Every one of these is deliberate; none is a silent approximation.

  • E3L, E8Q and E9Q are refused, and the whole file with them, naming the element. Treating a mid-side or centre node as a corner would distort the element without any error, so no mapping is guessed.
  • E6T is kept as a six-node face. Its node order is corner, mid-side, corner, mid-side, corner, mid-side, so the hexagon through those points is the element outline; it is not demoted to its corner triangle.
  • One read returns one topology. MeshDataset and Mesh1d are separate types, so a file holding both is read twice, once per mesh_name (see above). Reading either half warns about what the other half leaves behind rather than omitting it silently.
  • No elevation coordinate. The pyramids mesh model is planar, so on the surface path z survives as a node-located node_z variable. Anything consuming the mesh geometry sees the planar projection.
  • A 1D read cannot carry z, variables or global attributes at all. [Mesh1d][pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.Mesh1d] holds a topology and a CRS and has no parameter for data, so reading the network half of a file reports each of those by name in a warning and returns without them. This is a pyramids-core limitation, not a decision of this driver: it will be carried properly once Mesh1d has somewhere to put it.
  • No elevation is invented. If no ND record carries a z column, node_z is omitted entirely rather than filled with zeros a consumer could not tell from a real zero datum. A file whose ND records disagree about the z column is refused, since the ones without it would need a datum invented.
  • Records this driver does not model are skipped: MESHNAME, the BEGPARAMDEF block and anything else beyond the nodes, elements and NUM_MATERIALS_PER_ELEM. One consequence is that a file naming its own mesh loses that name — the topology is always built as mesh2d.
  • A malformed record is refused, never guessed. A record short of the fields its keyword requires, a non-numeric coordinate, id or material, and a NUM_MATERIALS_PER_ELEM below one all raise and name the file and the record. An element short of its declared material columns is the one exception: the missing columns read as 0.0, because a writer omitting a trailing column is common and refusing the file would cost more than it buys.
  • Two nodes, faces or line elements sharing an id are refused: the connectivity would be ambiguous.
  • No CRS. 2DM carries none, so crs is always None; it is never inferred from the coordinate magnitudes.
  • Read-only for now. write_mesh arrives with the 2DM writer (task W1).
  • Values are read eagerly: the format is text, so there is nothing to defer and lazy_data is not declared.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text:
MeshDataset.to_file("out.2dm", driver="2dm") writes the mesh back. It emits MESH2D, one ND per node, and one E3T/E4Q/E6T per face — the element keyword chosen from the face's real vertex count, ignoring -1 fill.

  • The recorded connectivity base is re-applied. A file read 1-based is written back 1-based (original_start_index on the connectivity), so a read/write round trip preserves the numbering.
  • Node elevation comes from a node-located node_z variable when present, else 0.0; the material column from a face-located material variable, else 0.
  • Full precision by default. Coordinates are written with Python's shortest exact float64 representation, because a fixed number of decimals silently loses position for projected coordinates in the millions. Pass precision=<n> for n significant digits when a smaller file matters more than an exact round trip.
  • A face whose real vertex count is not 3, 4 or 6 has no 2DM element keyword and is refused; a dataset with no face connectivity is not a 2DM mesh and is refused.
from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import MeshDataset

mesh = MeshDataset.read_file("domain.2dm")
mesh.to_file("copy.2dm", driver="2dm")              # exact round trip
mesh.to_file("small.2dm", driver="2dm", precision=8)  # 8 significant digits

docs.title: 3Di — results NetCDF
docs.text:
The 3Di reader. 3Di stores each 2D cell by its corner coordinates rather than a node list, so the driver deduplicates the corners into shared nodes and builds face connectivity. Read through the vendored GDAL multidimensional API (no declared dependency).

Driver name 3di Suffixes .nc Capabilities read_mesh, read_data, lazy_data Extra required none Returns MeshDataset

3Di results use .nc, which is not UGRID. MeshDataset.read_file tries its built-in UGRID reader first and, finding no topology, falls back to a driver claiming the suffix (pyramids-core 0.69.0's dispatch) — which is how this driver is reached.

from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import MeshDataset

mesh = MeshDataset.read_file("results_3di.nc")
water_level = mesh.get("Mesh2D_s1")   # face-located, over time

docs.title: Documented limitations
docs.text:
• Corner dedup uses a rounded key, not float equality. Shared corners are matched after rounding to a fixed tolerance; raw float comparison would leave duplicate nodes and split edges. The unique nodes are sorted, so the node order is deterministic.
  • A coupled 1D network is reported, not represented. A file with Mesh1D* arrays carries a 1D model coupled to the 2D mesh; pyramids has no coupling relation (design §10), so the 2D mesh is returned and the 1D part is announced in a warning rather than dropped silently.
  • Flow-line variables are not shipped — a result on the nMesh2D_lines dimension lives on flow links between cells, which the mesh model has no place for; only per-cell (face) variables are read.
  • Values are lazy; the loader reopens the file per read. CRS comes only from a validated grid-mapping attribute, else None.

docs.title: pyramids_mesh.drivers.threedi.ThreeDiDriver
docs.text:
Bases: BaseDriver

Reader for 3Di result NetCDF.

3Di stores 2D cell contours -- each cell's corner coordinates -- rather than a node list and connectivity. The driver deduplicates the corners into a shared node table and builds face-node connectivity into it, so a 3Di result becomes an ordinary :class:~pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset. Per-cell result arrays become face-located variables over time.

Documented limitations
  • Corner dedup uses a rounded key, not float equality. Shared corners are matched after rounding to a fixed tolerance; raw float comparison would leave duplicate nodes and split edges. The unique nodes are sorted, so the same file gives the same node order every run -- downstream indices stay stable.
  • A coupled 1D network is reported, not represented. A 3Di file with Mesh1D* arrays carries a 1D model coupled to the 2D mesh; pyramids has no coupling relation (design section 10), so the 2D mesh is returned and the 1D part is announced in a warning naming Mesh1d rather than dropped silently.
  • Flow-line variables are not shipped. A result on the nMesh2D_lines dimension lives on flow links between cells, which the mesh model has no place for; only per-cell (face) variables are read.
  • Values are lazy: the loader reopens the file per read and seeks to its array, closing over a path, never an open handle (design section 7).
  • No CRS is read. This result carries no grid-mapping, and 3Di's CF grid-mapping variant is not extracted without a real sample to verify it against, so crs is None rather than guessed.
Example

Read a 3Di result. It is reached through read_file's NetCDF fallback because its .nc is not UGRID; shown rather than run as a doctest since it needs a real NetCDF file::

from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import MeshDataset

mesh = MeshDataset.read_file("results_3di.nc")   # cells -> shared nodes
water_level = mesh.get("Mesh2D_s1")               # face-located, over time
Source code in src/pyramids_mesh/drivers/threedi.py 
class ThreeDiDriver(BaseDriver):
    """Reader for 3Di result NetCDF.

    3Di stores 2D cell *contours* -- each cell's corner coordinates -- rather than a node
    list and connectivity. The driver deduplicates the corners into a shared node table
    and builds face-node connectivity into it, so a 3Di result becomes an ordinary
    :class:`~pyramids.netcdf.ugrid.MeshDataset`. Per-cell result arrays become
    face-located variables over time.

    Documented limitations:
        - **Corner dedup uses a rounded key, not float equality.** Shared corners are
          matched after rounding to a fixed tolerance; raw float comparison would leave
          duplicate nodes and split edges. The unique nodes are sorted, so the same file
          gives the same node order every run -- downstream indices stay stable.
        - **A coupled 1D network is reported, not represented.** A 3Di file with
          ``Mesh1D*`` arrays carries a 1D model coupled to the 2D mesh; pyramids has no
          coupling relation (design section 10), so the 2D mesh is returned and the 1D
          part is announced in a warning naming ``Mesh1d`` rather than dropped
          silently.
        - **Flow-line variables are not shipped.** A result on the ``nMesh2D_lines``
          dimension lives on flow links between cells, which the mesh model has no place
          for; only per-cell (face) variables are read.
        - Values are lazy: the loader reopens the file per read and seeks to its array,
          closing over a path, never an open handle (design section 7).
        - **No CRS is read.** This result carries no grid-mapping, and 3Di's CF
          grid-mapping variant is not extracted without a real sample to verify it
          against, so ``crs`` is ``None`` rather than guessed.

    Example:
        Read a 3Di result. It is reached through ``read_file``'s NetCDF fallback because
        its ``.nc`` is not UGRID; shown rather than run as a doctest since it needs a real
        NetCDF file::

            from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import MeshDataset

            mesh = MeshDataset.read_file("results_3di.nc")   # cells -> shared nodes
            water_level = mesh.get("Mesh2D_s1")               # face-located, over time
    """

    name = "3di"
    long_name = "3Di results"
    suffixes = (".nc",)
    api_version = MESH_DRIVER_API_VERSION
    capabilities = frozenset({"read_mesh", "read_data", "lazy_data"})

    def _sniff(self, path: str) -> bool:
        """Report whether the file is a 3Di result, by its defining contour arrays.

        Keyed on ``Mesh2DContour_x`` so a plain NetCDF or another model's ``.nc`` is not
        claimed; opening a non-NetCDF file raises inside GDAL and is reported as "not
        3Di" rather than propagated.

        Args:
            path: The file to inspect.

        Returns:
            bool: ``True`` when the contour arrays are present.
        """
        with gdal.ExceptionMgr(useExceptions=True):
            try:
                dataset = gdal.OpenEx(path, gdal.OF_MULTIDIM_RASTER | gdal.OF_READONLY)
            except RuntimeError:
                return False
            try:
                names = set(dataset.GetRootGroup().GetMDArrayNames())
            finally:
                dataset.Close()
        return {_CONTOUR_X, _CONTOUR_Y} <= names

    def _parse(self, path: str, *, lazy: bool) -> ParsedMesh:
        """Read a 3Di file into a :class:`ParsedMesh`.

        Args:
            path: The 3Di ``.nc`` file.
            lazy: When ``True``, leave each variable behind a loader.

        Returns:
            ParsedMesh: Nodes deduplicated from the cell contours, face connectivity, the
                cell centres and the per-cell variables.

        Raises:
            FileFormatNotSupportedError: If the contour arrays are missing.
        """
        return _ThreeDiReader(path, lazy=lazy).build()

docs.title: can_open(path)
docs.text:
Report whether this driver recognises the file, without ever raising.

A missing path or a directory answers False, and so does a suffix this driver does not claim. Everything about the file's content is the subclass's _sniff to judge, and the default _sniff judges nothing -- so on BaseDriver itself an empty file with a claimed suffix answers True. A driver that means to decline an empty or foreign file reads a header signature, as :meth:~pyramids_mesh.drivers.sms.TwoDmDriver._sniff does.

A _sniff that fails for any reason is reported as a warning and the file declined, so a broken candidate cannot abort driver dispatch. Only _sniff sits inside that guard: a TypeError from being handed something that is not a path is the caller's mistake, not a verdict about a file, so it propagates.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default path str

The filesystem path to test.

required

Returns:

Name Type Description bool bool

True only when the suffix matches and _sniff accepts the file.

Examples:

  • The path checks and the suffix are all the base class decides. With the default _sniff, which accepts whatever reaches it, an empty file under a claimed suffix is recognised and a missing one is not:

    import os import tempfile from pyramids_mesh._base import BaseDriver class TinyDriver(BaseDriver): ... name = "tiny" ... suffixes = (".tiny",) driver = TinyDriver() with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory: ... empty = os.path.join(directory, "empty.tiny") ... open(empty, "wb").close() ... verdicts = ( ... driver.can_open(empty), ... driver.can_open(os.path.join(directory, "gone.tiny")), ... driver.can_open(directory), ... ) verdicts (True, False, False)

  • A _sniff that raises never escapes: the file is declined and the driver named, so one broken candidate cannot abort dispatch for the rest:

    import os import tempfile import warnings from pyramids_mesh._base import BaseDriver class BrokenSniffDriver(BaseDriver): ... name = "broken" ... suffixes = (".tiny",) ... ... def _sniff(self, path): ... raise RuntimeError("header parser is wrong") with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory: ... path = os.path.join(directory, "f.tiny") ... with open(path, "wb") as handle: ... _ = handle.write(b"anything at all") ... with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught: ... warnings.simplefilter("always") ... verdict = BrokenSniffDriver().can_open(path) verdict False str(caught[0].message).split(" and ")[-1] 'is treated as declining it: RuntimeError: header parser is wrong'

def can_open(self, path: str) -> bool:
    """Report whether this driver recognises the file, without ever raising.

    A missing path or a directory answers ``False``, and so does a suffix this
    driver does not claim. Everything about the file's *content* is the subclass's
    ``_sniff`` to judge, and the default ``_sniff`` judges nothing -- so on
    ``BaseDriver`` itself an empty file with a claimed suffix answers ``True``. A
    driver that means to decline an empty or foreign file reads a header signature,
    as :meth:`~pyramids_mesh.drivers.sms.TwoDmDriver._sniff` does.

    A ``_sniff`` that fails for any reason is reported as a warning and the file
    declined, so a broken candidate cannot abort driver dispatch. Only ``_sniff``
    sits inside that guard: a ``TypeError`` from being handed something that is not
    a path is the caller's mistake, not a verdict about a file, so it propagates.

    Args:
        path: The filesystem path to test.

    Returns:
        bool: ``True`` only when the suffix matches and ``_sniff`` accepts the file.

    Examples:
        - The path checks and the suffix are all the base class decides. With the
          default ``_sniff``, which accepts whatever reaches it, an empty file
          under a claimed suffix is recognised and a missing one is not:

            >>> import os
            >>> import tempfile
            >>> from pyramids_mesh._base import BaseDriver
            >>> class TinyDriver(BaseDriver):
            ...     name = "tiny"
            ...     suffixes = (".tiny",)
            >>> driver = TinyDriver()
            >>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
            ...     empty = os.path.join(directory, "empty.tiny")
            ...     open(empty, "wb").close()
            ...     verdicts = (
            ...         driver.can_open(empty),
            ...         driver.can_open(os.path.join(directory, "gone.tiny")),
            ...         driver.can_open(directory),
            ...     )
            >>> verdicts
            (True, False, False)

        - A ``_sniff`` that raises never escapes: the file is declined and the
          driver named, so one broken candidate cannot abort dispatch for the rest:

            >>> import os
            >>> import tempfile
            >>> import warnings
            >>> from pyramids_mesh._base import BaseDriver
            >>> class BrokenSniffDriver(BaseDriver):
            ...     name = "broken"
            ...     suffixes = (".tiny",)
            ...
            ...     def _sniff(self, path):
            ...         raise RuntimeError("header parser is wrong")
            >>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
            ...     path = os.path.join(directory, "f.tiny")
            ...     with open(path, "wb") as handle:
            ...         _ = handle.write(b"anything at all")
            ...     with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
            ...         warnings.simplefilter("always")
            ...         verdict = BrokenSniffDriver().can_open(path)
            >>> verdict
            False
            >>> str(caught[0].message).split(" and ")[-1]
            'is treated as declining it: RuntimeError: header parser is wrong'
    """
    # Outside the guard on purpose: a bad argument type is the caller's error, not a
    # verdict about a file, so it propagates rather than becoming a warning.
    if not os.path.isfile(path):
        return False
    if not self._has_suffix(path):
        return False
    try:
        return self._sniff(path)
    except Exception as error:  # noqa: BLE001 - the contract is never to raise
        # Narrower than this (OSError alone) left the guarantee false for a _sniff
        # that hit a decoding or parsing error. Declining is the right answer, but
        # a driver whose sniff raises is a bug, so it is named rather than hidden.
        warnings.warn(
            f"{self.name or type(self).__name__} failed to sniff {path!r} and is "
            f"treated as declining it: {type(error).__name__}: {error}",
            stacklevel=2,
        )
        return False

def mesh_names(self, path: str) -> list[str]:
    """List the topology names in the file.

    A single-mesh format returns a one-item list; ``multi_mesh`` drivers override
    this to read the names from the file.

    Args:
        path: The filesystem path, unused by the single-mesh default.

    Returns:
        list[str]: The configured mesh name, as a one-item list.

    Examples:
        - A single-mesh driver names one topology, so the list it returns is the
          set of values ``read``'s ``mesh_name`` will accept:

            >>> from pyramids_mesh._base import BaseDriver
            >>> class TinyDriver(BaseDriver):
            ...     name = "tiny"
